unistr_label: Greetings and farewells
label: Saluti e congedi

en.title: Greetings and Farewells in Italian
en.explanation: In Italian, you use different greetings depending on the time of day and how formal the situation is. **Ciao** is a friendly, informal word that means both "hello" and "goodbye" — you can use it with friends and family. For more formal situations, or when meeting someone for the first time, use **buongiorno** (good morning/good day) or **buonasera** (good evening). - **Ciao, Marco!** (Hi, Marco! / Bye, Marco!) - **Buongiorno, signora Rossi.** (Good morning, Mrs. Rossi.) - **Buonasera a tutti!** (Good evening, everyone!) When saying goodbye, **arrivederci** is a polite way to say "goodbye" (literally "until we see each other again"), and **a presto** means "see you soon" — a warm way to end a conversation with someone you expect to meet again.

unistr_label: Italian pronunciation basics
label: Pronuncia italiana fondamentale

en.title: Italian Pronunciation Basics
en.explanation:
## How to Pronounce Italian

Italian is a very **phonetic** language — almost every letter is always pronounced the same way, so once you learn the sounds, you can read any Italian word out loud!

### The Five Vowels

Italian has five vowels, and each one has only **one** clear, pure sound:

| Letter | Sound | Example |
|--------|-------|---------|
| **a** | like 'ah' | **a**more (love) |
| **e** | like 'eh' | **e**state (summer) |
| **i** | like 'ee' | **i**sola (island) |
| **o** | like 'oh' | **o**ra (hour/now) |
| **u** | like 'oo' | **u**va (grape) |

Every vowel is **always** pronounced clearly — never swallowed or skipped.

### Hard and Soft C and G

The letters **c** and **g** change their sound depending on the vowel that follows:

- **Hard sound** (like English *k* / *g*) — before **a, o, u**:
  - **ca**sa (house), **co**sa (thing), **cu**ore (heart)
  - **ga**tto (cat), **go**mma (rubber), **gu**sto (taste)

- **Soft sound** (like English *ch* / *j*) — before **e, i**:
  - **ce**na (*cheh*-na — dinner), **ci**ao (*chow* — hi/bye)
  - **ge**lato (*jeh*-lato — ice cream), **gi**ro (*jee*-ro — tour)

### Double Consonants

When you see a double consonant (like **tt**, **ll**, **nn**), you hold the sound **slightly longer**. This matters because it can change the meaning of a word!

- **fato** (fate) vs. **fatto** (done/fact)
- **nono** (ninth) vs. **nonno** (grandfather)
- **pala** (shovel) vs. **palla** (ball)

Think of it like a tiny pause or extra emphasis on that consonant.

### Quick Tips
- Every letter in Italian is **pronounced** — there are almost no silent letters.
- Stress usually falls on the **second-to-last** syllable: *pa-**sta***, *ca-**sa***, *a-**mi**-co*.
- Practice saying the vowels out loud every day — they are the heart of Italian pronunciation!

unistr_label: Numbers 0–20
label: Numeri da zero a venti

en.title: Numbers from Zero to Twenty
en.explanation:
Numbers in Italian from 0 to 20 are essential building blocks for everyday communication. Learning them allows you to count, give your age, talk about quantities, and much more. Here are the numbers to memorize:

| Number | Italian |
|--------|----------|
| 0 | zero |
| 1 | uno |
| 2 | due |
| 3 | tre |
| 4 | quattro |
| 5 | cinque |
| 6 | sei |
| 7 | sette |
| 8 | otto |
| 9 | nove |
| 10 | dieci |
| 11 | undici |
| 12 | dodici |
| 13 | tredici |
| 14 | quattordici |
| 15 | quindici |
| 16 | sedici |
| 17 | diciassette |
| 18 | diciotto |
| 19 | diciannove |
| 20 | venti |

**Examples:**

- *Ho due gatti.* (I have two cats.)
- *Lei ha quindici anni.* (She is fifteen years old.)
- *Ci sono venti studenti in classe.* (There are twenty students in class.)

> **Tip:** Notice that numbers 11-16 end in **-dici** (from *dieci*, meaning ten), and numbers 17-19 start with **dici-**. This can help you remember them more easily!

unistr_label: Yes, no, not
label: Affermazione, negazione e negativo

en.title: How to Say Yes, No, and Not
en.explanation:
In Italian, you use **si** to say yes and **no** to say no. When you want to make a verb negative (say you do *not* do something), you put **non** directly before the verb.

**Examples:**

- *Si, parlo italiano.* (Yes, I speak Italian.)
- *No, non parlo francese.* (No, I do not speak French.)
- *Non capisco.* (I do not understand.)

**Tip:** Remember that **no** is used on its own as a short answer, while **non** always comes right before a verb to make it negative. You will use both of them all the time!

unistr_label: Simple sentences
label: Frasi semplici dichiarative

en.title: Building a Simple Italian Sentence
en.explanation:
In Italian, a basic sentence follows a simple order: **subject** (who does the action) + **verb** (the action) + **object** (what the action is done to). This is very similar to English, so it is easy to get started! Just put the pieces together in the right order.

**Examples:**

- *Marco mangia una pizza.* (Marco eats a pizza.)
- *Io bevo il caffè.* (I drink the coffee.)
- *La bambina legge un libro.* (The little girl reads a book.)

**Tip:** In Italian, you can often leave out the subject pronoun (like *io*, *tu*, *lui*) because the verb ending already tells you who is doing the action. For example, *Mangio una pizza* means **I** eat a pizza — the *-o* ending on *mangio* shows it is "I".

unistr_label: Vorrei (I would like)
label: Condizionale presente di volere per cortesia

en.title: Vorrei: Making Polite Requests
en.explanation:
**Vorrei** means **"I would like"** and is the polite way to ask for something in Italian. It is much more common and courteous than simply saying "I want" (*voglio*). Use it whenever you are ordering food, shopping, or making a request.

**How to use it:**
Just say **vorrei** + the thing you want.

**Examples:**
- *Vorrei un caffè.* (I would like a coffee.)
- *Vorrei un biglietto, per favore.* (I would like a ticket, please.)
- *Vorrei dell'acqua.* (I would like some water.)

> **Tip:** You can always add **per favore** (please) at the end to sound extra polite!

unistr_label: Polite expressions
label: Espressioni di cortesia e ringraziamento

en.title: Polite Words: per favore, grazie and More
en.explanation:
Italian has a few very important **polite words** that you will use every day. Learning these words first will help you be friendly and respectful right away.

**The key polite words:**

| Italian | English |
|---|---|
| per favore | please |
| grazie | thank you |
| prego | you're welcome |
| scusi / scusa | excuse me / sorry |
| mi dispiace | I'm sorry |

**Examples:**

- *Un caffè, per favore.* (A coffee, please.)
- *Grazie!* — *Prego!* (Thank you! — You're welcome!)
- *Scusi, dov'è la stazione?* (Excuse me, where is the train station?)

**Quick tip:** Use **scusi** with strangers or adults you don't know (formal), and **scusa** with friends or people your own age (informal). Use **mi dispiace** when you feel genuinely sorry about something, for example: *Mi dispiace, non lo so.* (I'm sorry, I don't know.)

unistr_label: Articles: il and la
label: Articoli determinativi singolari il e la

en.title: Articles il and la: Masculine and Feminine
en.explanation:
In Italian, every noun (person, place, or thing) is either **masculine** or **feminine**. The word for **"the"** changes depending on the gender: use **il** before masculine nouns and **la** before feminine nouns. You will need to learn the gender of each new word as you go — it is usually shown in a dictionary.

**Examples:**
- *il ragazzo* (the boy) — masculine, so we use **il**
- *la ragazza* (the girl) — feminine, so we use **la**
- *il libro* (the book) — masculine, so we use **il**
- *la porta* (the door) — feminine, so we use **la**

**Quick tip:** Most masculine nouns end in **-o** and most feminine nouns end in **-a**, but there are exceptions, so always check!

unistr_label: What is it? (Che cos'è?)
label: Domanda identificativa che cos'è

en.title: Asking What Something Is: Che cos'è?
en.explanation:
## Asking "What is it?" in Italian

**Che cos'è?** is how you ask *"What is it?"* or *"What is this?"* in Italian. You can also say **Che cos'è questo?** when you want to point at something specific and ask what it is. It is one of the most useful questions for beginners!

### Examples

- **Che cos'è?** (What is it?)
- **Che cos'è questo?** (What is this?)
- **Che cos'è quella cosa?** (What is that thing?)

### How to answer

To answer, you use **È** (it is) followed by the name of the thing:

- — Che cos'è questo? *(What is this?)*
  — **È un libro.** *(It is a book.)*
- — Che cos'è? *(What is it?)*
  — **È una mela.** *(It is an apple.)*

> **Tip:** **È** comes from the verb *essere* (to be). You don't need to say a word for "it" — **È** alone already means *"It is."*

unistr_label: Subject pronouns: io, tu, lui/lei
label: Pronomi personali soggetto io tu lui lei

en.title: Subject Pronouns: io, tu, lui, lei
en.explanation:
In Italian, subject pronouns tell us *who* is doing the action in a sentence. The most common ones are: **io** (I), **tu** (you), **lui** (he), and **lei** (she). Unlike in English, Italian speakers often leave these pronouns out, because the verb ending already shows who is doing the action — but they are still very useful to know!

**Examples:**
- **Io sono Marco.** (I am Marco.)
- **Tu parli italiano.** (You speak Italian.)
- **Lui si chiama Luca.** (He is called Luca.)
- **Lei è studentessa.** (She is a student.)

> **Quick tip:** Notice that **lei** (she) is written with a lowercase *l*. When **Lei** is written with a capital *L*, it means *you* in a formal/polite context — but don't worry about that just yet!

unistr_label: To be: sono, sei, è
label: Indicativo presente di essere forme sono sei è

en.title: The Verb essere: sono, sei, è...
en.explanation:
## The verb *essere* (to be)

In Italian, the verb **essere** means *to be*. Here are all six forms:

| Italian | English |
|---|---|
| io **sono** | I am |
| tu **sei** | you are |
| lui/lei **è** | he/she is |
| noi **siamo** | we are |
| voi **siete** | you (plural) are |
| loro **sono** | they are |

> Focus on io/tu/lui for now — you'll practice the others soon!

> Notice that **è** has an accent mark — this helps distinguish it from the word *e*, which means *and*.

**Examples:**

- *Io sono Marco.* (I am Marco.)
- *Tu sei italiana.* (You are Italian.)
- *Lei è studentessa.* (She is a student.)

Just match the correct form to the person you are talking about, and you are ready to go!

unistr_label: I like / I don't like
label: Indicativo presente di piacere forme mi piace non mi piace

en.title: Likes and Dislikes: mi piace / non mi piace
en.explanation:
## Saying What You Like and Don't Like

In Italian, you don't say "I like pizza" the way you do in English. Instead, you say **mi piace**, which works more like "pizza pleases me." Think of it as the thing you like *doing the action* — it pleases you!

- Use **mi piace** to say you like something.
- Use **non mi piace** to say you don't like something.
- Use **ti piace?** to ask someone else if they like something.

### With a noun (a thing)

When you like **one thing**, use **mi piace** + the noun:

- **Mi piace la pizza.** (I like pizza.)
- **Non mi piace il caffè.** (I don't like coffee.)

> Notice that Italian uses **la** or **il** (the) before the noun — this is normal and required in Italian!

### With a verb (an activity)

When you like **doing something**, use **mi piace** + the infinitive (the base form of a verb, like *mangiare* = to eat):

- **Mi piace mangiare.** (I like eating / I like to eat.)
- **Non mi piace studiare.** (I don't like studying / I don't like to study.)

### Asking a question

To ask someone if they like something, just use **ti piace?**:

- **Ti piace la musica?** (Do you like music?)

### Quick summary

| Italian | English |
|---|---|
| Mi piace la pizza. | I like pizza. |
| Non mi piace il caffè. | I don't like coffee. |
| Mi piace mangiare. | I like eating. |
| Ti piace la musica? | Do you like music? |

> **Tip:** To make it negative, just add **non** before **mi piace**. Easy!

unistr_label: Where is it? (Dov'è?)
label: Domanda di localizzazione dov'è

en.title: Asking Where Something Is: Dov'è?
en.explanation:
## Asking "Where is...?" in Italian

**Dov'è** is how you ask "Where is...?" in Italian. It is a combination of **dove** (where) and **è** (is), joined together with an apostrophe. Use it whenever you want to find out the location of a person, place, or thing.

### How to use it

Simply say **Dov'è** and then the person or thing you are looking for:

> **Dov'è** + [the thing/person you want to find]

### Examples

- **Dov'è il bagno?**
(Where is the bathroom?)

- **Dov'è la stazione?**
(Where is the train station?)

- **Dov'è Marco?**
(Where is Marco?)

### Useful tip

In Italian, nouns have a gender — they are either **masculine** or **feminine**. This affects the small word before the noun (the article):

- **il** is used before most masculine nouns
- **la** is used before most feminine nouns

But don't worry about this too much right now — just start using **Dov'è?** and you will pick it up naturally!

### Quick answer phrases

When someone answers your question, they might say:
- **È qui.** (It is here.)
- **È lì.** (It is there.)
- **È a destra.** (It is on the right.)
- **È a sinistra.** (It is on the left.)

unistr_label: Prepositions of place: a, in, di
label: Preposizioni di luogo: a, in, di

en.title: Prepositions of Place: a, in, di
en.explanation:
## Prepositions of Place: a, in, di

In Italian, small words called **prepositions** tell us where something or someone is, or where they are going. The three most common ones are **a** (to / at), **in** (in / inside), and **di** (of / from). Think of them as location connectors — they link a person or thing to a place.

### a — to / at
Use **a** before the name of a city, or to say you are at a specific place.

- *Vado **a** Roma.* (I am going **to** Rome.)
- *Sono **a** scuola.* (I am **at** school.)

### in — in / inside
Use **in** before the name of a country, region, or a general space you are inside.

- *Abito **in** Italia.* (I live **in** Italy.)
- *Il gatto è **in** giardino.* (The cat is **in** the garden.)

### di — of / from
Use **di** to show where someone comes from or that something belongs to a place.

- *Sono **di** Milano.* (I am **from** Milan.)
- *È la pizza **di** Napoli.* (It is the pizza **of** Naples.)

> **Quick tip:** Use **a** with cities and **in** with countries — this is the most common pattern for beginners!

unistr_label: My name is... (Mi chiamo)
label: Verbo chiamarsi al presente indicativo per l'autopresentazione

en.title: Introducing Yourself: Mi chiamo...
en.explanation:
## Saying Your Name in Italian

In Italian, you don't say *"I am called..."* word for word — instead, you use the phrase **mi chiamo** followed by your name. Think of it like saying *"I call myself..."* It is the most natural and common way to introduce yourself in Italian.

**The formula is simple:**
> **Mi chiamo + [your name]**

### Examples

- **Mi chiamo Marco.** (My name is Marco.)
- **Mi chiamo Sofia.** (My name is Sofia.)
- **Mi chiamo Anna. E tu?** (My name is Anna. And you?)

### How to Use It

When you meet someone new, you can say **mi chiamo** and add your name right after. That's it! No other words are needed. You can also ask someone else their name by saying:

- **Come ti chiami?** (What is your name? / literally: What do you call yourself?)

And they will answer:
- **Mi chiamo Luca.** (My name is Luca.)

### Quick Tip

*Mi chiamo* comes from the verb **chiamarsi** (to call oneself). For now, you don't need to learn the whole verb — just remember this one ready-made phrase and use it every time you introduce yourself!

unistr_label: La distinzione genere e numero dei nomi regolari a suffisso –O –A e a suffisso –E
label: Genere e numero regolari di nomi suffissi O A E

en.title: Plural forms of Italian nouns
en.tip: Most Italian nouns change their final vowel to form the plural. Nouns ending in -o or -e change to -i, and nouns ending in -a change to -e. Learning these three patterns lets you talk about more than one person, animal, or thing.
en.explanation: ## The three regular patterns Italian nouns belong to one of three groups based on their singular ending. To make them plural, replace that final vowel as follows: | Singular ending | Plural ending | Typical gender | |---|---|---| | -o | -i | masculine | | -a | -e | feminine | | -e | -i | masculine or feminine | The article changes alongside the noun. Masculine singular il becomes i, and feminine singular la becomes le. Nouns whose singular form uses the article lo (used before certain consonant clusters) take gli in the plural. --- ## Pattern 1: -o → -i (mostly masculine) Most nouns ending in -o are masculine. Replace -o with -i and change il to i: | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | il libro | i libri | book / books | | il ragazzo | i ragazzi | boy / boys | | il cane | — | (see Pattern 3) | --- ## Pattern 2: -a → -e (mostly feminine) Most nouns ending in -a are feminine. Replace -a with -e and change la to le: | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | la mela | le mele | apple / apples | | la sorella | le sorelle | sister / sisters | | la preda | le prede | prey / (instances of) prey | --- ## Pattern 3: -e → -i (masculine or feminine) Nouns ending in -e can be either masculine or feminine — you need to learn each noun's gender individually. Both genders replace -e with -i: | Singular | Plural | Meaning | Gender | |---|---|---|---| | il cane | i cani | dog / dogs | masculine | | la madre | le madri | mother / mothers | feminine | | il padre | i padri | father / fathers | masculine | --- ## Examples in context 1. Il bambino mangia una mela. — The child eats an apple. I bambini mangiano le mele. — The children eat the apples. 2. Ho un fratello e due sorelle. — I have one brother and two sisters. 3. Il cane è grande; i cani sono grandi. — The dog is big; the dogs are big. 4. C'è un libro sul tavolo. Ci sono tre libri sul tavolo. — There is a book on the table. There are three books on the table. 5. La madre e il padre sono a casa. Le madri e i padri sono a casa. — The mother and father are at home. The mothers and fathers are at home. 6. (Contrastive pair) la mano (hand) ends in -o but is feminine, and its plural is le mani — an irregular form covered separately at a higher level. --- ## Nouns whose plural is identical to their singular Some nouns do not change at all in the plural. This happens with: - Nouns ending in an accented vowel: la città → le città (city / cities), la tribù → le tribù (tribe / tribes). - Nouns ending in a consonant (mostly foreign words): il bar → i bar, lo sport → gli sport. - Monosyllabic nouns: il re → i re (king / kings), la gru → le gru (crane / cranes). In all these cases, the article is the only signal that the noun is plural, so learning the article alongside every noun is essential. --- ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Applying the wrong pattern to -e nouns:** Learners sometimes write *i padres or *i padree. The correct form is i padri. All -e nouns, whether masculine or feminine, take -i in the plural. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting to change the article:** Writing *la sorelle is wrong even though the noun ending is correct. The article must agree: le sorelle. The article and the noun always change together. **Mistake 3 — Assuming all -o nouns are masculine:** A small number of -o nouns are feminine (e.g. la mano, hand). These are exceptions to be memorised; the three-pattern system above covers the vast majority of everyday nouns. **Mistake 4 — Adding a plural ending to an invariable noun:** Do not write *le cittàe or *le città with a changed ending. Nouns with a final accented vowel never change: una città, due città. --- ## Quick-reference summary | Singular | Plural | Example | |---|---|---| | -o | -i | libro → libri | | -a | -e | mela → mele | | -e | -i | cane → cani | | accented vowel or consonant | no change | città → città |
en.why_this_matters: Almost every sentence you say in Italian will include a noun, and Italian nouns almost always signal whether you mean one thing or many by changing their final vowel — the ending grammarians call the desinenza (ending). Without this rule you cannot say 'two friends', 'some apples', or 'my sisters' — you will be stuck talking about only one of everything. Mastering these three patterns removes one of the most frequent sources of beginner errors immediately. ---

unistr_label: I principali nomi invariabili (es. caffè, cinema, città, università )
label: Nomi invariabili caffè cinema città università

en.title: Nouns that never change in the plural
en.tip: Some Italian nouns look exactly the same in the singular and the plural — only the article changes to show whether you mean one or many. This happens with short, clipped words, words ending in a stressed vowel, and foreign borrowings.
en.explanation: ## The core rule Most Italian nouns change their ending to form the plural (ragazzo → ragazzi, porta → porte). But a category called nomi invariabili (invariable nouns) keeps exactly the same form in both singular and plural. The article is the only thing that changes. Singular: il caffè → Plural: i caffè (the coffees) Singular: la città → Plural: le città (the cities) ## Which nouns are invariable? ### 1. Words ending in a stressed (accented) vowel Any noun whose final vowel carries a written accent is invariable. These are called polisillabi tronchi (words 'cut short' with stress on the last syllable). This is the largest and most important group for A1 learners. | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | il caffè | i caffè | coffee(s) | | la città | le città | city/cities | | l'università | le università | university/universities | | l'età | le età | age(s) | | la virtù | le virtù | virtue(s) | | il bignè | i bignè | cream puff(s) | ### 2. Monosyllables (one-syllable words) All nouns of just one syllable are invariable. | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | il re | i re | king(s) | | la gru | le gru | crane(s) (the bird or machine) | ### 3. Shortened (clipped) words Italian often shortens longer words. The clipped form — called a nome accorciato (shortened noun) — is always invariable, even though the full original word would have a regular plural. | Singular | Plural | Full form | |---|---|---| | l'auto | le auto | automobile → automobili | | la bici | le bici | bicicletta → biciclette | | il cinema | i cinema | cinematografo → cinematografi | | la foto | le foto | fotografia → fotografie | | la moto | le moto | motocicletta → motociclette | ### 4. Nouns of foreign origin Words borrowed from other languages and used without adaptation keep their original form and do not add any Italian plural ending. | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | il bar | i bar | bar(s) / café(s) | | il film | i film | film(s) | | lo sport | gli sport | sport(s) | ### 5. Other invariable groups (less common at A1) There are a few additional categories you may encounter: - Nouns ending in -i in the singular (e.g. l'analisi → le analisi, 'analysis/analyses'; la tesi → le tesi, 'thesis/theses') - Feminine nouns ending in -ie (e.g. la serie → le serie, 'series'; la carie → le carie, 'cavity/cavities') — but note that -cie, -gie, and -glie endings follow different rules - Masculine animal nouns ending in -a (e.g. il gorilla → i gorilla, 'gorilla/gorillas') ## Examples in sentences Vorrei due caffè, per favore. (I would like two coffees, please.) — The noun caffè is identical in singular and plural; only the number word tells you there are two. Quante città hai visitato? (How many cities have you visited?) — città does not change, even though the question clearly refers to multiple places. C'è un'università in questa città. / Ci sono tre università in questa città. (There is one university in this city. / There are three universities in this city.) — A perfect contrastive pair: the noun stays the same; the verb and numeral carry the plural meaning. Andiamo al cinema stasera? (Shall we go to the cinema tonight?) — cinema is a clipped word and never changes. Ho due bici: una rossa e una blu. (I have two bikes: a red one and a blue one.) — bici is the clipped form of bicicletta and stays invariable. In questo paese ci sono tre bar. (In this town there are three bars.) — Foreign borrowing bar takes no ending in the plural. ## Common learner mistakes **Adding a regular plural ending** Mistake: *le cittàe*, *i caffèi*, *i bars* Correction: le città, i caffè, i bar — these nouns never take a plural suffix. **Pluralising the clipped form as if it were a full word** Mistake: *le auti* (treating auto like a regular -o noun) Correction: le auto — once a word is clipped, it becomes invariable. **Forgetting to change the article** Mistake: *la città sono belle* Correction: le città sono belle (the cities are beautiful) — the noun stays the same, but the article must still agree in number. **Confusing foto and moto with masculine nouns** Because -o endings are usually masculine, learners sometimes say *il foto* or *il moto*. Both are feminine: la foto / le foto, la moto / le moto. They inherit the gender of their full forms (la fotografia, la motocicletta). ## Quick-reference summary | Type | Key feature | Example | |---|---|---| | Stressed final vowel | written accent on last vowel | città, caffè, università | | Monosyllable | one syllable only | re, gru | | Clipped word | shortened from a longer word | auto, bici, cinema, foto | | Foreign borrowing | kept in original form | bar, film, sport | | Singular ending in -i | already ends in -i | analisi, tesi | | Feminine -ie nouns | ends in -ie (not -cie/-gie) | serie, carie |
en.why_this_matters: A huge number of everyday Italian words — caffè, città, università, cinema, bar — belong to this group. If you try to add a regular plural ending to them, you will produce errors that native speakers immediately notice. Understanding this rule also trains you to watch the article carefully, because it is often the only signal that tells you whether someone means one thing or many.

en.title: Nouns used only in the plural
en.tip: Some Italian nouns exist only in the plural — they have no singular form. You must always use a plural article and plural adjective with them, even when you mean just one item.
en.explanation: ## The rule In Italian, some nouns are called nomi difettivi (defective nouns) — nouns that are 'defective' in that they lack one of the two number forms. The group that matters most at A1 level is nouns that exist **only in the plural**: they have no singular form and cannot be used with a singular article. The reason is logical: many of these nouns name objects that are physically made of two matching parts — two lenses, two legs, two blades. Italian treats the whole object as inherently plural. Because the object itself implies two parts, there is no 'one unit' form to express. The practical consequence is straightforward: **always use the plural article and plural agreement** with these words. You say gli occhiali sono (the glasses are), never *l'occhiale è. ## Core vocabulary: the most common plural-only nouns Learn these as fixed plural forms from the start: | Forma plurale | English | Article to use | |---|---|---| | gli occhiali | glasses (spectacles) | gli / i | | i pantaloni | trousers / pants | i | | i calzoni | trousers (informal) | i | | le mutande | underwear / underpants | le | | le forbici | scissors | le | | le pinze | pliers / tongs | le | | le tenaglie | pincers / tongs | le | | le cesoie | shears / garden scissors | le | | le redini | reins (for a horse) | le | | le manette | handcuffs | le | At A1 level, focus especially on gli occhiali and i pantaloni, as these come up in everyday conversation about clothing and personal items. ## Examples Gli occhiali sono sul tavolo. (The glasses are on the table.) I pantaloni sono neri. (The trousers are black.) Dove sono le forbici? (Where are the scissors?) Ho comprato i pantaloni nuovi. (I bought new trousers.) — note: nuovi, not *nuovo, because the adjective must agree in the plural. I miei occhiali sono rotti. (My glasses are broken.) — both the possessive miei and the adjective rotti are plural. Questi pantaloni sono troppo grandi. (These trousers are too big.) — questi (these), not *questo, because the noun is always plural. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — using a singular article:** Incorrect: *un occhiale, il pantalone. Correct: degli occhiali, i pantaloni. These nouns have no singular form, so a singular article is never correct. **Mistake 2 — singular adjective agreement:** Incorrect: *i pantaloni è bello. Correct: i pantaloni sono belli. Both the verb and the adjective must be plural, because the noun is always plural. **Mistake 3 — translating 'a pair of' literally to make a singular:** In English you can say 'a pair of trousers' to signal one item. In Italian, if you want to be explicit you can say un paio di pantaloni (a pair of trousers), but the noun pantaloni stays plural. Do not invent a singular form like *un pantalone to mean a single garment. **Mistake 4 — applying this rule too broadly:** Not every clothing word is plural-only. For example, la maglietta (the T-shirt) and la scarpa (the shoe) have normal singular and plural forms. Only memorise the specific words in the table above as exceptions. ## A note on everyday speech You may occasionally hear Italian speakers use forms like il pantalone in very informal speech, treating the noun as if it had a singular. This does happen in casual conversation, but it is considered non-standard. In writing and in careful speech, always use the plural forms listed above.
en.why_this_matters: A handful of very common Italian words — including everyday items like glasses and trousers — are always plural, even when you are talking about a single object. Getting this wrong produces immediate errors, because pairing these words with a singular article or adjective sounds unnatural to any native speaker. Mastering this small group removes a persistent source of mistakes from the very first weeks of learning Italian.

en.title: Irregular plurals: uomo and similar nouns
en.tip: A small group of Italian nouns ending in -o do not follow the regular -o → -i pattern in the plural. The most important one at A1 level is uomo (man) → uomini (men). You simply have to learn these forms by heart.
en.explanation: ## The regular rule (and why these nouns break it) Most masculine nouns ending in -o form their plural by changing -o to -i: | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | libro | libri | book / books | | ragazzo | ragazzi | boy / boys | A small but very important group of nouns does **not** follow this pattern. Their plurals must be memorised individually. ## The key irregular plural: uomo → uomini uomo (man) has the completely irregular plural uomini (men). The change is not a simple vowel swap — the entire word stem shifts. This is the single most important irregular plural at A1 level. ## Other irregular plurals in the same family The authoritative reference lists a set of nouns ending in -o (or closely related forms) whose plurals are irregular. Learn all of them: | Singular | Article | Plural | Article | Meaning | |---|---|---|---|---| | uomo | l' | uomini | gli | man / men | | uovo | l' | uova | le | egg / eggs | | mano | la | mani | le | hand / hands | | dio | il | dei | gli | god / gods | | paio | il | paia | le | pair / pairs | | miglio | il | miglia | le | mile / miles | | migliaio | il | migliaia | le | thousand / thousands | | centinaio | il | centinaia | le | hundred / hundreds | | riso (= laughing) | il | risa | le | laugh / laughs | | tempio | il | templi | i | temple / temples | | eco | la | echi | gli | echo / echoes | **Important notes on this table:** - uovo, paio, miglia, risa, centinaia, migliaia are unusual because they change gender in the plural — they are masculine in the singular but feminine in the plural. This affects the article too. - mano is feminine even in the singular (la mano) — it does not end in -a as most feminine nouns do, and its plural is le mani, not *le mane. - riso meaning 'rice' (the food) is a regular masculine noun: il riso / i risi. Only riso meaning 'laughter' has the irregular plural le risa. - At A1, the most important items to know are uomo/uomini, uovo/uova, and mano/mani. ## Examples 1. C'è un uomo alla porta. (There is a man at the door.) 2. Ci sono tre uomini alla porta. (There are three men at the door.) — Note: uomini, not *uomi or *uomos. 3. Vuoi un uovo per colazione? (Do you want an egg for breakfast?) 4. Ho comprato due uova al mercato. (I bought two eggs at the market.) — The article changes from il/l' to le in the plural. 5. Dammi la mano! (Give me your hand!) 6. Ho le mani fredde. (My hands are cold.) — Contrastive pair: la mano → le mani, not *le mane. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Applying the regular rule to uomo:** *gli uomi ✗ — Correction: gli uomini ✓. The plural is not formed by simply changing -o to -i. **Mistake 2 — Wrong article with uova:** *gli uova ✗ — Correction: le uova ✓. Because uova is feminine plural, it takes le, not gli. **Mistake 3 — Wrong plural of mano:** *le mane or *le manos ✗ — Correction: le mani ✓. **Mistake 4 — Treating riso (rice) as irregular:** The food 'rice' is regular: il riso has no common plural in everyday use. Only riso meaning 'laughter' has the feminine plural le risa. ## Practical advice Uomo/uomini is the form you will encounter most at A1 level — prioritise it. For the others, learn uovo/uova and mano/mani next, since they appear in everyday food and body-part vocabulary. When in doubt about any irregular plural, consult a dictionary — there is no shortcut rule that predicts all of them.
en.why_this_matters: The word uomo (man) is one of the most common nouns in Italian — you will need it from your very first conversations. Because its plural uomini looks nothing like the singular, students who have only learned the regular rule will produce errors every time. Learning this small set of exceptions now will save you constant embarrassment and confusion.

en.title: Foreign words that don't change in the plural
en.tip: Many Italian nouns borrowed from other languages — like 'bar', 'film', and 'computer' — have the same form in both singular and plural. Only the article changes to show whether you mean one or more than one.
en.explanation: ## The rule Nouns borrowed from foreign languages — mostly English, but also French and others — that have kept their original spelling do **not** change their ending in the plural. They are called nomi invariabili (invariable nouns). The only thing that changes is the **article** in front of the noun. > Singular: il bar → Plural: i bar (not *i bari) ## How to form the plural Keep the noun exactly as it is. Change only the article from singular to plural. | Singular article | Plural article | Noun (unchanged) | |---|---|---| | il | i | bar, film, computer, autobus | | lo | gli | sport, stress, yogurt | | la | le | email, chat | | l' | gli / le | hotel (gli hotel) | The article follows normal Italian rules for gender and the first letter of the noun, just as with any Italian word. ## Common examples at A1 level These are the foreign-origin nouns you will meet most often at beginner level: | Singular | Plural | Meaning | |---|---|---| | il bar | i bar | café / bar | | il film | i film | film / movie | | il computer | i computer | computer | | lo sport | gli sport | sport | | l'autobus | gli autobus | bus | | l'hotel | gli hotel | hotel | | il weekend | i weekend | weekend | | lo yogurt | gli yogurt | yogurt | ## Examples in sentences 1. C'è un bar vicino a casa mia. (There is a café near my house.) 2. Ci sono due bar vicino a casa mia. (There are two cafés near my house.) — notice: bar does not change. 3. Guardo un film stasera. (I am watching a film tonight.) 4. Guardo tre film nel weekend. (I watch three films at the weekend.) — film and weekend both stay the same. 5. Ho un computer nuovo. (I have a new computer.) 6. In questa scuola ci sono venti computer. (In this school there are twenty computers.) — the noun is unchanged; only context and number words tell you it is plural. ## Why only the article changes Italian nouns normally signal singular or plural through their ending (-o / -i, -a / -e, etc.). Foreign words end in consonant clusters or vowels that do not fit the Italian pattern, so Italian leaves the word untouched and relies on the article — and on context or numbers — to show quantity. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Adding an Italian plural ending:** *i filmi, i bari, i computeri — these forms do not exist. The noun never changes: i film, i bar, i computer. **Mistake 2 — Keeping the singular article:** *il computer sono nuovi — wrong; if the noun is plural, the article must be plural too: i computer sono nuovi (the computers are new). **Mistake 3 — Using the wrong article for sport and yogurt:** Because these words begin with s + consonant (sp-, st-), they take lo / gli, not il / i. So it is lo sport → gli sport, not *il sport / *i sport. **Mistake 4 — Forgetting that the noun is still singular or plural in agreement:** Even though the noun looks the same, adjectives and verbs must still agree in number: il film è bello (the film is good) vs. i film sono belli (the films are good). ## Quick reference To check whether a foreign word is invariable, ask: does it end in a consonant, or in a vowel that does not match a standard Italian ending? If yes, leave it unchanged and adjust only the article and any adjectives.
en.why_this_matters: Italian borrows many everyday words from English and other languages, and these words appear constantly in daily life — at the café, talking about technology, discussing hobbies. Because their plural form looks identical to the singular, students who try to add -i or -e endings will always be wrong. Mastering this small rule means you can speak and write these very common words correctly from day one.

en.title: Masculine and feminine noun suffixes
en.tip: Many Italian nouns that name people have two forms: one for males and one for females. Learning the most common pairs — especially -tore/-trice and -e/-essa — lets you talk about people and their jobs correctly from day one.
en.explanation: ## The core rule A noun with differentiated gender (nome a genere differenziato, a noun that has separate masculine and feminine forms) changes its ending to show whether it refers to a male or a female. The ending you swap out is called the desinenza (suffix or ending). The table below shows the main patterns. ## The main suffix patterns ### Pattern 1: -o (masculine) → -a (feminine) This is the largest and most common group. | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | maestro | maestra | teacher (primary school) | | ragazzo | ragazza | boy / girl | | cuoco | cuoca | cook | ### Pattern 2: -e (masculine) → -a (feminine) A sizeable group, but watch out: many nouns ending in -e do not change (see the exception note below). | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | cameriere | cameriera | waiter / waitress | | panettiere | panettiera | baker | | padrone | padrona | owner / boss | ### Pattern 3: -tore (masculine) → -trice (feminine) Nouns built on Latin agent suffixes follow this pattern reliably. It covers many job and role words. | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | direttore | direttrice | director / headteacher | | pittore | pittrice | painter | | salvatore | salvatrice | saviour / rescuer | A related group replaces -sore with -itrice: | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | difensore | difenditrice | defender | ### Pattern 4: adding -essa to the masculine Some nouns — especially for professions and titles — form the feminine by adding -essa to the masculine base. This group is most important at A1 for a small set of very common words. | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | dottore | dottoressa | doctor / graduate (title) | | professore | professoressa | professor / secondary-school teacher | | avvocato | avvocatessa | lawyer | | leone | leonessa | lion / lioness | | poeta | poetessa | poet | Notice that dottore and professore both end in -tore, yet they take -essa rather than -trice. These two words are the most important exceptions to Pattern 3 and must simply be memorised. ## Irregular and special pairs A handful of very common nouns are completely irregular — the feminine is not derived from the masculine at all: | Masculine | Feminine | Meaning | |---|---|---| | re | regina | king / queen | | dio | dea | god / goddess | | abate | badessa | abbot / abbess | | cane | cagna | dog / female dog | ## Important exception: nouns that do not change Some nouns ending in -e use the same form for both genders. The article or context shows the gender. The most common examples at A1 are: - insegnante (teacher) — il/la insegnante → l'insegnante - giovane (young person) - cantante (singer) These are called nomi di genere comune (common-gender nouns) and are covered in their own entry. Do not try to add -a to them. ## Examples in context 1. Il maestro spiega la lezione. — The (male) teacher explains the lesson. 2. La maestra spiega la lezione. — The (female) teacher explains the lesson. 3. Mia madre è dottoressa. — My mother is a doctor. (Note: -essa, not -trice.) 4. Il professore è in aula; la professoressa è in biblioteca. — The (male) teacher is in the classroom; the (female) teacher is in the library. 5. La direttrice della scuola si chiama Anna. — The (female) headteacher is called Anna. (direttore → direttrice, Pattern 3.) 6. Contrastive pair: il cameriere / la cameriera (Pattern 2) vs. il professore / la professoressa (Pattern 4) — both end in -e in the masculine, but they form the feminine differently. Always check which group a word belongs to. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Applying -trice to professore and dottore:** Learners who have just learned the -tore/-trice rule often write *professorice or *dottrice. These do not exist. The correct forms are professoressa and dottoressa. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting to change the article:** Changing only the noun ending is not enough. The article must also agree: il direttore → la direttrice, not *il direttrice. **Mistake 3 — Adding -a to a common-gender noun:** Writing *insegnanta for a female teacher is wrong. Use la insegnante / l'insegnante and let the article carry the gender. **Mistake 4 — Using the masculine form as a 'neutral' title for a woman:** In everyday Italian at A1, use the feminine form when referring to a woman: say la professoressa, not *la professore. The feminine forms exist precisely for this purpose and are the expected choice.
en.why_this_matters: Italian nouns that refer to people almost always have a masculine form and a feminine form. If you use the wrong ending, you may accidentally say the wrong thing about a person's identity. The suffix pairs covered here — especially -tore/-trice and -e/-essa — appear constantly when talking about jobs, roles, and titles, so mastering them early removes one of the most common A1 mistakes.

en.title: Subject personal pronouns in Italian
en.tip: In Italian, you usually leave out the subject pronoun ('I', 'you', 'he', etc.) because the verb ending already shows who is acting. Use the pronoun only when you need to make a contrast, add emphasis, or avoid confusion.
en.explanation: ## The subject pronouns — full list These are the Italian subject pronouns — the words that tell you *who* performs the action of the verb. | Person | Italian form(s) | English equivalent | |---|---|---| | 1st singular | io | I | | 2nd singular | tu | you (informal, one person) | | 3rd singular masc. | lui / egli / esso | he / it | | 3rd singular fem. | lei / ella / essa | she / it | | 1st plural | noi | we | | 2nd plural | voi | you (plural) | | 3rd plural masc./mixed | loro / essi | they | | 3rd plural fem. | loro / esse | they (all female) | At A1, the forms you will use and hear every day are: io, tu, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro. The others (egli, ella, esso, essa, essi, esse) appear mainly in literary or formal written Italian and are explained below under 'Variants and formal forms'. ## The core rule: usually omit the pronoun Unlike English, where 'I speak', 'you speak', 'she speaks' all need a pronoun to show who is acting, Italian verb endings already carry that information. The pronoun is therefore *optional in most sentences* and is routinely left out in speech and informal writing. Compare: English (pronoun obligatory): I work → I work (you cannot say just 'work') Italian (pronoun optional): (Io) lavoro. — 'I work.' The ending -o already signals first-person singular, so io adds no new information. ## When the pronoun IS required There are three clear situations in which you must include the subject pronoun: ### 1. Contrast between two different subjects When two clauses in a row have *different* subjects, use pronouns to signal the switch clearly. > Lui va in montagna, io vado al mare. > (He is going to the mountains; I am going to the seaside.) ### 2. Emphasis or focus on the subject When you want to stress *who* is performing the action — 'it was specifically *you*, not someone else' — the pronoun must be present. This use is also required after words such as anche ('also/too'), neanche ('not even/neither'), and pure ('too/also'). > Sei stato tu a dire questo. > (It was *you* who said that — emphasising 'you and no one else'.) > È venuta anche lei. > (She came too.) ### 3. Avoiding ambiguity When leaving out the pronoun would make the sentence unclear about who is involved, include it. > È bene che vada. > (It is good that [someone] goes.) — Without context, this could mean I, you, he or she should go. If the subject needs to be clear, say: È bene che vada lui. (It is good that *he* goes.) ## Third-person singular and plural: which form to choose The third person has several competing forms. Here is the practical guidance for A1 students: **Singular — lui and lei** Use lui for 'he' and lei for 'she'. These are the standard forms in modern spoken and written Italian. Whenever a subject pronoun of the third person singular is *required* (contrast, emphasis, or clarity), lui and lei are the correct choices. > Io resto, lui parte. > (I am staying; he is leaving.) **Plural — loro** Use loro for 'they' when referring to people. Note that loro is the only plural third-person form permitted when a pronoun is required. > Noi siamo italiani, loro sono francesi. > (We are Italian; they are French.) ## Variants and formal forms The forms egli ('he', formal/literary), ella ('she', formal/literary), esso / essa ('it' — for animals or things, and in formal style also for people in the feminine), and essi / esse ('they', formal/literary, for groups of things or all-female groups) belong mainly to written, formal, or literary Italian. Historically, egli was prescribed for referring to a male person and esso for animals and things, but today even in formal writing egli is increasingly rare and lui has taken its place. As an A1 student, you do not need to *use* these forms, but you should recognise them when you see them in a text. **Reinforced forms** Any subject pronoun can be reinforced by adding stesso ('myself/yourself/himself' etc.) immediately after it: io stesso, tu stesso, lui stesso, lei stessa, and so on. There are also the old reinforced forms noialtri and voialtri (written as one word), used in some regional varieties to add emphasis, though these are rarely needed at A1. ## Examples covering the main uses 1. Normal sentence — pronoun omitted (most common situation): > Mangio la pasta. > (I eat pasta.) — No pronoun needed; the -o ending identifies the speaker. 2. Contrast between subjects — pronoun required: > Lei beve il caffè, io bevo il tè. > (She drinks coffee; I drink tea.) 3. Emphasis — pronoun required: > Sei tu il professore? > (Are *you* the teacher? — 'you specifically, not someone else') 4. After anche — pronoun required: > Anche lui parla italiano. > (He speaks Italian too.) 5. Avoiding ambiguity — pronoun added for clarity: > È importante che lei risponda. > (It is important that *she* answers. — Without lei, we would not know who must answer.) 6. Contrastive pair showing the difference between using and omitting the pronoun: > Lavoro ogni giorno. (I work every day. — neutral, no pronoun.) > Io lavoro ogni giorno, tu no. (I work every day; you don't. — pronoun added for contrast.) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Always inserting the pronoun, as in English:** Because English requires 'I', 'you', 'he' etc. in every sentence, English speakers often add them in Italian even when they are not needed. This is not wrong, but it sounds unnatural and over-emphatic, as if you are stressing the subject every single time. Avoid: Io mi chiamo Marco. Io ho diciotto anni. Io abito a Roma. (sounds forced) Better: Mi chiamo Marco. Ho diciotto anni. Abito a Roma. **Mistake 2 — Using egli or ella in conversation:** These forms sound archaic or literary in spoken Italian. Use lui and lei instead. Avoid in speech: Egli è mio fratello. Natural: Lui è mio fratello. (He is my brother.) **Mistake 3 — Confusing lei ('she') with Lei (formal 'you'):** In written Italian, Lei with a capital letter is the formal polite form of 'you' (used with strangers, teachers, etc.), while lei with a lower-case letter means 'she'. In speech the two sound identical, so context tells you which is meant. At A1, simply note that when someone writes Lei with a capital in the middle of a sentence, it signals formality, not 'she'. **Mistake 4 — Using essi / esse where loro is needed:** When referring to people and a pronoun is required (contrast, emphasis), only loro is acceptable. Essi and esse are reserved for objects or formal writing. Avoid in a contrast sentence: *Noi mangiamo, essi bevono. Correct: Noi mangiamo, loro bevono. (We eat; they drink.)
en.why_this_matters: Subject pronouns are among the very first words you meet in Italian, yet Italian uses them very differently from English or French — leaving them out is not lazy, it is the normal, correct thing to do. Understanding when to drop them and when to keep them will immediately make your Italian sound natural and will prevent one of the most common A1 mistakes. Mastering these pronouns also unlocks the ability to contrast two people ('I am staying, you are going') and to add emphasis ('It was *you* who said that').

en.title: Reflexive pronouns in Italian
en.tip: Reflexive pronouns go with reflexive verbs to show that the subject is doing something to or for themselves — like getting dressed or washing yourself. Each subject pronoun has its own matching reflexive pronoun, and it usually comes directly before the verb.
en.explanation: ## The rule A reflexive pronoun is used when the action performed by the subject falls back onto that same subject. In other words, the subject and the object of the action are the same person. In Italian these pronouns always accompany a reflexive verb — a verb whose infinitive ends in -si (for example lavarsi, 'to wash oneself'; alzarsi, 'to get up'; chiamarsi, 'to be called'). The reflexive pronoun must **agree with the subject** — each person has one fixed form. In a normal statement the pronoun is placed **directly before the conjugated verb**. ## Forms | Subject pronoun | Reflexive pronoun | Meaning | |---|---|---| | io | mi | myself | | tu | ti | yourself | | lui / lei / Lei | si | himself / herself / yourself (formal) | | noi | ci | ourselves | | voi | vi | yourselves | | loro | si | themselves | ## How to form a sentence Take the infinitive (e.g. lavarsi), remove -si, conjugate the verb normally, and place the correct reflexive pronoun immediately before it. Full conjugation of lavarsi ('to wash oneself') in the present tense: | | | |---|---| | io mi lavo | I wash myself | | tu ti lavi | you wash yourself | | lui / lei si lava | he / she washes himself / herself | | noi ci laviamo | we wash ourselves | | voi vi lavate | you (plural) wash yourselves | | loro si lavano | they wash themselves | ## Examples Mi chiamo Marco. (My name is Marco. Literally: I call myself Marco.) — the most common reflexive phrase at A1 level. Mi alzo alle sette. (I get up at seven o'clock.) — alzarsi is a key verb for daily routines. Lei si veste in fretta. (She gets dressed quickly.) — note that si covers both 'himself' and 'herself'. Ci sediamo qui. (We sit down here.) — sedersi, 'to sit down', is another very common reflexive verb. Vi svegliate tardi la domenica? (Do you all wake up late on Sundays?) — reflexive pronoun in a question; position does not change. Contrastive pair — reflexive vs. non-reflexive: Lavo la macchina. (I wash the car.) — no reflexive pronoun; the action falls on an external object. Mi lavo. (I wash myself.) — reflexive pronoun required because the subject is washing themselves. ## Common mistakes **Omitting the pronoun.** Learners sometimes conjugate the verb but forget the pronoun entirely. This produces a grammatically incomplete or wrong sentence. Mistake: *Chiamo Marco. — this means 'I call Marco' (someone else named Marco), not 'my name is Marco'. Correct: Mi chiamo Marco. **Using the wrong pronoun for the subject.** Because the reflexive pronoun must match the subject, mixing them is a very common error. Mistake: *Lei mi lava. — this means 'she washes me', not 'she washes herself'. Correct: Lei si lava. **Placing the pronoun after the verb in a normal statement.** In a standard present-tense sentence the pronoun comes before the verb, not after it. Mistake: *Alzo mi alle sette. Correct: Mi alzo alle sette. **Confusing si with se.** The reflexive pronoun for third-person singular and plural is always si, never se (which is a conjunction meaning 'if'). Mistake: *Se chiama Anna. Correct: Si chiama Anna. (Her name is Anna.)
en.why_this_matters: Reflexive pronouns are everywhere in everyday Italian. Dozens of the most common verbs — getting up, getting dressed, washing, sitting down, being called — are reflexive verbs, and they cannot work at all without their matching reflexive pronoun. Without this rule you cannot say your name, describe your morning routine, or talk about how you feel.

en.title: Interrogative pronouns: chi, che, quanto, quale
en.tip: Italian has four main question pronouns: 'chi' (who), 'che' (what, for things), 'quale' (which one), and 'quanto' (how much/many). Each one covers a specific type of question, so choosing the right one depends on whether you are asking about a person, a thing, an identity, or a quantity.
en.explanation: ## The four interrogative pronouns Italian has four core interrogative pronouns. Unlike interrogative adjectives, which accompany a noun, interrogative pronouns stand alone in place of a noun — they replace it entirely. | Pronoun | Meaning | Refers to | |---|---|---| | chi | who / whom | people and animate beings only | | che | what | things only | | quale / quali | which one / which ones | people or things (asking for identity) | | quanto / quanta / quanti / quante | how much / how many | people or things (asking for quantity) | ## Chi — who, whom Use chi to ask about a person or animate being. It is invariable — it never changes its form, regardless of number or gender. It can function as the subject of the sentence ('who') or as the object ('whom'), including after a preposition ('to whom', 'with whom', 'for whom', etc.). As subject: Chi è quella ragazza? (Who is that girl?) As object: Chi cerchi? (Who are you looking for?) After a preposition: A chi parli? (Who are you talking to? / To whom are you talking?) Con chi vieni? (Who are you coming with?) Important: chi is always singular in form, even when the answer might be plural. The verb that follows agrees with the expected answer, not with chi itself — but in simple A1 questions this rarely causes difficulty. ## Che — what Use che to ask about things. Like chi, it is completely invariable. It cannot refer to people when used as an interrogative pronoun. Che dici? (What are you saying?) Che mangi stasera? (What are you eating tonight?) You will also see the longer form che cosa ('what thing') and the form cosa used alone. All three — che, che cosa, and cosa — mean 'what' and are interchangeable in everyday speech. Che cosa fai? = Cosa fai? = Che fai? (What are you doing?) ## Quale / Quali — which one, which ones Use quale (singular) or quali (plural) to ask someone to identify a specific person or thing from a set. It can refer to both people and things. Ho due fratelli. Quale preferisci? (I have two brothers. Which one do you prefer?) Ci sono molte pizze. Quali vuoi? (There are many pizzas. Which ones do you want?) Note: before the verb è (is), quale drops the final -e and becomes qual — no apostrophe is used: Qual è il tuo nome? (What is your name? / Which is your name?) — NOT *quale è and NOT *qual'è. ## Quanto / Quanta / Quanti / Quante — how much, how many Use quanto to ask about quantity or number. Unlike chi and che, quanto changes to agree in gender and number with the noun it replaces: | Form | Gender / Number | Example | |---|---|---| | quanto | masculine singular | Quanto costa? (How much does it cost?) | | quanta | feminine singular | Quanta ne vuoi? (How much of it do you want?) | | quanti | masculine plural | Quanti siete? (How many of you are there?) | | quante | feminine plural | Quante sono? (How many are there?) | ## Use as exclamatory pronouns All four pronouns can also be used in exclamations rather than questions. The form and meaning stay the same — only the context and punctuation change. Chi l'avrebbe detto! (Who would have thought it!) Quanti sono! (There are so many of them!) ## Examples covering the main uses 1. Chi è tua madre? — Who is your mother? (chi as subject, referring to a person) 2. A chi scrivi? — Who are you writing to? (chi after a preposition) 3. Che mangi a colazione? — What do you eat for breakfast? (che referring to a thing) 4. Qual è la tua borsa? — Which one is your bag? (quale asking for identity, with elision before è) 5. Quanti vengono alla festa? — How many people are coming to the party? (quanti, masculine plural, asking for number) 6. Contrastive pair — chi vs che: Chi hai incontrato? — Who did you meet? (a person) Che hai mangiato? — What did you eat? (a thing) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using che to ask about people** Incorrect: *Che è tuo padre? Correct: Chi è tuo padre? (Who is your father?) Remember: che refers only to things; chi refers only to people. **Mistake 2: Writing qual'è with an apostrophe** Incorrect: *Qual'è il problema? Correct: Qual è il problema? — no apostrophe. This is not an elision (vowel dropped); it is simply the standard short form of quale before è. **Mistake 3: Treating quanto as invariable** Incorrect: *Quanto persone vengono? Correct: Quante persone vengono? — persone is feminine plural, so quanto must become quante. **Mistake 4: Confusing quale (pronoun) with quale (adjective)** As a pronoun, quale stands alone: Quale preferisci? (Which one do you prefer?) As an adjective, it accompanies a noun: Quale pizza preferisci? (Which pizza do you prefer?) Both are correct — just make sure you are not omitting the noun by accident when you need the adjective form.
en.why_this_matters: Every conversation involves questions. Without interrogative pronouns — the words for 'who', 'what', 'which one', and 'how much' — you cannot ask who someone is, what they want, which option they prefer, or how many people are coming. These four pronouns appear in almost every exchange you will have in Italian, from greetings to shopping to making plans, so getting them right from the start saves you from constant confusion.

en.title: Saying 'nobody' and 'nothing' in Italian
en.tip: Use 'nessuno' for 'nobody/no one' and 'niente' for 'nothing'. When they come after the verb, you must also put 'non' before the verb — but never use both together before the verb.
en.explanation: ## The two pronouns **nessuno** means 'nobody,' 'no one,' or 'not anyone.' **niente** (also nulla, which is slightly more formal) means 'nothing' or 'not anything.' Both are **indefinite pronouns** — they refer to a person or thing in a completely unspecified, zero-quantity way. ## The double-negative rule Italian uses a double negative that English does not. The rule works like this: - If nessuno or niente comes **before** the verb, no non is needed. - If nessuno or niente comes **after** the verb, you **must** add non before the verb. This is not an error — it is correct, standard Italian grammar. ### Position before the verb (no 'non' needed) | Italian | English | |---|---| | Nessuno è a casa. | Nobody is home. | | Niente è pronto. | Nothing is ready. | ### Position after the verb ('non' required before the verb) | Italian | English | |---|---| | Non c'è nessuno a casa. | There is nobody home. | | Non ho niente. | I have nothing. | The second pattern (non + verb + nessuno/niente) is by far the more common word order in everyday Italian. You will see and hear it constantly. ## Examples **1.** Non c'è nessuno in cucina. (There is nobody in the kitchen.) — Everyday situation; nessuno follows the verb, so non is required. **2.** Nessuno mangia la verdura. (Nobody eats the vegetables.) — Nessuno is the subject before the verb; no non needed. **3.** Non ho niente da mangiare. (I have nothing to eat.) — Common daily-life sentence; double negative is correct and required. **4.** — Cosa c'è nel frigo? — Niente. (— What is in the fridge? — Nothing.) — As a one-word answer, niente stands alone with no verb, so no non is needed. **5.** Non conosco nessuno qui. (I don't know anyone here.) — Contrastive note: in English you switch to 'anyone' after a negative; in Italian you keep nessuno, not a separate word. **6.** Niente è difficile per lei. (Nothing is difficult for her.) — Niente as subject before the verb; no non needed. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Omitting non when the negative word follows the verb:** *Ho niente. ✗ Non ho niente. ✓ English speakers drop non because they think 'I have nothing' already contains one negative. In Italian, both are required. **Mistake 2 — Using non when the negative word is already before the verb:** *Non nessuno è a casa. ✗ Nessuno è a casa. ✓ When nessuno or niente leads the sentence, do not also add non. **Mistake 3 — Using 'anything' logic and choosing a different word:** Learners sometimes try to say 'I don't know anyone' by inventing a word like *qualcuno in a negative sentence. This is wrong. Italian keeps nessuno even in sentences that are already negative: Non conosco nessuno. ✓ **Mistake 4 — Confusing niente (pronoun) with nessuno (pronoun):** nessuno refers only to **people**; niente refers only to **things**. Do not swap them: Non vedo nessuno (I see nobody) vs. Non vedo niente (I see nothing). ## Quick-reference summary | Pronoun | Refers to | Before verb | After verb | |---|---|---|---| | nessuno | people | Nessuno viene. | Non viene nessuno. | | niente | things | Niente cambia. | Non cambia niente. |
en.why_this_matters: From your very first conversations in Italian, you will need to say things like 'Nobody is home' or 'I have nothing.' These two words — nessuno and niente — are among the most common indefinite pronouns in the language. Getting their position and double-negative rule right will immediately make your Italian sound natural and prevent one of the most persistent errors learners make.

en.title: Qualifying adjectives: forms and agreement
en.tip: Qualifying adjectives must match the noun they describe in both gender and number. Most adjectives have four forms ending in -o, -a, -i, -e. Always change the ending to match the noun.
en.explanation: ## What a qualifying adjective is A qualifying adjective (aggettivo qualificativo, 'quality adjective') is a word that describes a quality of a noun: its size, colour, character, or condition. In Italian, every adjective must accordarsi ('agree') with the noun it modifies — that is, it must take the same gender (masculine or feminine) and the same number (singular or plural) as that noun. ## The four-form adjective (-o type) Most Italian adjectives belong to the -o class. They have four distinct forms: | | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | Masculine | -o | -i | | Feminine | -a | -e | Take the adjective alto ('tall') as a model: | | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | Masculine | alto | alti | | Feminine | alta | alte | The same pattern applies to adjectives such as piccolo ('small'), nuovo ('new'), brutto ('ugly'), stanco ('tired'), buono ('good'), and cattivo ('bad'). ## The two-form adjective (-e type) A second group of adjectives ends in -e in the singular and -i in the plural. These adjectives have the same form for masculine and feminine: | | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | Masculine | -e | -i | | Feminine | -e | -i | Take grande ('big, great') as a model: | | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | Masculine | grande | grandi | | Feminine | grande | grandi | Other common adjectives of this type: felice ('happy'), triste ('sad'), verde ('green'), dolce ('sweet'), giovane ('young'), forte ('strong'). ## How adjectives agree with nouns The rule is simple: look at the noun, identify its gender and number, then choose the matching adjective ending. - A masculine singular noun takes an adjective in -o (or -e for the second group). - A feminine singular noun takes an adjective in -a (or -e for the second group). - A masculine plural noun takes an adjective in -i. - A feminine plural noun takes an adjective in -e (first group) or -i (second group). When an adjective modifies two or more nouns of different genders, use the masculine plural form: Marco e Maria sono stanchi. (Marco and Maria are tired.) ## Where the adjective goes In Italian, the qualifying adjective usually comes after the noun: un ragazzo alto ('a tall boy'), una pizza buona ('a good pizza'). This is the safe, default word order for A1 learners. Some very common adjectives — such as bello ('beautiful'), buono ('good'), grande ('great'), piccolo ('small'), and brutto ('ugly') — can also precede the noun without changing the essential meaning, though adjective-before-noun tends to sound more descriptive and adjective-after-noun tends to be more specific or contrastive. At A1, placing the adjective after the noun is always correct. ## Invariable adjectives (no ending change) A small but important group of adjectives never change their ending, regardless of the gender or number of the noun. The most common at A1 are certain colour adjectives: rosa ('pink'), blu ('blue'), viola ('violet'), lilla ('lilac'). These are called aggettivi invariabili ('invariable adjectives'): una scarpa rosa / due scarpe rosa / un fiore rosa / tre fiori rosa. ('a pink shoe / two pink shoes / a pink flower / three pink flowers') — the adjective stays rosa throughout. ## Examples 1. Il fratello è alto. — 'The brother is tall.' (masculine singular: alto) 2. La sorella è alta. — 'The sister is tall.' (feminine singular: alta) 3. I bambini sono stanchi. — 'The children are tired.' (masculine plural: stanchi) 4. Le ragazze sono felici. — 'The girls are happy.' (feminine plural, -e type adjective: felici — same form as masculine plural) 5. Contrastive pair — -o type vs -e type in the feminine: La pizza è buona e dolce. — 'The pizza is good and sweet.' (buona: feminine singular of buono, -o type; dolce: feminine singular of dolce, -e type — no change from masculine) 6. Invariable colour adjective: Ho una borsa blu e due scarpe blu. — 'I have a blue bag and two blue shoes.' (blu does not change) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — treating all adjectives as four-form:** Learners sometimes add an -a ending to a two-form adjective in the feminine: ✗ La ragazza è felica. ✓ La ragazza è felice. — 'The girl is happy.' Adjectives ending in -e do not change between masculine and feminine. Only the singular → plural change (-e → -i) applies. **Mistake 2 — forgetting to change the adjective at all:** Using the masculine singular form everywhere is a very frequent error: ✗ Le ragazze sono stanco. ✓ Le ragazze sono stanche. — 'The girls are tired.' (feminine plural: stanche) **Mistake 3 — changing invariable colour adjectives:** ✗ Ho due scarpe rosei. ✓ Ho due scarpe rosa. — 'I have two pink shoes.' (rosa never changes) Note: rosso ('red') is a regular four-form adjective (rosso, rossa, rossi, rosse) — do not confuse it with invariable rosa ('pink'). **Mistake 4 — mixed-gender nouns: using feminine plural:** ✗ Il papà e la mamma sono alte. ✓ Il papà e la mamma sono alti. — 'Dad and mum are tall.' (at least one masculine noun → use masculine plural adjective)
en.why_this_matters: Adjectives are everywhere in Italian. You need them to describe people, places, food, and feelings — the most basic things you want to say. Without knowing how to change the adjective ending to match the noun, almost every descriptive sentence you produce will contain an error. Master this rule and a huge part of Italian description becomes available to you immediately.
