en.title: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her…
en.tip: Possessive adjectives in Italian agree in gender and number with the thing owned, not the owner. They almost always appear with a definite article in front of them — except with singular, unmodified family members.
en.explanation: Possessive adjectives tell you who something belongs to. Italian has a full set of them, and they work quite differently from English ones — they must agree with the noun they describe, and they almost always travel with a definite article. Getting these right will let you talk about your family, your things, and your daily life from your very first conversations. ## The full set of forms Each possessive has four forms: masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural. The article in front agrees with the noun in gender and number in the normal way. | Person | Masc. sg. | Fem. sg. | Masc. pl. | Fem. pl. | |---|---|---|---|---| | I (my) | il mio | la mia | i miei | le mie | | you sg. (your) | il tuo | la tua | i tuoi | le tue | | he/she/it (his/her/its) | il suo | la sua | i suoi | le sue | | we (our) | il nostro | la nostra | i nostri | le nostre | | you pl. (your) | il vostro | la vostra | i vostri | le vostre | | they (their) | il loro | la loro | i loro | le loro | Notice that loro never changes its ending — only the article changes. All other possessives agree fully with the noun. ## The key rule: agreement follows the object, not the owner In English, 'his' or 'her' depends on the sex of the owner. In Italian, suo / sua / suoi / sue depends entirely on the gender and number of the thing owned. So 'his bag' and 'her bag' are both la sua borsa — because borsa (bag) is feminine. Context or earlier mention tells you whose it is. ## The article rule — and the big exception Italian possessive adjectives are almost always preceded by the appropriate definite article (il, la, i, le, etc.). **Exception — singular, unmodified family members:** When the noun is a singular family-member noun in its basic, unmodified form, the article is dropped. Family-member nouns that trigger this rule include: madre (mother), padre (father), sorella (sister), fratello (brother), figlia (daughter), figlio (son), moglie (wife), marito (husband), nonna (grandmother), nonno (grandfather), zia (aunt), zio (uncle). The article **stays** when any of the following is true: - the noun is **plural**: i miei fratelli (my brothers) - the possessive is **loro**: il loro padre (their father) - the noun has a **suffix** (diminutive, etc.): il mio fratellino (my little brother) - the noun is modified by an **adjective**: la mia cara sorella (my dear sister) ## Examples Dov'è il mio zaino? (Where is my backpack?) — article present; zaino is not a family noun. Questa è mia sorella. (This is my sister.) — no article; singular, unmodified family noun with mio/mia. Ho parlato con i miei genitori. (I spoke with my parents.) — article present because the noun is plural. Lui mangia a casa sua ogni sera. (He eats at his own home every evening.) — sua agrees with casa (feminine), not with 'he'. Come si chiama il loro cane? (What is their dog's name?) — article stays because the possessive is loro. La nostra scuola è grande. (Our school is big.) — nostra agrees with scuola (feminine singular). ## The special possessive 'proprio' The adjective proprio (one's own) can replace suo or loro when the possessive refers back to the subject of the same sentence. It is especially preferred when using suo or loro would be ambiguous, or when the subject is indefinite (e.g. ognuno — everyone, nessuno — no one). Compare these two sentences: Francesco parlò con Giuseppe, poi telefonò a sua sorella. (Francesco spoke with Giuseppe, then called his sister.) — Ambiguous: whose sister? Francesco parlò con Giuseppe, poi telefonò alla propria sorella. (Francesco spoke with Giuseppe, then called his own sister.) — Clear: Francesco's sister. With an indefinite subject: Ognuno ha il diritto di seguire la propria strada. (Everyone has the right to follow their own path.) Like all other possessives, proprio agrees in gender and number with the noun it modifies: proprio, propria, propri, proprie. ## The invariable 'altrui' Italian also has altrui (someone else's / other people's), which functions as a possessive adjective. It has only one form — it never changes for gender or number — and it usually follows the noun rather than preceding it: fare la volontà altrui (to do another's will); acconsentire agli altrui desideri (to agree to other people's wishes). At A1 level you mainly need to recognise it; active use comes later. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Agreeing with the owner instead of the object:** ❌ Maria ha perso il suo borsa. — wrong; borsa is feminine. ✅ Maria ha perso la sua borsa. (Maria lost her bag.) **Mistake 2 — Forgetting the article with non-family nouns:** ❌ Dov'è mio libro? ✅ Dov'è il mio libro? (Where is my book?) **Mistake 3 — Adding the article with singular, unmodified family nouns:** ❌ Questa è la mia madre. ✅ Questa è mia madre. (This is my mother.) **Mistake 4 — Changing loro to agree with the noun:** ❌ la lora casa / i lori libri — loro is invariable. ✅ la loro casa (their house), i loro libri (their books). **Mistake 5 — Translating 'his' / 'her' as different words:** ❌ Thinking that 'his book' and 'her book' use different Italian words. ✅ Both are il suo libro. The gender of the owner is irrelevant; only the noun matters.
en.why_this_matters: You will need possessive adjectives constantly — to say 'my bag', 'her mother', 'our house', 'their names'. Without them you cannot describe possession, relationships, or anything that belongs to someone. Because Italian possessives behave very differently from English ones (they agree with the object, not the owner; they carry an article; 'his' and 'her' are the same word), this is one of the rules where learners make the most errors — and getting it right early removes a huge source of confusion.

unistr_label: Aggettivi dimostrativi: questo, quello
label: Aggettivo dimostrativo questo e quello

en.title: Demonstrative adjectives: questo and quello
en.tip: Use 'questo' (this/these) for people or things close to you, and 'quello' (that/those) for people or things far away. Both adjectives must agree in gender and number with the noun they describe.
en.explanation: ## The core rule In Italian, demonstrative adjectives agree in **gender** (masculine or feminine) and **number** (singular or plural) with the noun they modify. The two main demonstrative adjectives are: - **questo** — 'this / these': points to someone or something **close to the speaker** - **quello** — 'that / those': points to someone or something **far from the speaker** ## Forms of questo The forms of questo follow the regular pattern of a first/second-declension adjective. Before a vowel, the singular forms questo and questa may drop their final vowel and add an apostrophe (quest'), though the full form is always acceptable too. | | Masculine | Feminine | |---|---|---| | Singular | questo | questa | | Plural | questi | queste | Before a vowel (optional elision): | | Masculine | Feminine | |---|---|---| | Singular before vowel | quest' | quest' | Example: quest'uomo (this man), quest'arancia (this orange). The plural forms questi and queste are **never** elided. ## Forms of quello The forms of quello follow the same pattern as the definite article (il, lo, la, i, gli, le). This is the trickiest part: the form changes depending on the first letter(s) of the noun that follows. | Context | Masculine Singular | Masculine Plural | Feminine Singular | Feminine Plural | |---|---|---|---|---| | before most consonants | quel | quei | quella | quelle | | before s+consonant, z, ps, gn, x, y | quello | quegli | quella | quelle | | before a vowel | quell' | quegli | quell' | quelle | A simple way to remember this: the form of quello before the noun mirrors whichever definite article (il → quel, lo → quello, l' → quell', i → quei, gli → quegli, la → quella, le → quelle) that noun would normally take. ## Examples **1. Pointing to something close vs. far away:** Questo libro è interessante. (This book is interesting. — the book is near the speaker.) Quel libro è interessante. (That book is interesting. — the book is far from the speaker.) **2. Feminine plural:** Queste scarpe sono nuove. (These shoes are new.) Quelle scarpe sono vecchie. (Those shoes are old.) **3. Elision of questo before a vowel:** Quest'arancia è buona. (This orange is good.) **4. quello before s+consonant:** Quello studente è bravo. (That student is good.) — note quello, not quel, because studente begins with st-. **5. Referring back to something already mentioned:** Ho un gatto. Questo gatto si chiama Micio. (I have a cat. This cat is called Micio.) — questo here refers back to the cat just mentioned. **6. Contrastive pair (near vs. far, masculine plural):** Questi ragazzi sono italiani, quei ragazzi sono francesi. (These boys are Italian, those boys are French.) ## A note on codesto The textbook lists a third demonstrative, codesto, which historically pointed to something near the **listener** ('that near you'). In modern standard Italian it is virtually obsolete — you will only hear it in Tuscany. In everyday speech, Italians use either questo or quello to cover all situations, relying on context or a pointing gesture to make the distance clear. You do not need to use codesto at this level. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Using quello instead of quel / quell':** *Quello libro è mio. ✗ — libro begins with a plain consonant, so the correct form is quel libro ✓. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting gender/number agreement:** *Questo ragazza è simpatica. ✗ — ragazza is feminine, so the correct form is questa ragazza ✓. **Mistake 3 — Eliding the plural:** *Quest'amici sono gentili. ✗ — Elision only applies in the singular. The correct form is questi amici ✓. **Mistake 4 — Using quegli before an ordinary consonant:** *Quegli ragazzi giocano. ✗ — quegli is reserved for nouns starting with a vowel or s+consonant, z, etc. The correct form is quei ragazzi ✓.
en.why_this_matters: Every time you point something out — 'this book', 'that table', 'these shoes', 'those people' — you need a demonstrative adjective. Without them you cannot distinguish between what is near and what is far, or refer back to something already mentioned in conversation. These two words appear in almost every Italian exchange, so getting their forms right early removes a persistent source of errors.

unistr_label: Aggettivi interrogativi: che, quanto
label: Aggettivo interrogativo che e quanto

en.title: Asking questions with 'che' and 'quanto'
en.tip: Use 'che' before a noun to ask 'what?' or 'which?' — it never changes its form. Use 'quanto' to ask 'how much?' or 'how many?' — it must agree in gender and number with the noun it describes.
en.explanation: ## The interrogative adjectives: what they are and how they work Interrogative adjectives (aggettivi interrogativi, literally 'asking adjectives') are placed directly before a noun to ask a question about it. Italian has three: che, quale, and quanto. This entry focuses on che and quanto, the two introduced at A1. ## 'Che' — what / which Che means 'what' or 'which' when placed before a noun. Its most important feature is that it is **invariable** — it has one single form for masculine, feminine, singular, and plural. It never changes. It works exactly like quale in questions with a noun: che giorno? and quale giorno? both mean 'which day?' and are fully interchangeable in this context. **Important exception — exclamations:** Che can also be used as an exclamative adjective (expressing surprise or emotion) before **another adjective**. In this use, quale cannot replace it. For example, you can say Che bello! ('How beautiful!'), but *Quale bello! is incorrect. **The phrase che cosa:** When asking 'what?' without a following noun, Italian often uses che cosa (literally 'what thing'). In everyday speech, che can be dropped and you can simply say cosa. All three forms — che cosa, che, and cosa — are correct and common. ## 'Quanto' — how much / how many Quanto means 'how much' (with uncountable nouns) or 'how many' (with countable nouns). Unlike che, it is **variable** — it must agree in gender and number with the noun it modifies, exactly like a regular adjective. Here are its four forms: | | Masculine | Feminine | |---|---|---| | **Singular** | quanto | quanta | | **Plural** | quanti | quante | Use the singular with uncountable nouns (things you cannot count individually, like water or time) and the plural with countable nouns. ## Examples Che libro leggi? — 'Which book are you reading?' (che + singular masculine noun; invariable) Che lingue parli? — 'What languages do you speak?' (che + plural feminine noun; still invariable — no change) Che bella giornata! — 'What a beautiful day!' (che as exclamative adjective before another adjective; quale could not replace it here) Quanto zucchero vuoi? — 'How much sugar do you want?' (quanto + singular masculine uncountable noun) Quante sorelle hai? — 'How many sisters do you have?' (quante + plural feminine noun — agreement is required) Dimmi cosa vuoi. — 'Tell me what you want.' (cosa used alone in an indirect question; che cosa or che would also be correct) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Changing che to agree with the noun:** Learners sometimes write *chi libro or try to make che plural. Remember: che is always che, regardless of the noun. Correct form: che libro, che libri, che pizza, che pizze — always the same. **Mistake 2 — Not changing quanto to agree with the noun:** Because che is invariable, learners sometimes treat quanto the same way. This is wrong. *Quanto sorelle hai? is incorrect. The noun sorelle is feminine and plural, so the correct form is Quante sorelle hai? **Mistake 3 — Using quale in exclamations before an adjective:** *Quale bello! is not Italian. Only che can introduce an exclamation before a bare adjective: Che bello!, Che buono!, Che strano! **Mistake 4 — Thinking only che cosa is correct:** All three forms — che cosa, che, and cosa — are equally acceptable when asking or saying 'what'. Do not hesitate to use cosa alone in conversation; it is not informal or incorrect.
en.why_this_matters: Two of the most basic things you need to do in Italian are ask questions and express surprise — and both depend on a small set of adjectives that appear constantly in everyday conversation. Without che and quanto, you cannot ask 'what time is it?', 'which pizza do you want?', or 'how many brothers do you have?' Mastering these two words immediately unlocks dozens of essential questions and exclamations.

unistr_label: Aggettivi indefiniti: poco, molto, tanto
label: Aggettivo indefinito poco, molto, tanto

en.title: Indefinite adjectives: poco, molto, tanto
en.tip: The adjectives poco, molto, and tanto tell you how much or how many of something there is. They must agree in gender and number with the noun they describe, just like regular adjectives.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what these adjectives mean The adjectives poco, molto, and tanto are called aggettivi indefiniti (indefinite adjectives). They go directly before a noun and express a vague, non-exact idea of quantity or degree: - poco — little, few, not much, not many - molto — much, many, a lot of - tanto — so much, so many; (without a correlating word) also equivalent to molto (a lot of) ## Formation: agreement with the noun All three adjectives follow the standard four-form pattern of Italian adjectives ending in -o. They must agree with the gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural) of the noun they modify. | | Masculine singular | Feminine singular | Masculine plural | Feminine plural | |---|---|---|---|---| | | poco | poca | pochi | poche | | | molto | molta | molti | molte | | | tanto | tanta | tanti | tante | Notice that the masculine plural forms of poco are pochi / poche — the -h- is added to keep the hard c sound, exactly as with adjectives like bianco → bianchi. ## Position: always before the noun As indefinite adjectives, poco, molto, and tanto must come directly before the noun they modify. Placing them after the noun changes their function or makes the sentence ungrammatical in this context. ## A note on tanto According to Italian grammar, tanto has a specific meaning of 'so much / so many' when it is used in a correlation with che (that) or quanto (as): for example, Ha tanti amici che non li ricorda tutti (He has so many friends that he cannot remember them all). Without this correlation, tanto is simply equivalent to molto and means 'a lot of'. At A1 level, you will mostly encounter tanto in this second, simpler sense. ## Examples Ho poca acqua. (I have little water.) — feminine singular noun, feminine singular form poca. Ci sono pochi studenti in classe oggi. (There are few students in class today.) — masculine plural noun, masculine plural form pochi. Mia madre ha molta pazienza. (My mother has a lot of patience.) — feminine singular noun, feminine singular form molta. Marco ha molti libri. (Marco has many books.) — masculine plural noun, masculine plural form molti. Ho tanto tempo libero. (I have a lot of free time.) — masculine singular noun, masculine singular form tanto; here tanto simply means 'a lot of'. Giorgio ha tanti soldi che non sa cosa farci. (Giorgio has so much money that he does not know what to do with it.) — edge case: tanto in correlation with che, meaning 'so many'. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — not agreeing the adjective with the noun:** Incorrect: *Ho molto amiche. Correct: Ho molte amiche. (I have many friends [female].) The noun amiche is feminine plural, so the adjective must also be feminine plural: molte, not molto. **Mistake 2 — forgetting the -h- in the plural of poco:** Incorrect: *poci studenti or *poce ragazze Correct: pochi studenti (few students), poche ragazze (few girls). The -h- preserves the hard c sound before -i and -e. **Mistake 3 — using molto as an adverb but keeping adjective agreement rules confused:** Note that molto, poco, and tanto can also work as adverbs modifying a verb or another adjective (e.g. Mangio molto — I eat a lot). When used as adverbs, they do not change form. This entry covers only their use as adjectives before a noun, where agreement is required. **Mistake 4 — placing the adjective after the noun:** Incorrect: *Ho tempo molto. Correct: Ho molto tempo. (I have a lot of time.) As indefinite adjectives, these words must precede the noun.
en.why_this_matters: These three words appear in almost every Italian conversation — you need them to say things like 'a little water', 'many friends', or 'so much time'. Without them, you cannot talk about quantities in everyday situations such as ordering food, describing your family, or explaining your daily routine. Getting their forms right also builds the habit of adjective agreement, which is one of the most important skills in Italian grammar.

unistr_label: Aggettivi numerali cardinali: da 1 a 100
label: Aggettivi numerali cardinali da uno a cento

en.title: Cardinal numbers: one to one hundred
en.tip: Cardinal numbers in Italian almost never change form — only 'uno' (one) has a feminine form, 'una'. All other cardinal numbers stay the same regardless of the gender or number of the noun they describe.
en.explanation: ## What cardinal numbers are I numerali cardinali (cardinal numbers) are the ordinary counting numbers: uno, due, tre... They answer the question 'how many?' They can be used before a noun like an adjective, or on their own as a number. ## The core rule: cardinal numbers are invariable With one important exception, all Italian cardinal numbers are **invariable** — they do not change for grammatical gender (masculine/feminine) or number (singular/plural). The same form is used with masculine and feminine nouns alike. > diciotto ragazzi — eighteen boys > diciotto ragazze — eighteen girls The number stays diciotto in both cases. ## The one exception: uno / una Uno (one) has a feminine form una. Use uno before masculine nouns and una before feminine nouns. > un fratello — one brother (masculine) > una sorella — one sister (feminine) Note: before a masculine noun beginning with a vowel or z, the form is uno: uno zaino (one backpack), uno studente (one student). Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel, una shortens to un': un'amica (one friend, female). ## The numbers from 1 to 100 | Numeral | Italian | | Numeral | Italian | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | uno / una | | 11 | undici | | 2 | due | | 12 | dodici | | 3 | tre | | 13 | tredici | | 4 | quattro | | 14 | quattordici | | 5 | cinque | | 15 | quindici | | 6 | sei | | 16 | sedici | | 7 | sette | | 17 | diciassette | | 8 | otto | | 18 | diciotto | | 9 | nove | | 19 | diciannove | | 10 | dieci | | 20 | venti | | Numeral | Italian | | Numeral | Italian | |---|---|---|---|---| | 20 | venti | | 60 | sessanta | | 30 | trenta | | 70 | settanta | | 40 | quaranta | | 80 | ottanta | | 50 | cinquanta | | 90 | novanta | | 100 | cento | | | | ## How compound numbers (21–99) are formed Compound numbers are built by joining the tens form and the units form into a single word. **Key spelling rules for compounds:** 1. When the units digit is uno or otto, drop the final vowel of the tens word before adding the units: venti + uno → ventuno, venti + otto → ventotto, trenta + uno → trentuno, trenta + otto → trentotto, and so on through all the tens. 2. In all other cases, simply join the two parts with no change: venti + due → ventidue, trenta + tre → trentatré (note the written accent on tré when it ends a compound number). 3. The feminine rule for uno carries through to compounds: ventuno studenti (masculine), ventuna studentesse (feminine). ### Selected compound examples | Numeral | Italian | |---|---| | 21 | ventuno | | 22 | ventidue | | 23 | ventitrè | | 28 | ventotto | | 31 | trentuno | | 33 | trentatré | | 38 | trentotto | | 44 | quarantaquattro | | 55 | cinquantacinque | | 68 | sessantotto | | 81 | ottantuno | | 99 | novantanove | ## Examples in context 1. Ho due fratelli e una sorella. — I have two brothers and one sister. *(due is invariable; una is feminine because sorella is feminine.)* 2. La classe ha ventidue studenti. — The class has twenty-two students. *(ventidue does not change.)* 3. Ho trentun anni. — I am thirty-one years old. *(trentuno drops the final -o before a noun beginning with a consonant; the full form trentuno is also widely accepted.)* 4. Il negozio apre alle otto. — The shop opens at eight. *(Used on its own without a noun — cardinal numbers work independently too.)* 5. Ci sono cinquanta ragazzi e cinquanta ragazze. — There are fifty boys and fifty girls. *(Contrastive pair: the same form cinquanta is used with both masculine and feminine nouns.)* 6. Ventotto studentesse sono in aula. — Twenty-eight female students are in the classroom. *(Ventotto — the tens vowel is dropped before otto — and the number is still invariable despite the feminine noun.)* ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Changing the number to match gender:** *due fratelli / *duei fratelli / *due sorelle → duE sorelle — wrong; the correct form is just due sorelle. Only uno/una changes. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting the feminine of uno:** *Ho uno sorella. — incorrect. Correct: Ho una sorella. Always use una (or un' before a vowel) with feminine nouns. **Mistake 3 — Not dropping the vowel before uno or otto in compounds:** *ventiuno, *ventiotto — incorrect spellings. Correct: ventuno, ventotto. **Mistake 4 — Forgetting the accent on trè in compounds:** *ventitre — missing accent. Correct written form: ventitrè. **Mistake 5 — Writing numbers as digits in ordinary prose:** In normal written Italian, numbers are preferred in full letters except for dates, technical contexts, and proper names: write ventidue alunni, not 22 alunni, in a standard sentence.
en.why_this_matters: Numbers are everywhere in Italian — telling the time, shopping, giving your age, counting people in a family. Without cardinal numbers you cannot handle the most basic everyday transactions. Because Italian numbers work differently from English in a few important ways (especially the single irregular form uno/una), learning the rule precisely now will save you from a persistent error that appears even at advanced levels.

unistr_label: Aggettivi numerali ordinali da primo a decimo Nota: principalmente prima singolare con i nomi di famiglia
label: Aggettivi numerali ordinali da primo a decimo

en.title: Ordinal numbers: primo to decimo
en.tip: Ordinal numbers (first, second, third…) tell you the position of something in a sequence. Unlike most cardinal numbers, they change their ending to match the noun they describe — just like regular adjectives.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what ordinal numbers are Ordinal numbers — called numerali ordinali (ordinal numerals) in Italian — answer the question 'which one in a series?' They correspond to English 'first', 'second', 'third', and so on. In Italian, they are adjectives, so they must agree in gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural) with the noun they modify. This is different from cardinal numbers like due or tre, which never change their form. ## The ten forms: primo to decimo Here are the ten ordinals with their four possible endings. The masculine singular form is the base form you should memorise first. | Cardinal | Masc. sg. | Fem. sg. | Masc. pl. | Fem. pl. | English | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | uno | primo | prima | primi | prime | first | | due | secondo | seconda | secondi | seconde | second | | tre | terzo | terza | terzi | terze | third | | quattro | quarto | quarta | quarti | quarte | fourth | | cinque | quinto | quinta | quinti | quinte | fifth | | sei | sesto | sesta | sesti | seste | sixth | | sette | settimo | settima | settimi | settime | seventh | | otto | ottavo | ottava | ottavi | ottave | eighth | | nove | nono | nona | noni | none | ninth | | dieci | decimo | decima | decimi | decime | tenth | ## How agreement works Treat ordinal numbers exactly like a regular adjective ending in -o (like rosso, red). Choose the ending that matches the noun: - masculine singular → -o (e.g. il primo giorno, the first day) - feminine singular → -a (e.g. la prima lezione, the first lesson) - masculine plural → -i (e.g. i primi giorni, the first days) - feminine plural → -e (e.g. le prime lezioni, the first lessons) ## Examples Abito al terzo piano. (I live on the third floor.) — masculine singular, agreeing with piano (floor, masc.). Oggi è la mia prima lezione di italiano. (Today is my first Italian lesson.) — feminine singular, agreeing with lezione (lesson, fem.). Marco arriva secondo e Luca arriva quinto. (Marco comes second and Luca comes fifth.) — both masculine singular, used without a noun after a verb. La quinta porta a sinistra è la cucina. (The fifth door on the left is the kitchen.) — feminine singular, agreeing with porta (door, fem.). I primi giorni di scuola sono difficili. (The first days of school are difficult.) — masculine plural, agreeing with giorni (days, masc.). Contrastive pair — ordinal vs. cardinal: Ho due sorelle (I have two sisters) uses the invariable cardinal due. But la mia seconda sorella (my second sister) uses the ordinal seconda, which agrees with the feminine noun sorella. ## Position in the sentence Ordinal numbers almost always come before the noun, just like in English: il primo caffè della mattina (the first coffee of the morning). They can also follow a verb directly — sono arrivato terzo (I arrived third) — where they still agree with the subject. ## Writing ordinals: words vs. symbols In normal writing, Italian prefers the word form: il terzo capitolo (the third chapter) is preferred over il 3° capitolo. Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV…) are used for popes, kings, and centuries: Giovanni Paolo II, il XX secolo. At A1 level, simply focus on knowing and using the word form. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — treating ordinals as invariable like cardinals:** Learners sometimes write *la primo lezione* by analogy with cardinals, which never change. Correction: ordinals always agree, so the correct form is la prima lezione. **Mistake 2 — using a cardinal where an ordinal is needed:** Saying *abito al tre piano* (using the cardinal tre) instead of abito al terzo piano (using the ordinal terzo) is a very common error, especially for floors of a building and numbered sequences. **Mistake 3 — wrong ending on a feminine noun:** Writing *la quinto strada* instead of la quinta strada (the fifth street). Always check the gender of the noun and choose the matching -o / -a / -i / -e ending. **Mistake 4 — forgetting the article:** In Italian, ordinal numbers used with a noun almost always require the definite article: il primo giorno, not *primo giorno* (unless in a title or heading). This is different from English, which sometimes drops 'the' ('first day of school').
en.why_this_matters: Ordinal numbers come up constantly in everyday Italian — telling someone you live on the third floor, talking about the first day of school, or describing the second street on the left. Without them, you cannot place things in order or talk about sequences, rankings, or positions. Mastering these ten forms also gives you the pattern you need to build every higher ordinal number later.

en.title: Definite and indefinite articles in Italian
en.tip: Every Italian noun needs an article, and the article must match the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural). The definite article ('the') points to something specific and known; the indefinite article ('a / an') introduces something new or unspecified.
en.explanation: Every Italian noun needs an article, and the article must match the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural). The definite article points to something specific and known; the indefinite article introduces something new or unspecified. ## What an article does The article (l'articolo, literally 'the article') is the small word placed directly before a noun. It tells the listener two things at once: whether the noun is specific and already known (definite) or general and newly introduced (indefinite), and whether the noun is masculine or feminine, singular or plural. ## The definite article — 'the' Use the definite article (l'articolo determinativo) when both speaker and listener know exactly which person or thing is meant — because it has already been mentioned, because there is only one of it, or because it is being discussed as a category in general. The form of the definite article changes depending on the gender and number of the noun that follows it, and also on the first sound of that noun. | Gender & number | Starts with… | Article | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Masculine singular | most consonants | il | il libro (the book) | | Masculine singular | s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y | lo | lo studente (the student) | | Masculine singular | any vowel | l' | l'amico (the friend) | | Masculine plural | most consonants | i | i libri (the books) | | Masculine plural | s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y, vowel | gli | gli studenti (the students) | | Feminine singular | any consonant | la | la madre (the mother) | | Feminine singular | any vowel | l' | l'amica (the female friend) | | Feminine plural | any sound | le | le madri (the mothers) | ## The indefinite article — 'a / an' Use the indefinite article (l'articolo indeterminativo) when you are introducing a noun for the first time, when you are talking about one unspecified example of something, or when you mean 'a certain kind of thing'. The indefinite article only has singular forms in Italian — to express 'some' in the plural, Italian uses the partitive article (del, della, dei, etc.), which is covered in a separate entry. | Gender | Starts with… | Article | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Masculine | most consonants or any vowel | un | un caffè (a coffee) | | Masculine | s + consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y | uno | uno zaino (a backpack) | | Feminine | any consonant | una | una pizza (a pizza) | | Feminine | any vowel | un' | un'arancia (an orange) | Notice that the masculine un does not add an apostrophe before a vowel (un amico, not *un'amico), while the feminine una always drops its final vowel and adds an apostrophe before a vowel (un'amica). ## When each article is used Use the definite article when: - the noun has already been mentioned or is clearly identified: Ho un cane. Il cane si chiama Leo. (I have a dog. The dog is called Leo.) - you refer to something as a whole category: Mi piace la pasta. (I like pasta — pasta in general.) - there is only one of the thing: Il sole è grande. (The sun is big.) Use the indefinite article when: - you introduce something for the first time: Ho un cane. (I have a dog — introducing it.) - you mean 'one of many', not a specific item: Vorrei una mela. (I would like an apple — any apple.) ## Examples Il bambino mangia la pizza. (The child is eating the pizza. — both are specific and known.) Ho una sorella e un fratello. (I have a sister and a brother. — introducing family members for the first time.) L'acqua è fredda. (The water is cold. — a specific glass of water already in view, or water as a substance in general.) Gli studenti sono in classe. (The students are in class. — a specific known group.) Voglio un caffè, per favore. (I want a coffee, please. — one unspecified coffee.) Mi piace il caffè. vs. Voglio un caffè. (I like coffee — coffee in general / I want a coffee — one specific cup. This contrast is crucial.) ## Common learner mistakes Mistake 1 — Omitting the article: English sometimes drops the article ('I like coffee', 'She is a teacher'), but Italian almost always requires one. Do not write *Mi piace caffè; write Mi piace il caffè. Mistake 2 — Wrong gender: *il problema looks masculine because problema ends in -a, but it is actually masculine (from Greek): il problema is correct. Always learn the article together with each new noun. Mistake 3 — Using il instead of lo: Before s + consonant or z, masculine singular nouns take lo, not il. Write lo zaino, not *il zaino. Mistake 4 — Apostrophe on masculine un: Only the feminine una takes an apostrophe before a vowel. The masculine form stays un without an apostrophe: un uomo (a man), never *un'uomo. Mistake 5 — Definite where indefinite is needed: Saying *Ho il gatto to introduce a pet for the first time sounds as if the listener already knows the cat. Use Ho un gatto (I have a cat) to introduce it.
en.why_this_matters: Articles appear in front of almost every noun in Italian, so you will meet them in the very first sentences you read or hear. Getting them right is not optional: the wrong article — or a missing one — makes a sentence sound ungrammatical to a native speaker. Mastering articles also forces you to learn the gender of every new noun, which unlocks agreement with adjectives and past-tense verbs later on.

en.title: Telling the time with the definite article
en.tip: In Italian, you always use a definite article — 'la' or 'le' — when saying what time it is. Without the article, a time expression sounds incomplete or wrong to a native speaker.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what article to use and when Italian treats each hour as a feminine noun. The hours are thought of as le ore (the hours), which is feminine plural. This is why the article is always feminine. Use l'una (the one) for 1:00, because una is singular — it uses the singular elided form l'. Use le + the number for every other hour (2:00 through 12:00 / midnight / noon), because all other numbers are plural. The verb used to express the time is essere (to be), and it must agree with the article: - È l'una. — singular verb è - Sono le due. — plural verb sono ## Full paradigm of the hours | Time | Italiano | |---|---| | 1:00 | È l'una. | | 2:00 | Sono le due. | | 3:00 | Sono le tre. | | 4:00 | Sono le quattro. | | 5:00 | Sono le cinque. | | 6:00 | Sono le sei. | | 7:00 | Sono le sette. | | 8:00 | Sono le otto. | | 9:00 | Sono le nove. | | 10:00 | Sono le dieci. | | 11:00 | Sono le undici. | | 12:00 (noon) | È mezzogiorno. | | 12:00 (midnight) | È mezzanotte. | Note: mezzogiorno (noon) and mezzanotte (midnight) are masculine and feminine nouns respectively, used without any article. ## Adding minutes To say minutes past the hour, add e (and) followed by the minutes: Sono le tre e venti. — It is twenty past three. For a quarter past, use e un quarto (and a quarter): Sono le otto e un quarto. — It is a quarter past eight. For half past, use e mezza or e mezzo (and a half — both forms are acceptable): Sono le sei e mezza. — It is half past six. For minutes to the hour, use meno (minus/less) followed by the minutes: Sono le cinque meno dieci. — It is ten to five (literally: five minus ten). For a quarter to, use meno un quarto: È l'una meno un quarto. — It is a quarter to one. ## Asking and answering 'What time is it?' The standard question is: Che ora è? or Che ore sono? — What time is it? Both forms are correct and very common. Che ore sono? (plural) is slightly more frequent in everyday speech. ## Saying 'at' a particular time To say something happens at a certain time, replace è / sono with the preposition a (at), which combines with the article: - a + l' → all': all'una (at one o'clock) - a + le → alle: alle tre (at three o'clock) The article is still required here — it just merges with a. ## Examples — Che ore sono? — Sono le sette. (— What time is it? — It is seven o'clock.) La scuola inizia alle otto e mezza. (School starts at half past eight.) Mangiamo all'una. (We eat at one o'clock.) Il treno parte alle nove e un quarto. (The train leaves at a quarter past nine.) — A che ora finisce il film? — Alle undici meno venti. (— At what time does the film end? — At twenty to eleven.) Il negozio chiude a mezzogiorno. (The shop closes at noon.) — Note: no article with mezzogiorno. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — omitting the article:** ❌ Sono tre. ✅ Sono le tre. The article is never optional. Dropping it sounds ungrammatical. **Mistake 2 — using è instead of sono for hours other than one:** ❌ È le due. ✅ Sono le due. Because le due is plural, the verb must be plural too. Only l'una, mezzogiorno, and mezzanotte use è. **Mistake 3 — forgetting that a contracts with the article:** ❌ a le cinque ✅ alle cinque ❌ a l'una ✅ all'una The preposition a always combines with the article — it never stands alone before a time. **Mistake 4 — adding an article before mezzogiorno or mezzanotte:** ❌ Sono le mezzogiorno. ✅ È mezzogiorno. These two words stand alone — they never take an article.
en.why_this_matters: Telling the time is one of the first practical tasks you face in Italian, and it works differently from English. Every time expression in Italian requires a definite article — la or le — in front of the number. Without it, sentences like 'Sono le tre' ('It is three o'clock') cannot be formed correctly. Mastering this small rule means you can immediately ask and answer questions about schedules, appointments, meals, and daily routines.

en.title: When to drop the definite article
en.tip: Italian normally uses definite articles before nouns, but there are important exceptions. Learning the main cases — family members with possessives, most city names, and titles before names — will help you sound natural from the very beginning.
en.explanation: ## The core rule Italian uses the definite article before most nouns, but omits it in several specific, predictable situations. The most important ones for beginners are family-member nouns combined with possessive adjectives, most city names, and personal names preceded by a title. Each case has its own logic — learn the pattern, not just a list. ## Case 1: Family members with possessive adjectives When a noun referring to a family member — padre ('father'), madre ('mother'), fratello ('brother'), sorella ('sister'), zio ('uncle'), zia ('aunt'), nonno ('grandfather'), cugino ('cousin') — is preceded by a possessive adjective (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro), the definite article is normally dropped. **Formation without article:** possessive adjective + family noun | Con articolo (SBAGLIATO) | Senza articolo (GIUSTO) | English | |---|---|---| | *il mio padre | mio padre | my father | | *la tua sorella | tua sorella | your sister | | *il suo fratello | suo fratello | his/her brother | | *la nostra zia | nostra zia | our aunt | ### Exceptions — when the article comes back The article **must** be used with family nouns in the following situations: **1. Plural family nouns always keep the article:** i miei nonni (my grandparents) — NOT *miei nonni i nostri cugini (our cousins) — NOT *nostri cugini le tue sorelle (your sisters) — NOT *tue sorelle **2. When the family noun has a descriptive adjective or modifier:** il nostro caro zio (our dear uncle) la mia sorella maggiore (my older sister) **3. When the noun is a diminutive or altered form (a word with a suffix like -ino/-etta):** la mia cuginetta (my little/dear cousin) **4. Mamma ('mum') and papà ('dad') always keep the article:** la mia mamma (my mum) — NOT *mia mamma il tuo papà (your dad) — NOT *tuo papà **5. With the third-person plural possessive loro, the article is always kept even in the singular:** il loro padre (their father) ## Case 2: City names Most Italian city names take **no** article: Roma è bella. (Rome is beautiful.) Abito a Milano. (I live in Milan.) However, a small number of city names include the article as a fixed part of the name itself. These must always be written with the article and a capital letter: | Città | English | |---|---| | L'Aquila | L'Aquila | | La Spezia | La Spezia | | Il Cairo | Cairo | | L'Aia | The Hague | | La Valletta | Valletta | Additionally, when **any** city name is accompanied by an adjective or a descriptive phrase, the article is required: la bella Napoli (beautiful Naples) la Roma dei papi (the Rome of the popes) ## Case 3: Surnames (family names) Italian has specific rules about using articles before surnames (cognomi): - **Masculine surnames:** In modern everyday Italian, the article is generally **not** used before a man's surname: Rossi abita qui. Using the article (il Rossi) is an older or more literary style, sometimes still seen with famous historical figures like il Petrarca or il Leopardi, but this usage is declining. - **Feminine surnames:** The article **is** used before a woman's surname, whether she is famous or not: la Callas, la Bianchi. - **Surnames referring to a whole family (plural):** The article is always used: i De Filippo, gli Alberti. ## Case 4: Titles before a name When a title (professore, dottore, signora, segretaria, etc.) appears directly before a person's name, the definite article is **required** before the title: il professor Rossi (Professor Rossi) la signora Bianchi (Mrs Bianchi) la segretaria Carla (the secretary Carla) **Exception:** A small group of traditional titles take **no** article. Learn these as fixed expressions: | Titolo | Meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | don | Don (clerical/respectful title) | don Giovanni | | mastro | Master (craftsman title) | mastro Geppetto | | fra | Brother (religious title) | fra Galdino | ## Examples in context 1. Mia madre lavora a Roma. (My mother works in Rome.) — No article before madre (singular family noun + possessive) and no article before Roma (city name). 2. I miei nonni abitano a La Spezia. (My grandparents live in La Spezia.) — Article required: nonni is plural, and La Spezia is one of the fixed city names. 3. Il professor Marini è gentile. (Professor Marini is kind.) — Article required before a title + name. 4. La mia mamma si chiama Anna. (My mum's name is Anna.) — Article required with mamma even though it is singular. 5. Ho uno zio simpatico, ma il mio caro zio Luca abita lontano. (I have a funny uncle, but my dear uncle Luca lives far away.) — The second example has an adjective (caro), so the article is required. 6. Conosci la Bianchi? — Sì, don Carlo la conosce bene. (Do you know Ms Bianchi? — Yes, Father Carlo knows her well.) — Article before a woman's surname; no article after the title don. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1:** Adding an article before a singular family noun with a possessive. *Il mio fratello è alto. ✗ → Mio fratello è alto. ✓ (My brother is tall.) **Mistake 2:** Forgetting the article when the family noun is plural. *Miei genitori sono a casa. ✗ → I miei genitori sono a casa. ✓ (My parents are at home.) **Mistake 3:** Treating mamma and papà like other family nouns and dropping the article. *Mia mamma cucina bene. ✗ → La mia mamma cucina bene. ✓ (My mum cooks well.) **Mistake 4:** Adding an article before a title that belongs to the no-article group. *Il don Giovanni è famoso. ✗ → Don Giovanni è famoso. ✓ **Mistake 5:** Omitting the article before a title in the general rule. *Professor Rossi spiega bene. ✗ → Il professor Rossi spiega bene. ✓ (Professor Rossi explains well.) **Mistake 6:** Dropping the article before a city name that contains it as a fixed part. *Abito ad Aquila. ✗ → Abito all'Aquila. ✓ (I live in L'Aquila.)
en.why_this_matters: Definite articles — il, lo, la, i, gli, le ('the') — appear constantly in Italian, far more often than in English. But certain very common situations call for no article at all, and getting this wrong is one of the most frequent mistakes learners make. Knowing exactly when to drop the article will make your Italian sound immediately more natural in everyday conversations about family, people's names, and places.

en.title: When to leave out the definite article
en.tip: Some words in Italian — especially possessives with family members, certain titles, and some place names — never take a definite article. Learning exactly where to drop 'il/la/i/le' removes one of the most frequent beginner mistakes.
en.explanation: ## The core rule In Italian the definite article is normally required before nouns. However, it is **omitted** in a number of specific, predictable cases. The most important ones for beginners are listed below. ## 1. Family members after a possessive adjective (singular only) When a **singular, unmodified** family noun follows a possessive adjective (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro), the definite article is dropped. | With article (wrong) | Without article (correct) | English | |---|---|---| | *il mio padre* | mio padre | my father | | *la tua sorella* | tua sorella | your sister | | *il suo fratello* | suo fratello | his/her brother | | *la nostra nonna* | nostra nonna | our grandmother | ### Exceptions — the article stays in four cases **a) Plural family nouns** always keep the article: i miei nonni (my grandparents), le tue sorelle (your sisters). **b) A modified family noun** (one with an adjective or other word added) keeps the article: il nostro caro zio (our dear uncle). **c) Diminutives and altered forms** keep the article: la mia cuginetta (my little cousin). **d)** Mamma (mum) and papà (dad) **always** keep the article even in the singular: la mia mamma, il tuo papà. ## 2. Titles before a name When a title or professional label directly precedes a person's name, the article **is required** in Italian — unlike English, which drops 'the' before titles. il professor Rossi (Professor Rossi), la dottoressa Bianchi (Dr Bianchi), la segretaria Carla (the secretary Carla). ### Exception — a small group of traditional titles takes **no** article: don, mastro, fra (and a handful of similar archaic or religious titles): don Giovanni, mastro Geppetto, fra Galdino. ## 3. Surnames **Women's surnames** always take the article, whether the person is famous or not: la Callas, la Bianchi. **Men's surnames** traditionally took the article (especially for famous figures: il Leopardi, il Petrarca), but this usage is declining in modern Italian. In everyday speech, men's surnames are normally used without an article. **A surname referring to more than one person** (a family or group) takes a plural article: i De Filippo, gli Alberti. ## 4. Place names This is a nuanced area; the key patterns to know at A1 are: **Cities**: most Italian city names take **no** article. A small number are exceptions because the article is actually part of the name: L'Aquila, La Spezia, Il Cairo. **Mountains, rivers, and lakes**: always take the article: il Po, il Trasimeno, il Monviso. **Islands**: some take the article (la Sicilia, l'Elba), others do not (Capri, Cipro). There is no simple rule here — learn each island name as you meet it. **Countries**: some always take an article (gli Stati Uniti, le Filippine); one refuses it entirely (Israele). Most countries follow the pattern 'article in some expressions, no article in others'. **Rule that overrides all of the above**: whenever a normally article-free place name is accompanied by a descriptive adjective or a qualifying phrase, the article returns: la bellissima Capri (beautiful Capri), la Roma dei papi (the Rome of the popes). ## Examples 1. Mia madre si chiama Anna. (My mother's name is Anna.) — singular, unmodified family noun: no article. 2. La mia mamma lavora in ufficio. (My mum works in an office.) — mamma always keeps the article. 3. I miei fratelli abitano a Milano. (My brothers live in Milan.) — plural family noun: article required. 4. Ho un appuntamento con il dottor Verdi. (I have an appointment with Dr Verdi.) — title + name: article required. 5. Don Camillo è un personaggio famoso. (Don Camillo is a famous character.) — don is one of the titles that never takes an article. 6. Il Po è un fiume importante. vs. Roma è bella. (The Po is an important river. / Rome is beautiful.) — rivers always take the article; most cities do not. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Adding the article before a singular possessive + family noun:** *il mio padre* ✗ → correct: mio padre ✓ **Mistake 2 — Dropping the article before a plural possessive + family noun:** *miei fratelli* ✗ → correct: i miei fratelli ✓ **Mistake 3 — Forgetting the article with mamma and papà:** *mia mamma* ✗ → correct: la mia mamma ✓ **Mistake 4 — Omitting the article before a title + name:** *professor Rossi arriva* ✗ → correct: il professor Rossi arriva ✓ **Mistake 5 — Adding the article before most city names:** *la Roma è bella* ✗ → correct: Roma è bella ✓ (unless a modifier follows: la Roma antica ✓)
en.why_this_matters: Italian uses the definite article (il, la, i, le, etc.) far more often than English uses 'the', so learners tend to add it everywhere. But several very common situations — talking about your family, addressing someone by title, or naming certain cities — require you to leave it out entirely. Getting this right makes your Italian sound natural from your very first conversations.

en.title: Definite articles with possessive adjectives
en.tip: In Italian, you usually drop the definite article before singular family nouns used with a possessive adjective — so 'my mother' is 'mia madre', not 'la mia madre'. But there are important exceptions: always keep the article in the plural, with 'mamma' and 'papà', and when an extra describing word is added.
en.explanation: ## The basic rule When a singular family noun is directly preceded by a possessive adjective (mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro — my, your, his/her, our, your, their), you do **not** use the definite article (il, la, l'). **Pattern:** possessive adjective + family noun (no article) | Italian | English | |---|---| | mio padre | my father | | tua sorella | your sister | | suo fratello | his/her brother | | nostra madre | our mother | | vostro zio | your uncle | | loro figlia | their daughter | This pattern applies to the most common singular family terms: padre (father), madre (mother), figlio/figlia (son/daughter), fratello (brother), sorella (sister), nonno/nonna (grandfather/grandmother), zio/zia (uncle/aunt), cugino/cugina (cousin), nipote (nephew/niece/grandchild). ## When you MUST keep the article There are four important exceptions — situations where the definite article is **required** even with a possessive adjective and a family noun. ### 1. Plural family nouns In the plural, the article always returns. | Italian | English | |---|---| | i miei nonni | my grandparents | | i nostri cugini | our cousins | | le tue sorelle | your sisters | | i suoi fratelli | his/her brothers | ### 2. 'Mamma' and 'papà' — always take the article The everyday words mamma (mum) and papà (dad) always keep the article, even in the singular. | Italian | English | |---|---| | la mia mamma | my mum | | il tuo papà | your dad | ### 3. When an adjective is added If any describing word (adjective) accompanies the family noun, the article is required. | Italian | English | |---|---| | il nostro caro zio | our dear uncle | | la mia piccola sorella | my little sister | ### 4. When an altered form (diminutive or similar) is used Italian family nouns can take suffixes that add a shade of meaning — for example, making a word sound smaller or more affectionate. These altered forms (alterati) always keep the article. | Italian | English | |---|---| | la mia cuginetta | my little/dear cousin | | il mio fratellino | my little brother | ## Examples in context Mio fratello si chiama Marco. (My brother's name is Marco.) — singular, no adjective: no article. I miei fratelli si chiamano Marco e Luca. (My brothers are called Marco and Luca.) — plural: article required. La mia mamma cucina bene. (My mum cooks well.) — 'mamma' always takes the article. Il nostro caro nonno abita a Roma. (Our dear grandfather lives in Rome.) — adjective 'caro' present: article required. Tua sorella parla italiano? (Does your sister speak Italian?) — singular, no adjective: no article. La mia sorellina dorme. (My little sister is sleeping.) — diminutive form: article required. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Adding the article in the simple singular case:** Learners often write *la mia sorella by analogy with English 'my sister', not realising Italian drops the article here. Correct form: mia sorella. **Mistake 2 — Dropping the article in the plural:** Having learned the 'no article' rule, learners then wrongly say *miei nonni without an article. Correct form: i miei nonni. **Mistake 3 — Forgetting the article with 'mamma' and 'papà':** Because madre and padre drop the article, learners assume the same for mamma and papà. Incorrect: *mia mamma. Correct: la mia mamma. **Mistake 4 — Dropping the article when an adjective is present:** Learners sometimes write *nostro caro zio instead of il nostro caro zio. Any time a describing word joins the phrase, the article comes back. ## Quick summary table | Situation | Article? | Example | |---|---|---| | Singular family noun, no adjective | No | mio padre | | Plural family noun | Yes | i miei fratelli | | Mamma or papà, any number | Yes | la mia mamma | | Family noun + adjective | Yes | il nostro caro zio | | Diminutive / altered form | Yes | la mia sorellina |
en.why_this_matters: Talking about your family is one of the very first things you do in Italian — introducing your parents, siblings, and grandparents comes up constantly at A1 level. The rule about dropping or keeping the article with family nouns is one of the most frequent sources of errors for English speakers, because English always says 'my brother', 'your sister' with no article at all, whereas Italian has a nuanced pattern you need to follow from day one.

en.title: The present tense (indicativo presente)
en.tip: The Italian present tense covers what is happening right now, what happens regularly, and — very commonly in spoken Italian — what will happen in the future. One tense does the work of several English ones, so mastering its forms early unlocks a huge range of everyday conversation.
en.explanation: ## What the present tense expresses Unlike English, which splits these ideas across several forms ('I write', 'I am writing', 'I do write'), Italian uses one form — the presente — to cover four distinct situations: 1. **Something happening right now:** Carlo scrive means both 'Carlo writes' and 'Carlo is writing' — the Italian present covers both. 2. **A habitual or repeated action:** things that happen regularly, always, or as a general truth. 3. **A future action** (especially in spoken Italian): using the present with a future time word is natural and extremely common. 4. **The historic present** (presente storico): retelling past events as if they are happening now, to make the story feel vivid and immediate. ## How to form the present tense Italian verbs belong to three conjugation classes, identified by the infinitive ending: -are, -ere, or -ire. To form the present, drop the infinitive ending and add the endings for that class. ### Regular -are verbs (e.g. parlare, 'to speak') | Person | Ending | Full form | |---|---|---| | io (I) | -o | parlo | | tu (you, singular) | -i | parli | | lui/lei (he/she) | -a | parla | | noi (we) | -iamo | parliamo | | voi (you, plural) | -ate | parlate | | loro (they) | -ano | parlano | ### Regular -ere verbs (e.g. scrivere, 'to write') | Person | Ending | Full form | |---|---|---| | io | -o | scrivo | | tu | -i | scrivi | | lui/lei | -e | scrive | | noi | -iamo | scriviamo | | voi | -ete | scrivete | | loro | -ono | scrivono | ### Regular -ire verbs: two patterns -ire verbs split into two groups. Most everyday -ire verbs you meet at A1 follow the -isc- pattern (also called the 'inchoative' pattern), which inserts -isc- between the stem and the ending in four of the six forms. A smaller group conjugates without the insert. **With -isc- insert** (e.g. finire, 'to finish'): | Person | Full form | |---|---| | io | finisco | | tu | finisci | | lui/lei | finisce | | noi | finiamo | | voi | finite | | loro | finiscono | **Without -isc- insert** (e.g. dormire, 'to sleep'): | Person | Full form | |---|---| | io | dormo | | tu | dormi | | lui/lei | dorme | | noi | dormiamo | | voi | dormite | | loro | dormono | ## Common irregular verbs Several high-frequency verbs are irregular in the present. You will need these from day one — learn them as fixed forms rather than trying to apply regular rules. | Infinitive | io | tu | lui/lei | noi | voi | loro | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | essere ('to be') | sono | sei | è | siamo | siete | sono | | avere ('to have') | ho | hai | ha | abbiamo | avete | hanno | | andare ('to go') | vado | vai | va | andiamo | andate | vanno | | fare ('to do/make') | faccio | fai | fa | facciamo | fate | fanno | | venire ('to come') | vengo | vieni | viene | veniamo | venite | vengono | | volere ('to want') | voglio | vuoi | vuole | vogliamo | volete | vogliono | | potere ('to be able to') | posso | puoi | può | possiamo | potete | possono | ## Examples covering all four uses **1. Action happening right now** Carlo scrive una lettera. — 'Carlo is writing a letter.' (or 'Carlo writes a letter.') Mangio la pizza. — 'I am eating pizza.' / 'I eat pizza.' Notice that where English needs 'is writing' or 'am eating' to signal an ongoing action, Italian simply uses the present tense. **2. Habitual action or general truth** In montagna d'inverno nevica. — 'In the mountains it snows in winter.' La mia famiglia mangia insieme ogni sera. — 'My family eats together every evening.' **3. Future action (with a time marker)** L'estate prossima vado in vacanza in Sardegna. — 'Next summer I am going on holiday to Sardinia.' The time word l'estate prossima ('next summer') makes it clear this is future. This use is extremely common in spoken Italian — using the present here sounds completely natural, not sloppy. **4. The historic present** Dante nasce a Firenze nel 1265 e muore a Ravenna nel 1321. — 'Dante was born in Florence in 1265 and died in Ravenna in 1321.' The present tense here ('is born', 'dies') pulls the past into the foreground and is standard in historical writing and storytelling. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using the wrong ending for the wrong class.** Learners sometimes apply -are endings to -ere or -ire verbs. For example, writing *lui scriva instead of lui scrive. Always identify the infinitive class before adding endings. **Mistake 2: Translating 'I am eating' with a separate construction.** English has a continuous form ('I am eating') that Italian does not. Do not try to invent one — mangio already covers both 'I eat' and 'I am eating'. The construction sto mangiando (gerund with stare) does exist for emphasis, but the plain present is always correct and always natural. **Mistake 3: Reaching for the future tense when talking about plans.** When you have a clear future time word (domani 'tomorrow', la settimana prossima 'next week'), Italian speakers almost always use the present, not the future tense. Saying domani vado al mercato ('tomorrow I am going to the market') is more natural than domani andrò al mercato, especially in conversation. **Mistake 4: Forgetting the -isc- insert in -ire verbs.** Writing *finisco is actually correct, but writing *fino (missing the insert entirely) is a frequent error. If you are unsure whether a verb takes -isc-, check a dictionary or word list — there is no simple spelling rule to predict it. **Mistake 5: Omitting the subject pronoun thinking it is required.** In Italian, subject pronouns (io, tu, lui, etc.) are optional because the verb ending already shows who the subject is. Parlo italiano and io parlo italiano are both correct. Pronouns are kept mainly for contrast or emphasis: Io parlo italiano, tu parli spagnolo. ('I speak Italian, you speak Spanish.')
en.why_this_matters: The indicativo presente (indicative present tense) is the single most useful verb form in Italian. Nearly every sentence a beginner needs — describing yourself, talking about daily routines, making plans — uses this tense. Without it you cannot say who you are, what you do, or where you are going. Mastering it also removes one of the most common early mistakes: reaching for a future tense when Italians simply use the present.

en.title: Saying what you would like with 'vorrei'
en.tip: Use 'vorrei' — the conditional form of 'volere' — to say what you would like politely. It is softer and more natural than 'voglio' (I want) in most everyday situations, especially when asking for something.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what 'vorrei' is and how it works Vorrei is the first-person singular conditional form of the verb volere (to want). The conditional mood — il condizionale — expresses something you would do or would like under certain conditions. Think of it as the 'would' form in English. In Italian, the conditional has two tenses: a simple form (condizionale semplice, referring to the present or future) and a compound form (condizionale passato, referring to the past). At A1 level, you focus on the simple form, and specifically on the most important word in it: vorrei. The underlying logic is: vorrei un caffè means 'I would like a coffee' — that is, 'I would like one, if you have it, if I may.' The condition is often left unspoken, but it makes the sentence polite rather than demanding. ## Formation: the full conditional of 'volere' Even though you only need the first-person singular for now, it helps to see the complete pattern so you recognise all the forms when you hear them. Volere is an irregular verb in the conditional. Its conditional stem is vorr-, and the endings are the same for all conditional verbs: | Person | Forma | English | |---|---|---| | io | vorrei | I would like / I would want | | tu | vorresti | you would like | | lui / lei | vorrebbe | he / she would like | | noi | vorremmo | we would like | | voi | vorreste | you (plural) would like | | loro | vorrebbero | they would like | The stem vorr- is irregular — do not try to build it from the infinitive volere by a regular rule. Just learn vorrei as a single, ready-made word first. ## How to use 'vorrei' Vorrei is followed directly by a noun or by an infinitive verb: - With a noun: Vorrei + [noun] → 'I would like [thing]' - With an infinitive: Vorrei + [infinitive] → 'I would like to [do something]' ## Examples Vorrei un caffè, per favore. (I would like a coffee, please.) — ordering in a bar, the classic use. Vorrei una pizza margherita. (I would like a margherita pizza.) — ordering in a restaurant. Vorrei parlare con il professore. (I would like to speak with the teacher.) — polite request using an infinitive. Vorrei un chilo di pane, grazie. (I would like a kilo of bread, thank you.) — shopping at a bakery. Contrastive pair — notice the difference in tone: Voglio un caffè. (I want a coffee.) — direct, can sound blunt or even rude in a service context. Vorrei un caffè. (I would like a coffee.) — polite and natural; the form Italians actually use when ordering. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using voglio when ordering or asking for something.** Saying voglio una birra (I want a beer) is grammatically correct, but it is often too direct for a polite request. In Italian service situations, vorrei is the expected and natural choice. Use voglio when expressing a strong wish or general preference, not when addressing a waiter or shopkeeper. **Mistake 2: Trying to conjugate vorrei further or add a subject pronoun as if it changes the meaning.** Vorrei already means 'I would like.' You do not need to say *io vorrei io — the ending -ei already identifies the subject as first-person singular. The optional pronoun io can be added for emphasis, but it is not required: Io vorrei un tè is fine for emphasis, but Vorrei un tè is the normal, natural form. **Mistake 3: Spelling or pronouncing the stem incorrectly.** Some learners write *volerei or *voglerei, trying to keep the infinitive stem. The correct stem is vorr-, giving vorrei. The double r is both spelled and pronounced — do not drop it. **Mistake 4: Forgetting di or using it incorrectly before an infinitive.** Unlike some Italian verbs, volere connects directly to an infinitive with no preposition: Vorrei mangiare qualcosa (I would like to eat something) — NOT *vorrei di mangiare. Never insert di between vorrei and the infinitive.
en.why_this_matters: The single word vorrei (I would like) is one of the most useful words you will learn in Italian. You need it every time you order food, ask for something in a shop, or make a polite request. Without it, you risk sounding abrupt — knowing it immediately makes your Italian sound natural and courteous.

en.title: Formal and Informal Imperative of 'scusare'
en.tip: To ask someone to excuse you, say 'scusa' to a friend and 'scusi' to a stranger or someone older. These two forms come from different grammatical persons, so you cannot swap them without sounding rude or odd.
en.explanation: ## The rule: imperative of scusare The verb scusare (to excuse, to forgive) is a regular -are verb. Its imperative forms follow the standard pattern for -are verbs, but there is one important twist: the Lei (formal 'you') form is borrowed from the congiuntivo presente (present subjunctive), not the indicative. ## Imperative forms of scusare | Person | Form | When to use it | |---|---|---| | tu (informal singular) | scusa | one friend, family member, child, peer | | Lei (formal singular) | scusi | stranger, older person, professional context | | voi (informal plural) | scusate | a group of friends or peers | | Loro (formal plural, rare) | scusino | very formal, e.g. addressing a group of clients | Note: the first person singular (io) does not exist in the imperative — you cannot give an order to yourself. ## Informal imperative: scusa (tu) Use scusa when speaking to one person you address as tu. This is the standard second-person singular imperative of a regular -are verb: drop the -re from the infinitive scusare to get scusa. ## Formal imperative: scusi (Lei) Use scusi when speaking to one person you address as Lei (the formal singular 'you'). This form ends in -i because it is drawn from the present subjunctive. This -i ending is the key marker of the formal imperative for all regular -are verbs. ## Negative imperative To tell someone not to do something, the rule changes for the informal singular only: place non before the infinitive scusare, not before the imperative form. | Person | Negative form | |---|---| | tu (informal) | non scusare | | Lei (formal) | non scusi | | voi | non scusate | For Lei and voi, the negative is simply non + the same imperative form. Only the tu negative uses the infinitive. ## Examples Scusa, come ti chiami? (Sorry, what's your name?) — informal, talking to a friend. Scusi, dov'è la stazione? (Excuse me, where is the station?) — formal, asking a stranger for directions. Scusate, siete pronti? (Excuse me, are you ready?) — informal plural, addressing a group of friends. Non scusare sempre lui! (Don't always make excuses for him!) — informal negative, using the infinitive after non. Scusi, signora, questo posto è libero? (Excuse me, madam, is this seat free?) — formal, polite address to an older woman. Scusa, non scusare — contrastive pair: scusa is the affirmative imperative ('say sorry / excuse me'), while non scusare is the negative imperative ('don't excuse / don't apologise'). ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — using scusa in a formal situation:** Saying scusa to a professor or a shop assistant you have just met sounds too familiar. Always use scusi when in doubt about the relationship. **Mistake 2 — using scusi with friends:** Conversely, using scusi with a classmate or a sibling sounds comically stiff. Match the form to the relationship. **Mistake 3 — negative informal with the imperative form:** A common error is *non scusa! This is wrong. The correct informal negative is non scusare! — always use the infinitive after non for the tu form. **Mistake 4 — confusing scusa and scusi as simply 'polite vs. casual':** The difference is grammatical, not just social. Scusi is a subjunctive-derived form linked to the pronoun Lei, while scusa is a true imperative linked to tu. Understanding this helps you apply the same pattern to other verbs.
en.why_this_matters: 'Excuse me' and 'sorry' are among the first things you need in any language. In Italian, the word you choose depends on registro (register) — whether you are speaking informally to a friend or formally to a stranger. Getting this right immediately makes you sound polite and natural; getting it wrong can come across as rude or overly stiff.

en.title: Using 'let's' to make suggestions in Italian
en.tip: To suggest doing something together in Italian, use the 'noi' (we) form of the present tense as a command — the same form you already know. Just say it with the meaning 'let's do this!' No extra word is needed.
en.explanation: ## The rule: how to form it The imperative ('command mood') in Italian has only one tense: the present. Because you cannot give an order to yourself, the imperative has no first-person singular ('I') form. However, it does have a **first-person plural** form, used to include yourself in an invitation or suggestion — exactly like English 'let's'. **Formation:** The first-person plural imperative is identical to the present-tense noi ('we') form of the verb. You do not need to add any extra word like 'let's' — the verb form alone carries that meaning. noi present tense = first-person plural imperative ### Verb endings at a glance | Infinitive | Present noi form | Meaning as imperative | |---|---|---| | parlare (to speak) | parliamo | let's speak / let's talk | | mangiare (to eat) | mangiamo | let's eat | | prendere (to take/have) | prendiamo | let's take / let's have | | partire (to leave) | partiamo | let's leave | | andare (to go) | andiamo | let's go | | essere (to be) | siamo | let's be | | avere (to have) | abbiamo | let's have | ## How to make it negative: 'let's not…' To say 'let's not do something', simply place non ('not') directly before the same verb form. The verb form itself does not change. Non mangiamo lì. → Let's not eat there. **Important contrast:** For the second-person singular ('you') negative imperative, Italian uses the infinitive (e.g. non parlare! — don't speak!). But for the first-person plural, the rule is simpler: non + the ordinary noi present form, just like the positive command. ## Examples 1. Andiamo a casa! — Let's go home! 2. Mangiamo la pizza stasera. — Let's eat pizza tonight. 3. Parliamo con la maestra. — Let's talk to the teacher. 4. Prendiamo un caffè insieme. — Let's have a coffee together. 5. Non usciamo stasera, fa freddo. — Let's not go out tonight, it's cold. 6. Siamo pazienti! — Let's be patient! (edge case: essere is irregular in the present, so its noi form siamo is the one to remember) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Translating 'let's' word for word.** English learners sometimes try to invent a word for 'let's' in Italian. There is no separate word — the verb form itself does the job. ✗ *Lasciamo mangiare. (This means 'let them/us eat' in a different sense, not a natural suggestion.) ✓ Mangiamo! — Let's eat! **Mistake 2: Confusing the imperative with a simple statement.** Because the form is identical to the present tense, context and intonation do the work of showing it is a suggestion. In writing, an exclamation mark is common; in speech, a rising-then-falling intonation signals an invitation. ✗ Thinking Andiamo can only mean 'we go/we are going' — it also means 'let's go!' depending on context. **Mistake 3: Using the infinitive for the negative.** Some learners apply the second-person singular rule (non + infinitive) to the noi form. This rule does not apply here. ✗ *Non andare insieme. (This is a command to one person: 'don't go together.') ✓ Non andiamo insieme. — Let's not go together. ## Quick summary - Positive suggestion: noi present form alone → Mangiamo! (Let's eat!) - Negative suggestion: non + noi present form → Non mangiamo! (Let's not eat!) - No extra word for 'let's' is needed or used.
en.why_this_matters: The moment you want to say 'andiamo!' ('let's go!') or suggest a plan to a friend, you need the first-person plural imperative. It comes up constantly in everyday conversation — making plans, ordering food together, inviting someone to sit down — and the good news is that it is identical to a verb form you already know, so there is almost nothing new to memorise.

en.title: Modal verbs: potere, volere, dovere
en.tip: The verbs potere, volere, and dovere come before another verb in its infinitive form to say what someone can, wants, or must do. They change their ending to match the subject, but the second verb always stays in the infinitive. These three verbs appear in almost every Italian conversation.
en.explanation: ## What modal verbs are Potere, volere, and dovere are called verbi modali (modal verbs) — sometimes also verbi servili (auxiliary verbs, literally 'servant verbs'). They are called this because they 'serve' another verb: they always appear together with a second verb in the infinito (infinitive — the base form ending in -are, -ere, or -ire). Each modal adds a specific meaning to that second verb: - dovere → necessity or obligation: 'must / have to' - volere → desire or intention: 'want to' - potere → possibility or permission: 'can / may / be able to' ## How to form them The structure is simple: **modal verb (conjugated) + infinitive of the main verb** The modal verb changes to match the subject. The main verb never changes — it always stays in the infinitive. Here are the full present-tense forms of all three: | Subject | dovere (must) | volere (want) | potere (can) | |---|---|---|---| | io | devo | voglio | posso | | tu | devi | vuoi | puoi | | lui / lei | deve | vuole | può | | noi | dobbiamo | vogliamo | possiamo | | voi | dovete | volete | potete | | loro | devono | vogliono | possono | All three verbs are irregular — their forms must be learned individually. Notice that volere and potere have vowel changes in the stem for io, tu, lui/lei, and loro (the so-called 'boot' pattern), while noi and voi forms stay closer to the infinitive. ## Examples Devo studiare stasera. (I have to study tonight.) — obligation Vuoi mangiare la pizza? (Do you want to eat pizza?) — desire Marco può venire domani. (Marco can come tomorrow.) — possibility Dobbiamo parlare con la mamma. (We have to talk to Mum.) — obligation, plural subject Non posso bere il caffè. (I can't drink coffee.) — negation: non goes before the modal, not before the infinitive Loro vogliono dormire. (They want to sleep.) — third person plural ## Negation To make a modal sentence negative, place non directly before the modal verb: Non voglio mangiare. (I don't want to eat.) ✓ *Voglio non mangiare. ✗ — This is incorrect in standard usage at this level. ## Asking questions In Italian, questions are formed without changing the word order — simply raise your intonation, or add a question mark in writing: Puoi aprire la finestra? (Can you open the window?) Vuole un caffè? (Would you like a coffee? — formal, addressing one person as Lei) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: conjugating the second verb** *Voglio mangio la pasta. ✗ Voglio mangiare la pasta. ✓ The verb after the modal must stay in the infinitive. Never conjugate it. **Mistake 2: confusing puoi and puòi** The tu form of potere is puoi (no accent). The lui/lei form is può (with an accent, no i). These are two different words. **Mistake 3: using voglio as a direct translation of 'I would like'** Voglio un caffè. is grammatically correct but can sound abrupt in some social situations. At A1, it is perfectly acceptable — just be aware that Italian also has politer alternatives you will learn later. **Mistake 4: wrong form of dovere for noi** *Devemo andare. ✗ Dobbiamo andare. ✓ The noi form of dovere is irregular: dobbiamo, not devemo. This is one of the most common spelling errors with this verb.
en.why_this_matters: Without modal verbs, you cannot express some of the most basic things people say every day — that they devono lavorare (must work), vogliono mangiare (want to eat), or possono venire (can come). These three verbs appear constantly in Italian — in requests, offers, rules, invitations, and descriptions of daily life. Mastering them lets you move far beyond simple statements and start expressing intention, obligation, and ability.
