en.title: Using 'ci' with the verb 'essere'
en.tip: Use 'ci' in front of 'essere' to say that something exists or is present in a place. 'C'è' means 'there is' and 'ci sono' means 'there are'. This construction is one of the most common in everyday Italian.
en.explanation: ## The rule and how to form it Place the particle ci (meaning roughly 'here/there' in this use) directly before the present-tense forms of essere ('to be'). Only two forms are used in practice at this level: | Form | Used with | Meaning | |---|---|---| | c'è | one thing (singular noun) | 'there is' | | ci sono | more than one thing (plural noun) | 'there are' | Notice that ci è contracts to c'è (with an apostrophe) because ci ends in a vowel and è begins with one. Ci sono does not contract. ## Full present-tense paradigm Although only two forms appear in normal use, here is the complete picture for reference: | Italian | English | |---|---| | c'è | 'there is' (singular) | | ci sono | 'there are' (plural) | The forms ci sei, ci siamo, etc. exist but carry a different meaning ('are you there?', 'we are here') — they are not part of this construction and appear at higher levels. ## How to use it Put c'è or ci sono at the start of the sentence, followed by the noun (the thing that exists or is present). The noun after c'è / ci sono is the subject of the sentence — Italian treats it this way even though in English we say 'there is/are' first. Basic word order: C'è / Ci sono + [noun] + [optional: location or extra information] ## Examples C'è un gatto sul divano. (There is a cat on the sofa.) Ci sono tre sedie in cucina. (There are three chairs in the kitchen.) C'è latte nel frigorifero? (Is there any milk in the fridge?) — question formed simply by using a rising intonation or a question mark; no word order change is needed. No, non c'è latte, ma ci sono due uova. (No, there is no milk, but there are two eggs.) — negative formed by placing non directly before c'è or ci sono. C'è mia sorella a casa oggi. (My sister is at home today.) — note that c'è can refer to a person being present, not just an object existing. Ci sono molti bambini nel parco. (There are many children in the park.) ## Negatives and questions at a glance | Type | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | Positive | c'è | ci sono | | Negative | non c'è | non ci sono | | Question | c'è…? | ci sono…? | ## Articles after c'è and ci sono The noun that follows almost always carries an indefinite article (un, una, uno, un') when you are introducing something for the first time, or no article at all with uncountable nouns: C'è un bambino alla porta. (There is a child at the door.) — first mention, indefinite. C'è acqua sul tavolo. (There is water on the table.) — uncountable noun, no article. Using a definite article (il, la, i, le) is possible when the thing is already known to both speakers, but at A1 level you will mostly see the indefinite article or no article. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — using the singular form with a plural noun:** *C'è due ragazzi. ✗ — incorrect. The noun ragazzi is plural, so you must use ci sono: Ci sono due ragazzi. ✓ **Mistake 2 — forgetting the apostrophe in c'è:** *ci è un libro ✗ — in writing, this must always be contracted: c'è un libro. ✓ **Mistake 3 — confusing c'è (there is) with è (he/she/it is):** Il gatto è sul divano means 'The cat is on the sofa' (describing where a specific, known cat is). C'è un gatto sul divano means 'There is a cat on the sofa' (announcing its existence). Do not swap these two structures. **Mistake 4 — placing non in the wrong position:** *C'è non latte. ✗ — non must come before the verb, not after it: Non c'è latte. ✓
en.why_this_matters: The construction ci + essere — giving us c'è and ci sono — is the standard Italian way to say 'there is' and 'there are'. You will need it from your very first conversations: describing a room, asking what is on the menu, talking about your family, or checking whether a friend is home. Without it, you cannot describe the world around you in the most basic way.

en.title: The infinitive in purpose clauses
en.tip: To say why you do something, use 'per' followed by the infinitive — the base form of the verb ending in -are, -ere, or -ire. This works whenever the subject of both actions is the same person.
en.explanation: ## The rule A **purpose clause** answers the question 'why?' or 'what for?'. In Italian, when the subject of both verbs is the same person, you express purpose with: **per + infinito presente** (per = 'in order to / to' + the present infinitive — the dictionary form of the verb) The **present infinitive** is the base form of the verb. It has three endings depending on the verb group: | Group | Ending | Example | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | 1st (-are verbs) | -are | mangiare | to eat | | 2nd (-ere verbs) | -ere | prendere | to take | | 3rd (-ire verbs) | -ire | dormire | to sleep | The infinitive does **not** change for person or number. The same form is used whether the subject is io, tu, noi, or anyone else. ## Formation at a glance [main verb] + per + infinito Example structure: Vado al supermercato **per comprare** il pane. (I'm going to the supermarket **to buy** bread.) ## Examples **1. Everyday errands and movement** Vado in cucina per mangiare. (I'm going to the kitchen to eat.) **2. Study and learning** Studio ogni giorno per imparare l'italiano. (I study every day to learn Italian.) **3. Communication** Telefono a mia madre per parlare con lei. (I call my mother to talk to her.) **4. With a different main verb — the infinitive stays the same** Usciamo per prendere un caffè. (We're going out to get a coffee.) **5. Contrastive pair — same infinitive, different main subject (edge case)** Chiamo Marco per venire con noi. (I'm calling Marco to come with us. — Here 'to come' refers to *me*, not Marco. If you mean Marco should come, you need a different structure: Chiamo Marco perché venga con noi, which is beyond A1. At A1, only use per + infinito when both verbs share the same subject.) **6. Negation — put non before the infinitive** Parlo piano per non svegliare il bambino. (I speak quietly so as not to wake the baby.) ## The infinitive as a noun The textbook notes that the present infinitive can also act as a noun — functioning as the subject or object of a sentence. This is a separate use from purpose clauses, but good to recognise: Viaggiare è molto istruttivo. (Travelling is very educational.) Mangiare bene è importante. (Eating well is important.) In this noun use there is no per. The infinitive simply stands at the start of the sentence like an English gerund in '-ing'. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using a conjugated verb after per** ✗ Vado al bar per compro un caffè. (Wrong — compro is a conjugated form, not an infinitive.) ✓ Vado al bar per comprare un caffè. (Correct.) **Mistake 2: Omitting per entirely (copying English word order)** ✗ Vado al supermercato comprare il pane. (Wrong — Italian requires per before the infinitive in purpose clauses; you cannot simply place the infinitive after the main verb.) ✓ Vado al supermercato per comprare il pane. **Mistake 3: Changing the infinitive ending to match the subject** ✗ Noi andiamo fuori per mangiamo. (Wrong — the infinitive never takes a personal ending.) ✓ Noi andiamo fuori per mangiare. **Mistake 4: Using per + infinito when the subjects are different** If the person doing the second action is *different* from the person doing the first, per + infinito is not correct. This situation requires a perché ('so that') clause with a subjunctive, which is learned at a higher level. At A1, always check that both actions have the same subject before using this structure.
en.why_this_matters: Saying *why* you do something is one of the first things you need in any language. Without this rule, you cannot express even the simplest intentions — 'I'm going to the shop to buy bread', 'I'm studying to learn Italian'. Once you know this pattern, you can add a reason to almost any sentence, making your Italian immediately more expressive and natural.

en.title: Using 'di' to express where you are from
en.tip: Use 'di' before a city or place name to say where someone is from or where something comes from. It works like 'from' in English when talking about origin. This is one of the first prepositions you will need in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The rule The preposition di expresses **origin or provenance** — the idea that someone comes from a place, or that something comes from a source. In English this corresponds to 'from'. The structure is simple: **Subject + essere + di + place name** For example: Sono di Roma. — 'I am from Rome.' The verb used is always essere ('to be'). The place name follows di directly, with no article, when it is a city or town. ## Formation at a glance | Person | Verb form | Example | |---|---|---| | io (I) | sono | Sono di Napoli. | | tu (you, singular) | sei | Sei di Milano? | | lui / lei (he / she) | è | È di Torino. | | noi (we) | siamo | Siamo di Venezia. | | voi (you, plural) | siete | Siete di Bologna? | | loro (they) | sono | Sono di Firenze. | ## The key question form The standard question is Di dove sei? (informal, 'Where are you from?') or Di dov'è? (formal). Notice that dove ('where') contracts to dov' before è to avoid two vowels side by side. The preposition di stays at the front of the question — it does not move to the end as 'from' sometimes does in English. ## Examples — Di dove sei? — Sono di Roma. ('Where are you from?' — 'I am from Rome.') Marco è di Milano. ('Marco is from Milan.') Mia madre è di Napoli e mio padre è di Palermo. ('My mother is from Naples and my father is from Palermo.') Questo vino è di Toscana. ('This wine is from Tuscany.') — di can also express the origin of things, not just people. Siete di qui? ('Are you from here?') — di is used with qui ('here') and lì ('there') in exactly the same way. Non sono di Londra, sono di Manchester. ('I am not from London, I am from Manchester.') — negation is formed by placing non before the verb. ## Cities vs. countries: an important edge case With **city names**, use di directly and with no article: Sono di Parigi. ('I am from Paris.') With **country names**, Italian normally uses venire da ('to come from') rather than essere di: Vengo dall'Italia. / Vengo dalla Francia. This is because country names take a definite article in Italian, which combines with da (not di) to express national origin. You do not need to master this now, but it is good to know that Sono di Italia sounds unnatural to a native speaker. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Omitting di:** *Sono Roma. ✗ — This means nothing in Italian. Sono di Roma. ✓ **Mistake 2 — Adding an article after di with city names:** *Sono di la Roma. ✗ — City names do not take an article here. Sono di Roma. ✓ **Mistake 3 — Translating 'from' with da instead of di for city origin:** English speakers sometimes reach for da because it can also translate as 'from'. With cities and the verb essere, the correct choice for origin is di. *Sono da Roma. — possible in some contexts (e.g. 'I have come from Rome' as a journey), but Sono di Roma is the natural way to state where you are originally from. **Mistake 4 — Putting di at the end of the question:** *Dove sei di? ✗ — This does not exist in Italian. Di dove sei? ✓ — The preposition always stays at the beginning.
en.why_this_matters: The very first question an Italian speaker will ask you is Di dove sei? — 'Where are you from?' Without di, you cannot answer it. This small word unlocks introductions, descriptions of people and products, and dozens of everyday conversations. Getting it right from day one removes one of the most common errors beginners make.

en.title: Using 'a' to show who receives something
en.tip: The preposition 'a' marks the person or thing that receives or benefits from an action — the indirect object. It answers the question 'to whom?' or 'for whom?' and is essential any time you say you give, send, speak, or show something to someone.
en.explanation: ## The rule Place a directly before the noun or name of the person (or thing) that receives or benefits from the action. This use is called complemento di termine (indirect object complement) — it answers the questions a chi? (to whom?) or a che cosa? (to what?). **Basic word order:** soggetto + verbo + oggetto diretto + a + persona Example: Do il libro a Marco. (I give the book to Marco.) The indirect object introduced by a typically comes **after** the direct object, but it can also appear immediately after the verb for emphasis or when there is no direct object. ## Combining 'a' with the definite article When a is followed by a **definite article** (il, lo, la, l', i, gli, le), the two words **merge** into a single contracted form called an articolo preposizionale (prepositional article). These contractions are **mandatory** — you cannot keep them separate. | Preposition | + Article | Contracted form | Example | |---|---|---|---| | a | il | al | al bambino (to the child) | | a | lo | allo | allo studente (to the student) | | a | la | alla | alla bambina (to the girl) | | a | l' | all' | all'amica (to the friend) | | a | i | ai | ai ragazzi (to the boys) | | a | gli | agli | agli amici (to the friends) | | a | le | alle | alle sorelle (to the sisters) | Note: when a is followed by a **proper name** or an **indefinite article** (un, una), no contraction occurs: a Marco, a una ragazza. ## Common verbs that take 'a' + indirect object These are among the most frequent verbs at A1 level that require an indirect object introduced by a: | Italian verb | English meaning | |---|---| | dare | to give | | mandare | to send | | scrivere | to write | | parlare | to speak/talk | | dire | to say/tell | | mostrare | to show | | portare | to bring | | chiedere | to ask | | rispondere | to reply | | telefonare | to phone | ## Examples **1. Giving something to a named person:** Do il libro a Maria. (I give the book to Maria.) **2. Speaking to a person with a definite article (contraction required):** Parlo al professore. (I speak to the teacher.) — a + il = al **3. Writing to a group (plural contraction):** Scrivo una lettera agli amici. (I write a letter to my friends.) — a + gli = agli **4. Bringing something to a female person:** Porto il caffè alla mamma. (I bring the coffee to Mum.) — a + la = alla **5. Asking something — verb with no direct object:** Chiedo a Luca. (I ask Luca. / I'll ask Luca.) — a follows the verb directly because there is no direct object. **6. Contrastive pair — direct vs indirect object:** Chiamo Maria. (I call Maria. — direct object, no preposition.) Telefono a Maria. (I phone Maria. — indirect object, a required. With telefonare, Italian always uses a, unlike English 'I phone Maria'.) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Omitting a after telefonare:** ✗ Telefono Maria. ✓ Telefono a Maria. Because English says 'I phone Maria' with no preposition, learners drop a. In Italian, telefonare always requires a. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting the contraction:** ✗ Parlo a il professore. ✓ Parlo al professore. The forms a il, a lo, a la, etc. are not acceptable in standard Italian. Always use the contracted form when a definite article follows. **Mistake 3 — Adding a when the verb takes a direct object:** ✗ Chiamo a Maria. ✓ Chiamo Maria. The verb chiamare (to call) takes a **direct** object — no preposition. Do not confuse it with telefonare. **Mistake 4 — Using per instead of a:** ✗ Do il libro per Maria. ✓ Do il libro a Maria. English speakers sometimes use 'for' and 'to' interchangeably, but in Italian, the indirect object (the receiver of an action) always takes a, not per. (Per expresses purpose or benefit in a different sense.)
en.why_this_matters: Almost every conversation involves giving, telling, or showing something to someone. In Italian, the preposition a (to, at) is the word that connects the verb to the person who receives the action — the indirect object. Without it, sentences like 'I give the book to Maria' or 'She writes to her mother' are impossible to form correctly. Mastering this single preposition immediately unlocks dozens of everyday sentences.

en.title: Using 'a' to express time in Italian
en.tip: Use 'a' to say what time something happens or to name a specific point in time, like a holiday or a meal. It works like 'at' in English for clock times, but Italian also uses it in a few fixed time phrases that English handles differently.
en.explanation: ## The core rule Use a to indicate a precise, clock-like point in time — most importantly with hours of the day and with a set of fixed time-of-day or calendar expressions. It corresponds closely to English 'at', but the two languages do not always match exactly, so the fixed phrases below need to be memorised. ## Forming time phrases with 'a' The basic pattern is: **verb + a + time expression** When the time expression begins with a definite article (il, la, le), a contracts with that article to form a single word. These contracted forms are called preposizioni articolate (articulated prepositions): | a + | Result | Example | |---|---|---| | a + il | al | al mattino (in the morning) | | a + la | alla | alla sera (in the evening) | | a + le | alle | alle tre (at three o'clock) | | a + l' | all' | all'una (at one o'clock) | Note: a does **not** contract when the time expression has no article: a mezzogiorno (at noon), a mezzanotte (at midnight), a Natale (at Christmas). ## The main uses ### 1. Clock times For all hours except one o'clock, the article is le (because le ore, 'the hours', is plural). For one o'clock the article is la (singular), giving the contracted form all'una. - La lezione inizia alle nove. (The lesson starts at nine.) - Mangio alle tredici. (I eat at one p.m.) - Il treno parte all'una e mezza. (The train leaves at half past one.) ### 2. Fixed time-of-day expressions A small set of time-of-day nouns always take a (with contraction where there is an article): | Italian | English | |---|---| | al mattino / la mattina | in the morning | | al pomeriggio / il pomeriggio | in the afternoon | | alla sera / la sera | in the evening | | a mezzogiorno | at noon / at midday | | a mezzanotte | at midnight | Note that English says 'in the morning / evening' but Italian uses a for these — a common false-friend trap for learners. ### 3. Holidays and calendar reference points Italian uses a (no article, no contraction) before holiday names, matching English 'at': - a Natale — at Christmas - a Pasqua — at Easter - a Capodanno — at New Year ## Full examples 1. La colazione è alle sette e mezza. — Breakfast is at half past seven. 2. Ci vediamo a mezzogiorno. — We'll see each other at noon. 3. La sera guardo la televisione con la mia famiglia. — In the evening I watch television with my family. (Note: here la sera without a is also possible with the article alone when it has a habitual meaning, but alla sera is equally correct and very common.) 4. A Natale mangio molto! — At Christmas I eat a lot! 5. La farmacia apre all'otto. — The pharmacy opens at eight. (Contraction with le → alle, but before a vowel: alle otto — note that otto does not trigger elision because the contracted article is alle, not all'; all' appears only with una.) 6. Il negozio chiude alle venti. — The shop closes at eight p.m. (twenty hundred hours). ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Using in instead of a for clock times** ❌ La festa inizia in otto. ✅ La festa inizia alle otto. — The party starts at eight. Italian never uses in for a clock hour. Reserve in for months, years, seasons, and places. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting the contraction** ❌ Arrivo a le tre. ✅ Arrivo alle tre. — I arrive at three. The sequence a le is never written as two separate words. Contraction is obligatory. **Mistake 3 — Translating 'in the morning/evening' literally with in** ❌ In mattina bevo il caffè. ✅ Al mattino bevo il caffè. — In the morning I drink coffee. English 'in the morning' maps onto Italian al mattino or la mattina, not in mattina. **Mistake 4 — Using all' instead of alle before hours other than one** ❌ Mangio all'otto. ✅ Mangio alle otto. — I eat at eight. The elided form all' is used only before una (one o'clock), because that is the only singular hour. All other hours use alle.
en.why_this_matters: Telling the time, arranging to meet someone, and describing your daily routine are among the very first things you need to do in Italian. The preposition a ('at') is the key word that links an action to a specific point in time — without it, sentences like 'I eat lunch at noon' or 'The lesson starts at three o'clock' are simply impossible to form correctly. Getting this right from the start also prevents a persistent mistake: reaching for the wrong preposition, such as in or di, in contexts where Italian always uses a.

en.title: Using 'a' for near future time expressions
en.tip: Use 'a' to say something will happen in a set amount of time — like 'in ten minutes' or 'in two days'. It points forward from now to a specific, near moment. Think of it as a countdown to the next event.
en.explanation: ## The rule In Italian, when you want to express that something will happen after a short, specific amount of time — counting forward from now — you use the preposition a before certain fixed time expressions. This is called distanza temporale prossima (near future time distance). The structure is simple: **a + time expression** This pattern is especially common with: - domani — tomorrow - dopodomani — the day after tomorrow - fra/tra + number + time unit — in [X] minutes / hours / days (see note below) - più tardi — later - presto — soon The most frequent fixed phrases with a are farewells and short announcements: | Italiano | English | |---|---| | a domani | see you tomorrow / until tomorrow | | a dopodomani | see you the day after tomorrow | | a più tardi | see you later | | a presto | see you soon | | a lunedì / a martedì … | see you on Monday / Tuesday … | | a stasera | see you tonight | | a dopo | see you in a bit / until later | ## How it is used in speech These a-phrases appear in two main ways: **1. As a farewell (most common at A1)** You say the phrase on its own, like a goodbye. No verb is needed. > — Ciao, Anna! A domani! — Bye, Anna! See you tomorrow! > — Arrivederci! A presto! — Goodbye! See you soon! **2. Inside a sentence with a verb** The phrase can also follow a verb to say when something will happen. > Il treno parte a momenti. — The train is leaving any moment now. ## Examples **1.** A simple farewell between friends: Ciao, Marco! A stasera! (Bye, Marco! See you tonight!) **2.** Saying goodbye until a specific day: — Buona giornata! — Grazie, a lunedì! (— Have a good day! — Thanks, see you Monday!) **3.** A parent speaking to a child: A dopo, tesoro. Mamma torna presto. (See you in a bit, sweetheart. Mum is coming back soon.) **4.** Two colleagues at the end of the day: — Arrivederci a tutti! — A domani! (— Goodbye everyone! — See you tomorrow!) **5.** Contrastive pair — notice the difference in meaning between a and tra/fra: A domani. (See you tomorrow — farewell phrase, fixed expression.) Torno tra due giorni. (I am coming back in two days — counting a span of time, uses tra/fra instead.) **6.** Edge case — a momenti (any moment now): La nonna arriva a momenti. (Grandma is arriving any moment now.) Here a momenti means 'very soon / imminently', not 'at moments'. It is a fixed idiomatic phrase. ## Important distinction: 'a' vs. 'tra/fra' Students sometimes confuse a with tra or fra (both meaning 'in' when counting forward in time). The rule is: - **a** → used in **fixed, named time expressions** (a tomorrow, a Monday, a later, a soon). These are points on the calendar or clock you can name. - **tra/fra + number** → used when you count a **span** of time forward from now (in 5 minutes, in 3 days, in an hour). | Meaning | Correct Italian | Notes | |---|---|---| | See you tomorrow | A domani | fixed farewell with a | | In two days | Tra due giorni | counted span, use tra/fra | | See you in five minutes | A tra cinque minuti | farewell + counted span: both appear together | | See you soon | A presto | fixed farewell with a | Note the combined form a tra/fra: when you want to say 'see you in five minutes' as a farewell, Italian uses both prepositions together: A tra cinque minuti! or A fra poco! This is a natural, spoken combination — do not drop the a. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Dropping 'a' in farewells:** *Domani! ✗ — This sounds abrupt or incomplete as a farewell. A domani! ✓ — Always include a to signal 'see you / until'. **Mistake 2 — Using 'a' with a counted span:** *A due giorni. ✗ — You cannot say 'a two days'. Tra due giorni. ✓ — Use tra/fra for counted spans. **Mistake 3 — Translating 'in' directly as 'in':** English says 'in two days' — Italian says tra due giorni, not *in due giorni. The preposition in exists in Italian but is not used for counting forward in time. **Mistake 4 — Forgetting 'a' in the combined farewell form:** *Tra poco! ✗ as a farewell. A tra poco! ✓ — The a is required at the start of the farewell phrase.
en.why_this_matters: Telling someone when something is about to happen — 'tra cinque minuti' or 'a domani' — is one of the first practical things you need in Italian. The preposition a (to/at/in) is used constantly in these short, fixed time phrases, and getting it right instantly makes your speech sound natural. Without it, you cannot say things like 'see you tomorrow', 'in an hour', or 'in two days'.

en.title: Preposition 'a': place and movement
en.tip: Use 'a' to say where you are or where you are going when the destination is a city or a specific place. It means both 'at/in' (staying) and 'to' (moving towards) depending on the verb you use with it.
en.explanation: ## The rule The preposition a has two closely related uses that depend on the verb in the sentence, not on a different word for 'at' versus 'to'. **Stato in luogo** (being in a place): use a to say where someone or something **is**. The verb will typically be essere ('to be'), stare ('to stay/be'), or a verb of activity like lavorare ('to work') or studiare ('to study'). In this use, a translates as **'in'** or **'at'** in English. **Moto a luogo** (movement towards a place): use a to say where someone or something **is going**. The verb will typically be andare ('to go'), venire ('to come'), or tornare ('to return'). In this use, a translates as **'to'** in English. The preposition itself does **not change** — only the verb signals whether you are talking about being somewhere or going somewhere. ## When to use 'a' Use a before: - **Cities and towns**: a Roma ('in/to Rome'), a Milano ('in/to Milan'), a Napoli ('in/to Naples') - **Specific named places and venues**: a casa ('at home'), a scuola ('at school'), a lavoro ('at work'), a teatro ('at the theatre'), a letto ('in bed') Note that many of these fixed expressions — especially a casa, a scuola, a letto — are used **without an article**. This is normal and must be memorised. ## Important contrast: 'a' vs 'in' Both a and in can mean 'in' or 'to' in English, so students often confuse them. The key rule at A1 level: - Use **a** before **cities**: a Firenze ('in/to Florence') - Use **in** before **countries, regions, and continents**: in Italia ('in/to Italy'), in Toscana ('in/to Tuscany') This distinction is fundamental and will be reinforced as you learn more prepositions. ## Examples **Stato in luogo** (being in a place): Sono a Roma. — 'I am in Rome.' Mia madre è a casa. — 'My mother is at home.' I bambini sono a scuola. — 'The children are at school.' **Moto a luogo** (movement towards a place): Vado a Milano domani. — 'I am going to Milan tomorrow.' Andiamo a casa. — 'We are going home.' / 'Let's go home.' **Contrastive pair** — same preposition, different verb: Sono a scuola. — 'I am at school.' (stato in luogo) Vado a scuola. — 'I am going to school.' (moto a luogo) Notice that a scuola is identical in both sentences — only the verb changes the meaning. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Using 'in' before a city:** *Sono in Roma. ✗ — Incorrect. Cities always take a, not in. Sono a Roma. ✓ **Mistake 2 — Adding an article after 'a' with fixed expressions:** *Vado a la casa. ✗ — Incorrect. Fixed place expressions like casa, scuola, letto, and teatro do not take an article after a in their standard uses. Vado a casa. ✓ **Mistake 3 — Confusing 'a' with 'to go to' in English and dropping it:** *Vado Roma. ✗ — In Italian, the preposition cannot be omitted the way it sometimes is in casual English. You must always include a. Vado a Roma. ✓ ## Quick reference | Use | Italian term | Verb type | English equivalent | |---|---|---|---| | Being in a place | stato in luogo | essere, stare, lavorare… | 'in', 'at' | | Going to a place | moto a luogo | andare, venire, tornare… | 'to' | | Place type | Preposition | Example | |---|---|---| | City | a | a Napoli | | Country | in | in Italia | | Fixed place | a (no article) | a casa, a scuola |
en.why_this_matters: The preposition a is one of the most common words in Italian. You need it every time you say where someone is or where someone is going — two things that come up in almost every conversation. Without it, you cannot answer basic questions like 'Dove sei?' ('Where are you?') or 'Dove vai?' ('Where are you going?'), so mastering it immediately opens up a huge range of everyday sentences.

en.title: Using 'a' for location with city names
en.tip: To say you are in a city or going to a city, use the preposition 'a' directly before the city name — no article needed. This one small word does the work of both 'in' and 'to' when talking about cities.
en.explanation: ## The rule Use a (meaning 'in' or 'to', depending on context) directly before the name of a city. No article is needed between a and the city name. The formula is simply: **verb + a + city name** This applies whether you are talking about: - **location** — where someone is or lives (English: 'in') - **destination** — where someone is going (English: 'to') The preposition a does not change its form before city names. It stays a regardless of whether the city name begins with a vowel or a consonant. ## Forms at a glance | Use | Italian | English | |---|---|---| | Location | Abito a Roma. | I live in Rome. | | Location | Sono a Napoli. | I am in Naples. | | Destination | Vado a Milano. | I am going to Milan. | | Destination | Vai a Firenze? | Are you going to Florence? | ## Examples Mia madre abita a Torino. — My mother lives in Turin. Domani vado a Venezia. — Tomorrow I am going to Venice. Marco è a Roma per lavoro. — Marco is in Rome for work. Andiamo a Palermo in estate. — We are going to Palermo in the summer. Sei mai stato a Oslo? — Have you ever been to Oslo? (Note: a is used with foreign city names too.) Studio a Bologna, ma la mia famiglia è a Bari. — I study in Bologna, but my family is in Bari. (A single sentence using a twice, each time with a different city.) ## Important exception: countries and regions The rule above applies **only to cities**. For countries and regions, Italian uses in instead of a, usually with an article. Abito in Italia. — I live in Italy. (country → in) Abito a Roma. — I live in Rome. (city → a) Do not mix these up: *Abito a Italia* is incorrect. ## City names that look unusual A small number of city names are traditionally used with a definite article (il, la, i, le — the article words). The most common example is L'Aia (The Hague). When a combines with a definite article beginning with a consonant, it forms a single merged word called a 'contracted preposition': for example, a + la → alla. However, these cases are rare and you will not need them at A1 level. For the vast majority of city names, a is used alone. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — using in instead of a with cities:** *Vado in Roma.* ✗ → Vado a Roma. ✓ English speakers sometimes reach for 'in' because in English we say 'in Rome'. In Italian, 'in' is reserved for countries and regions, not cities. **Mistake 2 — adding an article before the city name:** *Vado a la Milano.* ✗ → Vado a Milano. ✓ City names in Italian do not take an article in ordinary use. Write a and then the city name directly — nothing in between. **Mistake 3 — confusing location and destination:** Both 'I am in Rome' and 'I am going to Rome' use a Roma in Italian. The difference is expressed by the verb, not by changing the preposition: Sono a Roma (I am in Rome) vs. Vado a Roma (I am going to Rome). The preposition itself stays the same in both cases.
en.why_this_matters: Saying where you are and where you are going are among the very first things you need to do in Italian. The preposition a — one of the nine core Italian prepositions — is the word that connects you to a city in both of these situations. Without it, you cannot say 'I live in Rome' or 'I'm going to Milan', so mastering this small word immediately unlocks dozens of everyday sentences.

en.title: Using 'in' with countries: location and movement
en.tip: Use 'in' before the name of a country to say you are there or going there. Unlike English, Italian uses the same word 'in' for both 'in a country' and 'to a country', and you do not use an article with most country names.
en.explanation: ## The rule The preposition in is used before country names in two distinct situations: **1. Stato in luogo** (location — being in a place): answering the question Dove sei? / Dove abiti? ('Where are you? / Where do you live?') **2. Moto a luogo** (movement toward a place — going to a place): answering the question Dove vai? / Dove andate? ('Where are you going?') In both cases the structure is simply: **in + country name (no article)** This is different from English, which uses 'in' for location but 'to' for movement. Italian uses in for both. ## Formation: no article with most countries The most important detail is that country names used with in for location or movement do **not** take a definite article. You do not say *in la Francia*; you say in Francia. The article is dropped. This applies to the overwhelming majority of country names you will meet at A1 level: | Country | in + country | |---|---| | Italia (Italy) | in Italia | | Francia (France) | in Francia | | Spagna (Spain) | in Spagna | | Germania (Germany) | in Germania | | Inghilterra (England) | in Inghilterra | | Cina (China) | in Cina | | Giappone (Japan) | in Giappone | | Portogallo (Portugal) | in Portogallo | | Brasile (Brazil) | in Brasile | ## Examples **Location (stato in luogo):** Abito in Italia. — I live in Italy. I miei genitori sono in Francia. — My parents are in France. **Movement toward (moto a luogo):** Domani vado in Spagna. — Tomorrow I am going to Spain. Quest'estate andiamo in Giappone. — This summer we are going to Japan. **Contrastive pair — same preposition, two meanings:** Sono in Germania. — I am in Germany. (location) Vado in Germania. — I am going to Germany. (movement) Notice that the in does not change; only the verb signals whether the meaning is location or movement. ## Important exception: countries with a plural name A small number of countries have a plural name. These keep their article even after in, and in combines with the article to form a contracted preposition: | Country | Full form (not used) | Contracted form (correct) | |---|---|---| | gli Stati Uniti (the United States) | in + gli | negli Stati Uniti | | i Paesi Bassi (the Netherlands) | in + i | nei Paesi Bassi | At A1 level the most important one to remember is negli Stati Uniti ('in/to the United States'). Vado negli Stati Uniti. — I am going to the United States. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using a instead of in with countries.** Learners who know that a is used with cities (a Roma, a Parigi) sometimes carry this over to countries. This is wrong. *Vado a Italia. ✗ — incorrect Vado in Italia. ✓ — correct **Rule of thumb:** a for cities; in for countries. **Mistake 2: Keeping the article after in with singular countries.** *Vado in la Francia. ✗ — incorrect Vado in Francia. ✓ — correct Drop the article with singular country names. (Remember: plural country names like gli Stati Uniti are the exception and do keep a contracted article.) **Mistake 3: Translating 'to' as a for countries.** English uses 'to' for movement ('I am going **to** Italy'), so students sometimes look for an Italian equivalent. There is none needed here — in covers both 'in' and 'to' for countries. *Vado a in Italia. ✗ — incorrect (never double the preposition) Vado in Italia. ✓ — correct
en.why_this_matters: Talking about where you live, where you are from, and where you are going are some of the very first things you do in Italian. The preposition in is your essential tool for all of these situations with country names. Getting this right removes one of the most frequent errors beginners make — reaching for a or adding an unnecessary article — and lets you talk about travel and home from day one.

en.title: Using 'in' to express means of transport
en.tip: In Italian, use 'in' before most forms of transport to say how you travel — for example, by car, by bus, or by train. This is different from English, which uses 'by'. The noun after 'in' has no article.
en.explanation: ## The rule To say you travel by a particular vehicle or mode of transport, place in directly before the noun naming that vehicle. Do not use an article (no il, la, un, etc.) between in and the noun. **Pattern:** viaggiare / andare / venire + in + [vehicle noun, no article] ## Common transport nouns used with 'in' | Italian | English | |---|---| | in macchina | by car | | in autobus | by bus | | in treno | by train | | in aereo | by plane | | in bici / in bicicletta | by bike | | in moto / in motocicletta | by motorbike | | in taxi | by taxi | | in metropolitana | by metro / underground | | in nave | by ship / by boat | | in pullman | by coach | ## The important exception: 'a piedi' and 'a piedi' When you travel on foot, Italian does **not** use in. Instead it uses the preposition a (at/to/by): a piedi — on foot / by foot Similarly, for a horse, Italian uses a cavallo (on horseback). These are fixed expressions with a, not in, and must simply be memorised. ## Examples Vado a scuola in autobus. (I go to school by bus.) Mia madre va al lavoro in macchina. (My mother goes to work by car.) Loro viaggiano in treno ogni settimana. (They travel by train every week.) Vieni in bici o in autobus? (Are you coming by bike or by bus?) Di solito vado al supermercato a piedi. (I usually go to the supermarket on foot.) — note a piedi, not in piedi. Andiamo a Roma in aereo, non in treno. (We are going to Rome by plane, not by train.) — a contrastive pair showing in used twice in one sentence. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — adding an article:** *Vado in la macchina. ✗ The preposition in for means of transport is always followed directly by the noun, with no article. Correct: Vado in macchina. ✓ **Mistake 2 — using 'con' instead of 'in':** *Vengo con il treno. ✗ English speakers sometimes translate 'I come with the train', but Italian uses in for this meaning. Correct: Vengo in treno. ✓ (Note: con is used in other contexts, but not for standard means of transport.) **Mistake 3 — using 'in piedi' for 'on foot':** *Vado al parco in piedi. ✗ The expression in piedi means 'standing up', not 'on foot'. Always use a piedi to mean travelling on foot. Correct: Vado al parco a piedi. ✓ **Mistake 4 — using 'by' logic for all vehicles:** Not every English 'by + vehicle' maps to in in Italian. As noted above, a piedi and a cavallo use a. When in doubt, check whether the noun appears in the standard list above.
en.why_this_matters: Talking about how you get from place to place is one of the first things you need to do in Italian. The preposition in (in/by) is the standard way to express means of transport, and it appears in everyday questions and answers from the very first lessons. Getting this right removes a whole category of small but persistent errors, because English learners often reach for con (with) or try to add an article — both of which sound unnatural to a native speaker.

en.title: Using 'con' to express 'with' (company)
en.tip: Use 'con' before a noun or pronoun to say you are doing something together with another person or thing. It never changes its form — just place it directly before the word that follows. This is one of the most common prepositions you will meet from your very first conversations.
en.explanation: ## The rule Con is a preposizione propria (a 'true' preposition — a word used exclusively as a preposition). Its core meaning is **company or accompaniment**: it tells you *who* or *what* is together with the subject of the sentence. **Formation:** con does not change. It stays exactly the same regardless of the gender or number of the noun that follows it. Place it directly before the noun, pronoun, or noun phrase: con + [person / thing] = 'with' [person / thing] ## Forms and combinations Unlike most Italian prepositions, con does **not** merge with the definite articles (il, lo, la, i, gli, le) to form a single combined word in modern standard Italian. You simply write the two words separately: | Preposition + article | Form used | Example | |---|---|---| | con + il | con il (two words) | con il bambino ('with the child') | | con + la | con la (two words) | con la mamma ('with mum') | | con + i | con i (two words) | con i miei amici ('with my friends') | | con + gli | con gli (two words) | con gli studenti ('with the students') | | con + le | con le (two words) | con le sorelle ('with the sisters') | **Note for advanced curiosity:** Older or literary Italian occasionally used the merged forms col (con + il) and coi (con + i). You may see these in old texts or set phrases, but at A1 level always use the two-word form — it is correct everywhere in modern Italian. ## With pronouns When con is followed by a personal pronoun, Italian uses the pronomi tonici (stressed/independent pronouns), not the short object pronouns: | Italian | English | |---|---| | con me | 'with me' | | con te | 'with you' (informal singular) | | con lui | 'with him' | | con lei | 'with her' | | con Lei | 'with you' (formal) | | con noi | 'with us' | | con voi | 'with you' (plural) | | con loro | 'with them' | ## Examples **1. Basic company (person + person):** Mangio con la mamma. (I am eating with mum.) **2. Going somewhere with someone:** Vieni con me al supermercato? (Are you coming with me to the supermarket?) **3. With a plural noun:** Gioco con i miei amici ogni pomeriggio. (I play with my friends every afternoon.) **4. With a stressed pronoun:** Maria studia con lui. (Maria studies with him.) **5. Contrastive pair — alone vs. with someone:** Oggi mangio da solo. (Today I am eating alone.) / Oggi mangio con un amico. (Today I am eating with a friend.) — notice only con expresses company. **6. With a thing (not a person):** Bevo il tè con il latte. (I drink tea with milk.) — con can link a thing to another thing, not only people. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — using a short object pronoun after con:** *con mi ✗ → correct form: con me ✓ *con ti ✗ → correct form: con te ✓ Always use the stressed (tonic) pronoun after any preposition in Italian. **Mistake 2 — trying to merge con with the article:** *col bambino — while not wrong in older Italian, avoid this at A1 and write con il bambino ✓ to keep things clear and consistent. **Mistake 3 — confusing con with e ('and'):** Vado con Marco e Sofia. ✓ (I am going with Marco and Sofia — all three go together.) Marco e Sofia vanno. ✓ (Marco and Sofia go — they are the subject, no 'with'.) Use con when *you* accompany someone; use e simply to list people or things without implying one accompanies another. **Mistake 4 — omitting con entirely (translating literally from English 'I'm going shopping Mum'):** *Vado a fare la spesa mamma. ✗ → Vado a fare la spesa con la mamma. ✓ Italian always requires con to express accompaniment; you cannot simply place the companion's name next to the verb.
en.why_this_matters: Almost every conversation involves other people — and Italian uses con ('with') to show who is present or involved. Without it, you cannot say 'I am eating with my mum', 'he lives with a friend', or 'she is coming with me'. It appears constantly in everyday speech and is one of the first prepositions you need to master.

en.title: Using 'per' to mean 'for someone'
en.tip: Use 'per' to show that something is intended for a person or done in their benefit. It is one of the nine core Italian prepositions and works much like English 'for' in this meaning.
en.explanation: ## The rule Italian has nine core prepositions called preposizioni proprie (proper prepositions). They are: di, a, da, in, con, su, per, fra/tra. These words function exclusively as prepositions (with the minor exception of su, which can also be an adverb). Among them, per has several uses. This entry focuses on its **value of advantage or benefit** — expressing that something is done, given, bought, prepared, or intended **for the benefit of a person or group**. In English this corresponds to 'for'. **Formation:** per is invariable — it never changes form regardless of gender, number, or the word that follows. Place it directly before the noun, pronoun, or noun phrase indicating the beneficiary. **Pattern:** per + [person / group / pronoun] Examples of what follows per: | Italian | English gloss | |---|---| | per me | for me | | per te | for you (singular) | | per lui / per lei | for him / for her | | per noi | for us | | per voi | for you (plural) | | per loro | for them | | per mia madre | for my mother | | per i bambini | for the children | Note: per **does not combine** with the definite article to form a contraction (unlike di, a, da, in, su, which do). You always write per il, per la, per i, etc. as two separate words. ## Examples **1. Giving or buying something for someone** Ho comprato un regalo per mia sorella. (I bought a gift for my sister.) **2. Preparing food for someone** La mamma cucina la pasta per i bambini. (Mum is cooking pasta for the children.) **3. Doing a favour for someone** Puoi aprire la porta per me? (Can you open the door for me?) **4. Something intended for a specific person** Questo caffè è per te. (This coffee is for you.) **5. Ordering or requesting on behalf of someone** Un succo di frutta per lui, per favore. (A fruit juice for him, please.) **6. Contrastive pair — distinguishing the beneficiary** Questo libro è per me, non per te. (This book is for me, not for you.) Here per is used twice in the same sentence to contrast two different beneficiaries — a very natural pattern in spoken Italian. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using a instead of per to express benefit** ❌ Ho comprato un regalo a mia sorella. ✅ Ho comprato un regalo per mia sorella. The preposition a can appear with verbs of giving (dare qualcosa a qualcuno — to give something to someone), but when you want to say something is 'for' someone in the sense of benefit or destination, use per. **Mistake 2: Trying to contract per with the article** ❌ pel bambino (an old literary form, never used in modern Italian) ✅ per il bambino Students sometimes assume per contracts like di + il = del or a + il = al. It does not. Always write per as a separate word. **Mistake 3: Omitting per entirely** ❌ Questo è te. ✅ Questo è per te. In English, informal speech sometimes drops 'for' ('This one's you'), but in Italian the preposition per must always be present to convey the beneficiary meaning.
en.why_this_matters: The preposition per with the meaning of advantage or benefit ('for someone') appears in everyday Italian from the very first conversations — buying a gift, ordering food, doing a favour. Without it, you cannot express who something is meant for or who benefits from an action. Mastering this single use of per immediately makes your Italian sound natural in dozens of common situations.

en.title: Using 'per' for destination and purpose
en.tip: Use 'per' to say where someone is heading or why they are doing something. It answers both 'where to?' and 'what for?' in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The rule: two main uses ### 1. Motion towards a destination Use per after a verb of motion to say where someone or something is headed — that is, their destination or direction of travel. This is sometimes called moto a luogo (motion to a place). **Pattern:** [verb of motion] + per + [place] The key idea is that the person or thing is on their way there — they have not necessarily arrived yet. Think of per here as meaning 'for' or 'to' in the sense of 'bound for'. ### 2. Purpose or goal Use per to say why something is done, what something is intended for, or who something is meant for. This answers the question perché? (why? / what for?). **Pattern A — followed by an infinitive:** [main verb] + per + [infinitive] → means 'in order to do something' **Pattern B — followed by a noun:** [noun or verb] + per + [noun] → means 'for (the purpose of / intended for) something/someone' ## Formation notes Unlike di, a, in, and su, the preposition per does **not** combine with the definite articles (il, la, i, le, etc.) to form contracted forms. You always write it as a separate word. | Article | Contracted? | Example | |---|---|---| | il | No — stays per il | per il treno (for the train) | | la | No — stays per la | per la mamma (for mum) | | i | No — stays per i | per i bambini (for the children) | | le | No — stays per le | per le vacanze (for the holidays) | This is an advantage for beginners: you never need to memorise merged forms for per. ## Examples **1. Destination (motion towards a place)** Parto per Roma domani. (I'm leaving for Rome tomorrow.) → The speaker is on their way to Rome; they haven't arrived yet. Il treno parte per Milano alle otto. (The train leaves for Milan at eight.) → Classic use with transport and departure. **2. Purpose followed by an infinitive** Studio l'italiano per parlare con la mia famiglia. (I study Italian in order to speak with my family.) → per + infinitive clearly states the goal of the action. Vado al supermercato per comprare il pane. (I'm going to the supermarket to buy bread.) → Note that this sentence combines both uses: al supermercato is the destination (expressed with a + article here), while per comprare states the purpose. **3. Purpose followed by a noun (intended for something/someone)** Questo regalo è per te. (This gift is for you.) → per + pronoun to say who something is intended for. Ho comprato il latte per la colazione. (I bought the milk for breakfast.) → per + noun to say what the milk is meant for. ## Contrastive pair: 'per' vs 'a' Both per and a can appear after verbs of motion, but they are not interchangeable: | Sentence | Meaning | Focus | |---|---|---| | Parto per Roma. | I'm leaving for Rome. | Destination — still travelling, not yet there | | Vado a Roma. | I'm going to Rome. | Movement towards and arrival in Rome | Use per especially with verbs like partire (to leave/depart) and prendere (to take), where the emphasis is on setting out rather than arriving. Use a with andare (to go) when you want to say you are going to and reaching a place. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Using per + infinitive with andare when the destination itself is enough:** *Vado per il supermercato. ✗ Vado al supermercato. ✓ (I'm going to the supermarket.) → With andare and a place name or noun, use a (+ article if needed), not per. Reserve per for verbs of departure or when you want to add a purpose clause. **Mistake 2 — Forgetting the infinitive and using a conjugated verb after per:** *Studio per parlo con la famiglia. ✗ Studio per parlare con la famiglia. ✓ (I study to speak with the family.) → After per expressing purpose, the verb must always be in the infinitive (the base form ending in -are, -ere, or -ire), never conjugated. **Mistake 3 — Trying to contract per with an article:** *pel treno ✗ (archaic / non-standard) per il treno ✓ (for the train) → You may occasionally see the old contracted form pel in literary texts, but it is not used in modern Italian. Always keep per separate from the article.
en.why_this_matters: The preposition per is one of the nine core prepositions in Italian — the ones that exist only to link words together. Two of its most frequent jobs at A1 level are expressing destination ('heading to a place') and purpose ('in order to do something' or 'intended for someone/something'). You will hear and read these uses in almost every conversation, from asking where someone is going to explaining why you are doing something. Without per, you cannot express these ideas naturally in Italian.

en.title: Idiomatic prepositions in common phrases
en.tip: Italian prepositions don't always match English ones — the same preposition can have many meanings depending on the phrase. Learning fixed combinations as whole chunks is the fastest way to get them right.
en.explanation: Italian has nine core prepositions — called preposizioni proprie (proper prepositions) — and they are: di, a, da, in, con, su, per, fra, tra. Unlike English prepositions, which often translate one-to-one, Italian prepositions are highly idiomatic: the 'correct' preposition depends on the fixed phrase, not on logic or direct translation. ## The nine core prepositions | Italian | Closest English equivalent(s) | |---|---| | di | of, from, about | | a | to, at, in (a city) | | da | from, since, at someone's place | | in | in, to (a country/region), by (transport) | | con | with | | su | on, about | | per | for, in order to | | fra / tra | between, among, in (time from now) | Note: fra and tra are completely interchangeable in meaning. Italians choose between them mainly for sound — to avoid awkward repetition of similar sounds in the same phrase. ## Key rule: learn phrases as fixed chunks Because preposition use is largely idiomatic, the most reliable strategy at A1 level is to learn each high-frequency combination as a single unit. The sections below group the most important ones by meaning area. ### Telling time and scheduling — a and di Use a to say what time something happens: a che ora? a mezzogiorno, alle tre (at what time? at noon, at three o'clock). Use di for parts of the day: di mattina, di sera, di notte (in the morning, in the evening, at night). ### Location — a, in, da Use a with cities and small places: a Roma, a casa (in/at Rome, at home). Use in with countries, regions, and rooms: in Italia, in cucina (in Italy, in the kitchen). Use da to mean 'at someone's place': da Marco, dal medico (at Marco's place, at the doctor's). ### Means of transport — in and a Use in for enclosed vehicles: in macchina, in autobus, in treno (by car, by bus, by train). Use a for non-enclosed or human-powered transport: a piedi, a bicicletta (on foot, by bicycle). ### Duration and purpose — per Use per to express how long something lasts or why you do it: per un'ora, per mangiare (for an hour, in order to eat). ### Time from now — fra / tra Use fra or tra to say something will happen after a given interval: fra cinque minuti, tra una settimana (in five minutes, in a week). ## Examples La lezione comincia alle nove di mattina. (The lesson starts at nine in the morning.) → alle = a + le for clock time; di mattina for part of the day. Vado a Roma in treno. (I'm going to Rome by train.) → a for a city; in for an enclosed vehicle. Mangio a casa di Marco. (I'm eating at Marco's house.) → a casa is a fixed phrase; di Marco specifies whose house. Arrivo fra dieci minuti. (I'll arrive in ten minutes.) → fra signals future time from now, not duration. Studio italiano per un'ora ogni sera. (I study Italian for one hour every evening.) → per expresses duration; ogni sera is another fixed time phrase worth learning as a chunk. Vado dal medico domani. (I'm going to the doctor's tomorrow.) → da meaning 'at/to someone's place' — never use a here. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — translating in literally for cities** English says 'in Rome', but Italian uses a: a Roma, not *in Roma. Reserve in for countries and regions: in Italia. **Mistake 2 — using a for 'by car'** English says 'by car', which might suggest a macchina, but the correct form is in macchina. Only non-enclosed transport uses a: a piedi. **Mistake 3 — using per for 'in five minutes' (future)** English 'in five minutes' (meaning 'after five minutes') is fra cinque minuti, not *per cinque minuti. Per cinque minuti means 'for five minutes' (duration). **Mistake 4 — forgetting da for 'at someone's place'** Saying 'at the doctor's' or 'at Anna's' requires da: dal medico, da Anna. Using a here is a common error with no direct English parallel to guide you — this one must be memorised. **Mistake 5 — confusing di mattina and alle … di mattina** Di mattina alone means 'in the morning (generally)'. When you give a clock time, you add both: alle otto di mattina (at eight in the morning). Don't drop alle when a specific hour is mentioned.
en.why_this_matters: Prepositions appear in almost every Italian sentence. Because they don't map neatly onto English equivalents, they are one of the most common sources of errors for beginners. Mastering the most frequent fixed combinations — for telling time, locations, means of transport, and daily routines — lets you build correct, natural-sounding sentences from day one instead of guessing and getting it wrong.

en.title: Simple prepositions in everyday formulas
en.tip: Italian has nine core prepositions — di, a, da, in, con, su, per, fra/tra — and you will meet them in fixed phrases from your very first lessons. Learning the most common phrase-by-phrase combinations now will let you speak naturally before you have mastered every grammatical rule behind them.
en.explanation: ## The nine core prepositions Italian grammarians call these the preposizioni proprie ('proper prepositions') because — with one small exception — they work exclusively as prepositions. They are: | Italian | Closest English equivalent(s) | |---|---| | di | of, from | | a | to, at | | da | from, by, since | | in | in, into, to | | con | with | | su | on, on top of | | per | for, through, in order to | | fra / tra | between, among, in (time) | Fra and tra are completely interchangeable in meaning; you may choose either one freely. The only reason to prefer one over the other is to avoid awkward-sounding repetition — for example, native speakers usually avoid saying tra treni and would choose fra treni instead. ## The one exception: su as an adverb All nine prepositions are used exclusively as prepositions, with one small exception: su can also function as an adverb meaning 'up'. You will see this in phrases like vieni su! ('come up!'). At A1 level you do not need to worry about this distinction — simply be aware that su sometimes stands alone without a following noun. ## Formulaic uses you need from day one At A1, the most practical approach is to learn these prepositions inside the fixed phrases you encounter most often. Below are the key formulas grouped by preposition. ### di — of, from Di shows possession or origin and appears in countless set expressions. - un bicchiere di acqua — a glass of water - Sono di Roma. — I am from Rome. - di mattina — in the morning (set time expression) ### a — to, at A expresses location (staying somewhere) or direction (going somewhere), and appears in greetings and time expressions. - a casa — at home - a scuola — at school - a domani! — see you tomorrow! (literally 'until tomorrow') - a presto! — see you soon! - alle tre — at three o'clock ### da — from, by, since, at someone's place Da is one of the most versatile prepositions. Its key formulaic uses at A1 are: - Vengo da Milano. — I come from Milan. - da quanto tempo? — since how long? / how long has it been? - da stamattina — since this morning - da Maria — at Maria's place (used like French chez) ### in — in, to, into In is used with countries, rooms, and means of transport. - in Italia — in Italy / to Italy - in cucina — in the kitchen - in autobus — by bus ### con — with Con is the most straightforward preposition — it almost always means 'with'. - con la famiglia — with the family - un caffè con latte — a coffee with milk ### su — on - Il libro è sul tavolo. — The book is on the table. (Note: sul = su + il, a contracted form — see the note on contracted prepositions below.) ### per — for, in order to - per favore — please (literally 'as a favour') — one of the most essential fixed phrases in Italian - per te — for you - Studiamo per imparare. — We study in order to learn. ### fra / tra — between, among, in (future time) - fra due giorni — in two days (time counted forward from now) - tra amici — among friends - fra me e te — between me and you ## Important: prepositions combine with articles Several prepositions merge with the definite article (il, la, lo, i, gli, le) to form a single contracted word called a preposizione articolata ('articulated preposition'). This is a separate rule, but you need to recognise these forms as soon as you start reading Italian. The most common contractions you will meet at A1: | Preposition + article | Contracted form | Example | |---|---|---| | di + il | del | del pane (some bread / of the bread) | | a + il | al | al bar (at the café) | | da + il | dal | dal medico (at the doctor's) | | in + il | nel | nel parco (in the park) | | su + il | sul | sul tavolo (on the table) | Con, per, fra, and tra do **not** contract with the article in modern Italian — they always stay separate. ## Full examples with translations 1. Vado a scuola con mia sorella. — I go to school with my sister. 2. Il gatto è sul divano. — The cat is on the sofa. 3. Abito in Italia da tre anni. — I have lived in Italy for three years. (da + time period = duration up to the present) 4. Un caffè per favore, senza zucchero. — A coffee please, without sugar. 5. Arriviamo fra cinque minuti. — We will arrive in five minutes. 6. Sei di Milano o di Roma? — Are you from Milan or from Rome? ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Confusing a and in for location.** English uses 'in' for most places, but Italian uses a with cities and in with countries and rooms. - ✗ *Sono in Roma. - ✓ Sono a Roma. — I am in Rome. - ✓ Sono in Italia. — I am in Italy. **Mistake 2 — Translating 'for + time' with per when you mean duration up to now.** When an action started in the past and is still happening, Italian uses da, not per. - ✗ *Studio italiano per due anni. - ✓ Studio italiano da due anni. — I have been studying Italian for two years. **Mistake 3 — Forgetting that fra and tra are identical in meaning.** Students sometimes assume one is more formal or more correct. They are fully interchangeable — choose whichever sounds better next to the words around it. **Mistake 4 — Writing contracted prepositions as two separate words.** - ✗ *a il bar - ✓ al bar — the contraction is mandatory, not optional.
en.why_this_matters: Prepositions are the small words that glue sentences together, and in Italian they appear constantly — in greetings, times, places, and everyday requests. Even at the very beginning, you will need fixed phrases like a casa ('at home') or per favore ('please') long before you understand every rule that governs prepositions. Recognising these nine core words and their most common formulaic uses removes a huge source of early confusion and lets you communicate from day one.

en.title: Adverbs of manner: bene and male
en.tip: The words 'bene' (well) and 'male' (badly) describe how an action is done. They never change their form — they look the same no matter who is doing the action or what tense the verb is in.
en.explanation: ## What adverbs of manner are An adverb of manner answers the question 'come?' (how?). It modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb, telling us in what way something happens. The textbook category of manner adverbs (avverbi di modo) is the largest class of adverbs in Italian. Bene and male are the two most essential members of this class at A1 level. ## The core rule Both bene and male are **invariable**: they have one fixed form only. They do not agree with any noun or pronoun in gender or number. They are placed **directly after the verb** they modify in a simple tense, or after the past participle in a compound tense. ### Forms at a glance | Adverb | Meaning | Changes form? | |---|---|---| | bene | well | never | | male | badly, poorly | never | ## How to use them ### Modifying a verb Place bene or male immediately after the conjugated verb: - Marco parla bene l'italiano. — Marco speaks Italian well. - Io canto male. — I sing badly. In compound tenses (e.g. the passato prossimo, present perfect), the adverb follows the past participle: - Hai dormito bene? — Did you sleep well? - Ho mangiato male ieri sera. — I ate badly last night. ### The greeting formula The single most common use of these two adverbs at A1 level is in greetings. When someone asks 'Come stai?' (How are you?), the standard replies use bene or male with the verb stare (to be, in the sense of feeling): - Sto bene, grazie. — I am well, thank you. - Sto male oggi. — I am not well / I feel bad today. Note that bene and male can also stand alone as short answers: 'Bene!' or 'Male...' ## Important variants and related forms ### Modifying an adjective or another adverb Less commonly at A1, bene can strengthen an adjective, where it means 'quite' or 'really': - È bene cotto. — It is well cooked / properly cooked. ### Comparative and superlative forms Like most adverbs, bene and male have irregular comparative and superlative forms. You will meet these at a higher level, but they are listed here for completeness: | Form | bene | male | |---|---|---| | base | bene (well) | male (badly) | | comparative | meglio (better) | peggio (worse) | | superlative | benissimo (very well) | malissimo (very badly) | At A1 you only need bene and male themselves, but recognising benissimo and malissimo (formed by adding -issimo to the stem) is useful from the start. ## Examples covering key uses 1. La bambina disegna bene. — The little girl draws well. *(verb modified)* 2. Mio fratello cucina male. — My brother cooks badly. *(verb modified)* 3. Come stai? — Sto bene! — How are you? — I am well! *(greeting formula)* 4. Hai capito bene la lezione? — Did you understand the lesson well? *(compound tense)* 5. Ho dormito male stanotte. — I slept badly last night. *(compound tense + time adverb)* 6. Parla bene lui, ma lei parla male. — He speaks well, but she speaks badly. *(contrastive pair — note: bene and male are identical in form whether the subject is masculine or feminine)* ## Common learner mistakes ### Mistake 1: Confusing the adverb with the adjective The adjective meaning 'good' is buono/buona, and the adjective meaning 'bad' is cattivo/cattiva. These describe nouns and must agree in gender and number. Bene and male describe actions (verbs) and never change. ❌ *Parla buono l'italiano. — Wrong: buono is an adjective; it cannot modify a verb. ✅ Parla bene l'italiano. — Correct: use the adverb bene to modify the verb. ❌ *Canta cattiva. — Wrong: cattiva is an adjective and cannot describe how someone sings. ✅ Canta male. — Correct. ### Mistake 2: Making the adverb agree with the subject Because Italian adjectives agree with nouns, beginners sometimes try to make adverbs agree too. This is never correct. ❌ *Le ragazze parlano beni. — Wrong: bene does not take a plural form. ✅ Le ragazze parlano bene. — Correct: the adverb stays bene regardless of the subject. ### Mistake 3: Using 'stare' vs 'essere' with bene When talking about health or how someone feels, Italian uses stare bene / stare male, not essere bene. ❌ *Sono bene. — Unnatural in this context. ✅ Sto bene. — Correct: I am well / I feel well. ### Mistake 4: Wrong word order In Italian, manner adverbs come after the verb (or after the past participle in compound tenses), not before it as sometimes happens in English ('she well understands'). ❌ *Bene parla italiano. ✅ Parla bene italiano. — Correct word order.
en.why_this_matters: The adverbs bene (well) and male (badly/poorly) are among the most frequently used words in everyday Italian. You will need them from your very first conversations — to say how someone is feeling, how well you understand something, or how a meal tastes. Because they are invariable (they never change form), learning them is straightforward, but knowing exactly where to place them and how they differ from similar adjectives removes one of the most persistent errors beginners make.

en.title: Adverbs of place: here, there, inside, outside…
en.tip: Italian adverbs of place tell you *where* something or someone is — words like 'here', 'there', 'inside', 'outside', 'near', 'far'. They never change their form, no matter what noun or verb they are used with.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what adverbs of place are and how they work An adverb of place (avverbio di luogo, an unchanging word that says *where*) is an **invariable** word — it has only one form. It never agrees with a noun like an adjective does. It modifies a verb, telling you where the action happens, or it modifies another word to give location. The core A1 adverbs of place are listed below with their meanings: | Italiano | English | |---|---| | qui / qua | here | | lì / là | there | | dentro | inside | | fuori | outside | | sopra | above / on top | | sotto | below / underneath | | davanti | in front | | dietro | behind / at the back | | vicino | near / nearby | | lontano | far / far away | | su | up | | giù | down | | avanti | forward / ahead | | indietro | back / backward | ## qui / qua and lì / là — what is the difference? Both pairs mean 'here' and 'there' respectively, and in everyday spoken Italian they are largely interchangeable. The traditional distinction is: - qui and lì point to a **precise** spot. - qua and là point to a **vaguer or wider** area. At A1 level, do not worry about this distinction — both forms are correct and understood. Just be consistent within a sentence. ## Examples Il gatto è qui. (The cat is here.) La borsa è là, sul tavolo. (The bag is there, on the table.) I bambini giocano fuori. (The children are playing outside.) Vieni dentro! Fa freddo. (Come inside! It's cold.) Il libro è sopra, il quaderno è sotto. (The book is on top, the notebook is underneath.) — a contrastive pair showing two adverbs of place in the same sentence. La scuola non è lontano; è vicino. (The school is not far; it is nearby.) — a contrastive pair with a negative. ## Adverbs of place used with a following noun (preposition + noun) Many of these adverbs can also work as **prepositions** when followed directly by a noun. When they stand alone (no noun after them), they are adverbs. Compare: - Adverb alone: Marco è davanti. (Marco is in front.) - Followed by a noun: Marco è davanti alla scuola. (Marco is in front of the school.) At A1 level you will mostly use these words as standalone adverbs. Just be aware that adding a ('to/at') or di ('of') after them is also possible and very common. ## Invariability — the key point Unlike adjectives, adverbs **never change**. Whether the subject is masculine, feminine, singular, or plural, the adverb stays the same: - Il papà è dentro. ✓ - La mamma è dentro. ✓ - I bambini sono dentro. ✓ There is nothing to agree with — the form never changes. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — trying to make the adverb agree with the noun** *Il gatto è fuora. ✗ — fuori has only one form. Write: Il gatto è fuori. ✓ **Mistake 2 — confusing qui/qua and lì/là with the pronouns ci and vi** You may soon meet ci and vi (also meaning 'there/here' in certain structures). At A1, stick to qui/qua and lì/là for simple location; ci and vi are covered at a higher level. **Mistake 3 — using su and giù for location instead of direction** In Italian, su ('up') and giù ('down') most naturally describe **movement or direction**, not a static position. For a static position, sopra and sotto are more natural: - Direction: Vai su! (Go up!) ✓ - Position: Il gatto è sopra il letto. (The cat is on top of the bed.) ✓ — not *su il letto ✗ **Mistake 4 — forgetting the accent on là** Write là (with a grave accent) for the adverb 'there'. Without the accent, la is the feminine definite article or an object pronoun — a completely different word.
en.why_this_matters: Every time you describe where something is, where you are going, or where someone is standing, you need an adverb of place. These words appear in almost every conversation — giving directions, describing your home, talking about people around you. Without them you cannot answer the most basic question of all: Dov'è? ('Where is it?')

en.title: Time adverbs: when, how often, how soon
en.tip: Italian time adverbs tell you when something happens or how often it happens. They never change their form — they are the same word whether the subject is singular or plural, masculine or feminine.
en.explanation: ## What a time adverb is An adverb (avverbio, an unchanging word that modifies a verb) of time tells you when or how often an action happens. Italian time adverbs are invariable — they have only one form. They never agree with a noun or verb, so there is nothing to conjugate or decline. ## Core time adverbs at A1 The table below groups the most important A1 time adverbs by meaning. | Italian | English meaning | Category | |---|---|---| | ora / adesso | now | point in time | | oggi | today | point in time | | ieri | yesterday | point in time | | domani | tomorrow | point in time | | dopo | after / later | point in time | | presto | soon / early | point in time | | tardi | late | point in time | | sempre | always | frequency | | spesso | often | frequency | | mai | never / ever | frequency | ## Where to place a time adverb in a sentence The most common position is after the verb (or after the object if there is one). This is the neutral, unmarked order. Mangio adesso. — I am eating now. You can also place a time adverb at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, especially with words like oggi, domani, and ieri. Oggi ho scuola. — Today I have school. Frequency adverbs (sempre, spesso, mai) most naturally sit after the verb in a simple tense. Mia madre cucina sempre. — My mother always cooks. ## Using mai ('never' / 'ever') This adverb has two distinct uses and is one of the trickiest at A1. 1. In a negative sentence, mai means never. Italian requires double negation: you must keep non before the verb and add mai after it. Non mangio mai la carne. — I never eat meat. 2. In a question, mai means ever. Mangi mai la pizza? — Do you ever eat pizza? ## ora and adesso: two words for 'now' Both ora and adesso mean now and are interchangeable in everyday speech. Neither is more formal than the other at this level. Sono a casa ora. — I am at home now. Sono a casa adesso. — I am at home now. (same meaning) ## presto: 'soon' or 'early' Context decides the meaning. When presto refers to how soon something will happen, it means soon. When it describes the time of day something happens, it means early. A presto! — See you soon! Mi alzo presto. — I get up early. ## Examples covering the main uses 1. Ieri ho mangiato la pasta. — Yesterday I ate pasta. 2. Domani c'è una festa. — Tomorrow there is a party. 3. Arrivo tardi oggi. — I am arriving late today. 4. Mio fratello studia sempre. — My brother always studies. 5. Non vado mai a letto presto. — I never go to bed early. 6. Dopo, beviamo il caffè. — Afterwards, we drink coffee. ## Common learner mistakes Mistake 1 — Dropping non with mai: ❌ Mangio mai la carne. ✅ Non mangio mai la carne. — Italian always needs non before the verb even when mai is present. You cannot drop non the way English drops 'not' when it uses 'never'. Mistake 2 — Treating domani or ieri as adjectives and trying to make them agree: ❌ la lezione domania ✅ la lezione di domani — When you want to say 'tomorrow's lesson', use the preposition di before the time adverb. The adverb itself never changes. Mistake 3 — Placing sempre or spesso before the verb in a simple tense, copying English word order: ❌ Io sempre mangio la colazione. ✅ Io mangio sempre la colazione. — In Italian the frequency adverb follows the conjugated verb, not precedes it. Mistake 4 — Confusing presto (early/soon) with prima (before/first): These are two different adverbs. Presto relates to how early or how soon; prima means before or first in a sequence. ✅ Prima mangio, poi studio. — First I eat, then I study.
en.why_this_matters: Time adverbs are among the very first words you need in Italian. Without them, you cannot say 'today', 'never', 'always', 'yesterday', or 'tomorrow' — words that appear in almost every conversation. Because they never change form, they are also one of the easiest building blocks to master, and getting them right immediately makes your Italian sound natural.
