en.title: Adverbs of quantity: molto, poco, tanto, and more
en.tip: Words like 'molto' (a lot), 'poco' (a little), and 'troppo' (too much) can describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs without ever changing their form. When used as adverbs, they stay the same no matter what word they modify — do not add endings to match gender or number.
en.explanation: ## The rule: what adverbs of quantity are and how they work An adverb of quantity tells you *how much* or *to what degree* something happens or is true. In Italian, adverbs are **invariable** — they never change their ending for gender or number. An adverb of quantity can modify: - a **verb**: Mangio molto. (I eat a lot.) - an **adjective**: È molto stanca. (She is very tired.) - another **adverb**: Parla troppo lentamente. (He speaks too slowly.) The key point: when one of these words functions as an **adverb**, it is frozen in one form. It does **not** agree with any noun or adjective it appears near. ## The most important adverbs of quantity at A1 Here are the core adverbs you need to know first, with their basic meanings: | Avverbio | English | |---|---| | molto | a lot, very, much | | poco | a little, not very, not much | | tanto | so much, a lot | | troppo | too much, too | | abbastanza | enough, quite | | quasi | almost, nearly | | più | more | | meno | less, fewer | | niente / nulla | nothing (also used to mean 'not at all' in some constructions) | | un po' | a little bit (short for un poco) | | assai | very, quite a lot (slightly formal) | | parecchio | quite a lot, rather a lot | | soltanto / solo | only, just | | almeno | at least | | piuttosto | rather, quite | ## Forming sentences: position and use **When modifying a verb**, the adverb usually comes directly after the verb: Dormo molto. — I sleep a lot. Mangi poco. — You eat very little. Studiamo tanto. — We study a lot. **When modifying an adjective or another adverb**, it comes directly before that word: Il caffè è troppo caldo. — The coffee is too hot. Parla abbastanza bene. — She speaks quite well. ## Examples covering the main uses **1. Modifying a verb** Mia sorella mangia poco. My sister eats very little. **2. Modifying an adjective** Questo esercizio è molto facile. This exercise is very easy. **3. Expressing excess** Bevi troppo caffè! You drink too much coffee! **4. Using un po' to soften a statement** Sono un po' stanco oggi. I am a little tired today. **5. Modifying another adverb** Arriva sempre molto tardi. He always arrives very late. **6. Contrastive pair — più and meno** Marco parla più di me, ma capisce meno. Marco talks more than me, but understands less. ## Critical exception: adverb vs. adjective Several of these words — molto, poco, tanto, troppo, parecchio, altrettanto — can also be used as **adjectives** that directly modify a noun. When they are adjectives, they **do** agree in gender and number with the noun. Compare: | Function | Italian | English | |---|---|---| | Adverb (modifies adjective) | una pizza molto buona | a very good pizza | | Adjective (modifies noun) | molta pizza | a lot of pizza | | Adverb (modifies verb) | mangio molto | I eat a lot | | Adjective (modifies noun) | molti bambini | many children | **Rule of thumb**: if the word comes before a noun and you could replace it with a number or 'many/much', it is an adjective and must agree. If it comes after a verb, or before another adjective or adverb, it is functioning as an adverb and stays invariable. ## Special note on 'un po'' Un po' is a contraction of un poco (a little bit) and is far more common in everyday speech. It is always written with an apostrophe showing the dropped syllable. It softens adjectives and verbs: Parla un po' piano, per favore. — Speak a little quietly, please. Ho un po' di fame. — I am a little hungry. (lit. I have a little of hunger.) Note: un po' di (a little of) is followed by a noun and is a fixed expression. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Adding adjective endings to an adverb.** Incorrect: *È multa brava. Correct: È molto brava. (She is very good.) When molto modifies an adjective like brava, it is an adverb. It does not change to match brava's feminine form. It is always molto, never *molta in this role. **Mistake 2: Confusing molto (adverb) with molti/molte (adjective).** Incorrect: *Ho molto amici. Correct: Ho molti amici. (I have many friends.) — here molti is an adjective agreeing with the masculine plural noun amici. **Mistake 3: Writing un po without the apostrophe.** Incorrect: *un po Correct: un po' — the apostrophe is always required because a syllable has been dropped. **Mistake 4: Using molto where English uses 'very much' after a verb, then trying to translate 'very' and 'much' separately.** Incorrect: *Mi piace molto molto. Correct: Mi piace molto. — I like it very much. One molto is enough; doubling it is non-standard (though informal repetition like tantissimo exists as a separate intensified form).
en.why_this_matters: Adverbs of quantity are among the most frequently used words in everyday Italian. You need them to say things like 'I eat a lot', 'she speaks a little', or 'this is very good' — sentences that come up from the very first day of learning. Without them, you cannot express degree or amount, and you will also avoid a very common error: adding adjective endings to words that must stay invariable.

label: Avverbi di giudizio: sì, no, non, certo, quasi

en.title: Adverbs of judgement: yes, no, not, and more
en.tip: Italian has a small set of words — like 'sì', 'no', 'non', 'certo', and 'forse' — that let you agree, disagree, or express doubt. The most important rule: 'non' always comes directly before the verb, while 'no' and 'sì' stand alone.
en.explanation: ## What adverbs of judgement are An avverbio di giudizio is an adverb that does not describe how, when, or where an action happens — instead, it expresses your verdict on what is being said. Italian grammar divides these into three groups: - **Affirmative** (you confirm or agree): sì, certo, certamente, davvero, naturalmente, sicuramente, proprio, esattamente - **Negative** (you deny or contradict): no, non, mica, neanche, nemmeno, neppure - **Dubitative** (you express doubt or possibility): forse, quasi, magari, probabilmente, eventualmente ## The core rule: 'sì' and 'no' stand alone; 'non' goes before the verb This is the single most important distinction in this group. - Sì and no are used **as a complete answer on their own**, or as a short tag. They never attach directly to a verb. - Non is the word that actually **negates a verb**. It must be placed **immediately before the verb** in the sentence. Think of them as having two different jobs: sì/no are replies, while non is a grammatical operator that flips the meaning of a verb. ## Forming negative sentences with 'non' Place non directly before the conjugated verb. Nothing comes between non and the verb (except object pronouns — see note below). | Affirmative | Negative | |---|---| | Parlo italiano. | Non parlo italiano. | | Hai fame. | Non hai fame. | | È mia sorella. | Non è mia sorella. | **Note on pronouns:** Object pronouns (mi, ti, lo, la, ci, vi, li, le) attach between non and the verb — for example, non lo so ('I don't know it'). This is simply how Italian works; do not let it confuse the basic rule. ## How the affirmative adverbs work Words like certo, certamente, davvero, sicuramente and naturalmente intensify or confirm a statement. They can stand alone as a reply, or appear inside a sentence — usually at the start or end, but sometimes mid-sentence. They do **not** change form (they are invariable). ## How the dubitative adverbs work Words like forse ('perhaps/maybe') and probabilmente ('probably') express uncertainty. They are invariable and typically placed at the beginning or end of a sentence, or before the verb. At A1 level, forse is by far the most useful to know. ## Examples **1. Answering yes or no:** — Parli italiano? — Sì, parlo italiano. (Do you speak Italian? — Yes, I speak Italian.) **2. Answering no — 'no' as a standalone reply:** — Hai un cane? — No, non ho un cane. (Do you have a dog? — No, I don't have a dog.) Notice: no is the reply; non negates the verb in the sentence that follows. **3. Confirming strongly with 'certo':** — Ti piace la pizza? — Certo, mi piace molto! (Do you like pizza? — Of course, I like it a lot!) **4. Expressing doubt with 'forse':** Forse Maria è a casa. (Maybe Maria is at home.) **5. Using 'davvero' to show surprise or sincerity:** Davvero non sai dov'è il bar? (Really? You don't know where the café is?) **6. Contrastive pair — 'no' alone vs. 'non' before the verb:** No, non mangio carne. (No, I don't eat meat.) Here both words appear: no is the standalone negative reply; non negates the verb mangio. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using 'no' before a verb instead of 'non'.** ❌ Io no parlo inglese. ✅ Io non parlo inglese. (I don't speak English.) The word no can never be placed directly in front of a verb to negate it. Only non does this job. **Mistake 2: Leaving out 'non' and using only 'no' inside a sentence.** ❌ Io no ho fame. ✅ Io non ho fame. (I'm not hungry.) **Mistake 3: Putting another word between 'non' and the verb (at A1 level).** ❌ Io non oggi mangio. ✅ Io non mangio oggi. (I'm not eating today.) Keep non and the verb together. **Mistake 4: Confusing 'forse' (perhaps) with 'magari'.** Both can translate as 'maybe', but magari often implies a wish or hope ('if only!'). At A1, stick with forse for simple 'maybe'. ## Quick-reference summary | Word | Type | Position | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | sì | affirmative | standalone or sentence start | 'yes' | | no | negative | standalone or sentence start | 'no' | | non | negative | directly before the verb | 'not' | | certo / certamente | affirmative | standalone or start/end of sentence | 'certainly / of course' | | davvero | affirmative | start/end of sentence | 'really / truly' | | forse | dubitative | start/end of sentence or before verb | 'perhaps / maybe' | | quasi | dubitative | before verb or adjective | 'almost / nearly' |}
en.why_this_matters: From your very first conversation in Italian, you need to say yes, no, maybe, and certainly — and you need to say them correctly. Italian has a dedicated group of adverbs called avverbi di giudizio (adverbs of judgement) that do exactly this job. Getting them right — especially knowing when to use no versus non — will immediately prevent one of the most common mistakes Italian learners make.

label: Avverbi interrogativi: come, dove, quando, quanto, perché

en.title: Question adverbs: come, dove, quando, quanto, perché
en.tip: Italian has five key question adverbs — come, dove, quando, quanto, and perché — that let you ask about manner, place, time, quantity, and reason. They always stay the same no matter what they describe, and they go at or near the start of a question. Mastering these five words unlocks most everyday questions in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The five Italian question adverbs Italian has five core question adverbs. They are **invariable** — they never change their form, regardless of the noun, verb, or tense they appear with. | Avverbio | English meaning | What it asks about | |---|---|---| | come | how / what (name) | manner, description | | dove | where | place, location | | quando | when | time | | quanto | how much / how many | quantity, price, degree | | perché | why / because | reason, cause | ## How to form a question with these adverbs Place the question adverb at the **beginning** of the sentence (or very close to the start), then add the verb and the rest of the sentence. In spoken Italian, the subject pronoun often comes after the verb, or is dropped entirely. Basic pattern: [avverbio interrogativo] + [verbo] + [soggetto / resto della frase]? Example structure: Dove abiti? (Where do you live?) ## Each adverb explained ### come — how, what Come (how) asks about the **manner** in which something happens, or — very commonly at A1 — it asks for a **name or description**. It is also the standard word used in greetings. - Come stai? — How are you? - Come si chiama tua madre? — What is your mother's name? (literally: How is your mother called?) - Come vai a scuola? — How do you get to school? **Note:** When come is followed by a verb beginning with a vowel, the final -e is sometimes dropped in informal writing and speech: com'è? (how is it? / what is it like?). ### dove — where Dove (where) asks about **location or destination**. Like come, it may drop its final vowel before a verb starting with a vowel: dov'è? (where is it?). - Dove abiti? — Where do you live? - Dov'è il bagno? — Where is the bathroom? ### quando — when Quando (when) asks about **time** — a moment, a day, a period. It does not elide (drop a vowel) before other vowels. - Quando mangi? — When do you eat? - Quando arriva il treno? — When does the train arrive? ### quanto — how much, how many Quanto (how much / how many) asks about **quantity, price, or degree**. As a question **adverb** modifying a verb or adjective, it is invariable and stays as quanto. (Be careful: when quanto is used as an **adjective** directly before a noun — meaning 'how many [things]?' — it must agree in gender and number with the noun: quanta acqua, quanti studenti. At A1, the adverb use with a verb is most common.) - Quanto costa? — How much does it cost? - Quanto è lontano? — How far is it? (literally: How far away is it?) ### perché — why (and also: because) Perché (why) asks for a **reason or cause**. Importantly, the same word perché is also the word for **'because'** in answers — so you will see it in both questions and replies. Context makes the meaning clear. - Perché sei stanco? — Why are you tired? - Perché non mangi? — Why aren't you eating? - Answer: Perché non ho fame. — Because I'm not hungry. ## Reinforcing with mai Any of these five adverbs can be strengthened by adding mai (ever / on earth) immediately after them. This makes the question feel more emphatic or impatient. - Come mai sei qui? — How come / Why on earth are you here? - Dove mai hai messo le chiavi? — Where on earth have you put the keys? - Perché mai piange? — Why on earth is he/she crying? ## Full examples covering all five adverbs 1. Come si chiama? — What is his/her name? (literally: How is he/she called?) 2. Dov'è la stazione? — Where is the station? 3. Quando apre il negozio? — When does the shop open? 4. Quanto costa questo panino? — How much does this sandwich cost? 5. Perché non vieni a cena? — Why aren't you coming to dinner? 6. Contrastive pair — question vs. answer with perché: Perché non studi? — Why don't you study? / Perché sono stanco. — Because I'm tired. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Confusing perché as only 'why'.** Learners sometimes try to use perché only for questions and search for a different word for 'because'. Remember: in Italian, perché does both jobs. Perché sei qui? — Perché ho fame. (Why are you here? — Because I'm hungry.) **Mistake 2 — Making quanto invariable in all uses.** As a question adverb before a verb (Quanto costa?), quanto does not change. But before a noun it works as an adjective and must agree: Quanta acqua? (How much water?), Quanti anni hai? (How old are you? — literally: How many years do you have?). Do not write *quanto anni. **Mistake 3 — Forgetting elision with come and dove.** Before è (is), both come and dove normally contract: com'è, dov'è. Writing come è or dove è is not incorrect, but com'è and dov'è are far more natural and what you will see in texts. **Mistake 4 — Putting the question adverb in the middle of the sentence.** In Italian, question adverbs go at or near the **beginning**: Dove lavori? — not *Lavori dove? (while technically interpretable in speech, it is non-standard in written Italian). **Mistake 5 — Using come to ask for a name in English word order.** English says 'What is your name?' using 'what'. Italian uses come: Come ti chiami? Do not translate literally and write *Cosa è il tuo nome? — this sounds very unnatural.
en.why_this_matters: Without question adverbs, you cannot ask most of the basic questions you need every day — 'Where is the bathroom?', 'When does the lesson start?', 'How much does it cost?', 'Why are you tired?'. These five words appear in almost every conversation, every sign, and every exercise at A1 level. Mastering them immediately makes you able to ask — and understand — a huge range of real questions.

en.title: Making affirmative and negative statements
en.tip: To say something is true, just use a normal sentence. To say something is NOT true, place 'non' directly before the verb — that single word makes any Italian statement negative.
en.explanation: ## What is a statement? A proposizione enunciativa (declarative clause) is a complete unit of meaning built around a verb. It states a fact, describes a situation, or reports information. When a statement asserts that something IS the case, it is affermativa (affirmative). When it asserts that something is NOT the case, it is negativa (negative). A statement is different from a question or a command: it simply tells you how things are — or are not. ## Forming affirmative statements An affirmative statement in Italian follows a straightforward order: **Subject + Verb (+ rest of sentence)** The subject can be a noun or a pronoun. Because Italian verb endings already signal who is speaking, the subject pronoun is often omitted — this is perfectly normal at every level. ## Forming negative statements To make any statement negative, place non (not) **immediately before the verb** — and nothing else changes. **Subject + non + Verb (+ rest of sentence)** This is the complete rule. There is no second negative word required in standard negation. Non never moves away from the verb; it always sits directly in front of it. ## The rule at a glance | Type | Structure | Example | |---|---|---| | Affirmative | Subject + Verb | Io mangio la pizza. | | Negative | Subject + non + Verb | Io non mangio la pizza. | | Affirmative (no pronoun) | Verb | Mangio la pizza. | | Negative (no pronoun) | Non + Verb | Non mangio la pizza. | ## Examples **1. Simple affirmative statement** Maria parla italiano. — Maria speaks Italian. **2. Simple negative statement** Maria non parla inglese. — Maria does not speak English. **3. Affirmative with essere (to be)** Io sono stanco. — I am tired. **4. Negative with essere** Io non sono stanco. — I am not tired. **5. Affirmative without subject pronoun (very common in Italian)** Abito a Roma. — I live in Rome. **6. Negative without subject pronoun — contrastive pair** Non abito a Milano, abito a Roma. — I do not live in Milan; I live in Rome. ## Important variants: double negatives with words like niente and nessuno When a negative word such as niente (nothing), nessuno (nobody), or mai (never) comes **after** the verb, non is still required before the verb. Italian uses this double negative construction — it is correct and mandatory, not a mistake. Non mangio niente. — I eat nothing. / I do not eat anything. Non viene nessuno. — Nobody is coming. However, if the negative word comes **before** the verb, non is dropped: Nessuno viene. — Nobody is coming. This variant is introduced here for awareness; you will practise it fully at a later level. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Putting non after the verb** ❌ Mangio non la pizza. ✅ Non mangio la pizza. Non must come directly **before** the verb, never after it. **Mistake 2 — Separating non from the verb with another word** ❌ Non io mangio la pizza. ✅ Io non mangio la pizza. Non belongs immediately before the verb, not before the subject. **Mistake 3 — Translating English 'do not' with two words** English needs a helper verb: 'I do not eat.' Italian does not. One word — non — placed before the verb is all that is needed. ❌ Io faccio non mangio. ✅ Io non mangio. — I do not eat. **Mistake 4 — Omitting non when a negative word follows the verb** ❌ Mangio niente. ✅ Non mangio niente. — I eat nothing. When niente, mai, or nessuno follows the verb, non before the verb is still compulsory.
en.why_this_matters: Every conversation requires you to confirm or deny things: 'Parlo italiano' versus 'Non parlo italiano.' These two sentence types — affirmative and negative statements — are the most basic building blocks of Italian. Without them you cannot introduce yourself, describe your family, order food, or correct a misunderstanding. Master this rule and every topic you study becomes expressible.

en.title: Expressing wishes with volitive verbs
en.tip: To say what you would like or want, use a verb like 'volere' or 'piacere' in the conditional tense. This softer form is more polite than a direct request and is the standard way to express a wish or desire in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The rule: expressing a wish with a volitive verb in the conditional A **volitive verb** is a verb that expresses wanting, wishing, or liking. The most important ones at A1 are: | Infinito | Meaning | |---|---| | volere | to want | | desiderare | to desire / wish | | piacere | to like (literally: to be pleasing) | To express a wish politely, put the volitive verb into the **conditional present** (condizionale presente) — the Italian equivalent of 'would like' or 'would love to'. The conditional signals that something is desired but depends on circumstances; it is also simply the polite, softened form used for everyday wishes. ## Forming the conditional present of the key verbs The conditional present is formed by taking the **infinitive stem** (with a small spelling change for most verbs: the final -e of the infinitive is dropped and the -a- of -are verbs changes to -e-) and adding the conditional endings: | Person | Ending | volere → vorr- | desiderare → desiderer- | |---|---|---|---| | io | -ei | vorrei | desidererei | | tu | -esti | vorresti | desidereresti | | lui/lei | -ebbe | vorrebbe | desidererebbe | | noi | -emmo | vorremmo | desidereremmo | | voi | -este | vorreste | desiderereste | | loro | -ebbero | vorrebbero | desidererebbero | **Important:** volere is **irregular** in the conditional. Its stem changes from vol- to vorr-. You simply need to learn this form. desiderare is regular. ### Piacere in the conditional Piacere works differently from volere. In Italian, 'I would like' using piacere is expressed as 'it would be pleasing **to me**'. The verb agrees with the thing liked (the grammatical subject), not with the person. At A1, the two forms you need are: - mi piacerebbe — I would like (singular thing) - mi piacerebbero — I would like (plural things) The indirect object pronoun changes with the person: mi (me), ti (you), gli/le (him/her), ci (us), vi (you all), gli (them). ## Structure of a wish sentence The most common pattern at A1 is simply: **[subject] + [conditional of volitive verb] + [noun / infinitive]** Io vorrei un caffè. Noi vorremmo mangiare adesso. The subject pronoun is often dropped in Italian because the verb ending makes it clear: Vorrei un caffè. is perfectly natural. ## Examples 1. Vorrei un caffè, per favore. — I would like a coffee, please. *(simple polite request in a bar)* 2. Desidererei parlare con tua madre. — I would like to speak with your mother. *(slightly more formal wish)* 3. Mi piacerebbe mangiare una pizza stasera. — I would like to eat a pizza tonight. *(expressing a personal wish using piacere)* 4. Mia sorella vorrebbe un gatto. — My sister would like a cat. *(third-person wish)* 5. Vorreste venire a cena con noi? — Would you (all) like to come to dinner with us? *(second-person plural; also used as a polite invitation)* 6. Vorrei un panino, ma non ho fame adesso. vs. Voglio un panino. — 'I would like a sandwich' (polite, hypothetical wish) vs. 'I want a sandwich' (direct, immediate demand). The conditional is softer and more polite than the plain present tense of volere. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using the present tense instead of the conditional for polite wishes.** *Voglio un caffè, per favore.* — This is grammatically correct but sounds blunt or childlike in a service context. Prefer: Vorrei un caffè, per favore. **Mistake 2: Using the wrong stem for volere.** *Volerei* — incorrect; the stem is vorr-, not vol-. The correct form is vorrei. **Mistake 3: Making piacere agree with the person instead of the thing liked.** *Mi piacerei una pizza.* — incorrect. The verb agrees with una pizza (singular), and the form is fixed as third person: Mi piacerebbe una pizza. **Mistake 4: Forgetting the indirect object pronoun with piacere.** *Piacerebbe una pizza.* — This sounds incomplete. Always include the pronoun: Mi piacerebbe una pizza. **Mistake 5: Confusing conditional with future tense.** The future of volere is vorrò ('I will want'), which expresses a future fact. The conditional vorrei expresses a present wish or polite request — these are different meanings. At A1, focus on vorrei for wishes.
en.why_this_matters: The moment you walk into a café, a shop, or a friend's home in Italy, you need to express what you would like. Without this pattern, you are limited to blunt demands or pointing — with it, you can make polite requests, state preferences, and express wishes naturally. This structure appears in almost every real-life conversation at A1 level and beyond.

en.title: Exclamatory phrases without a verb
en.tip: In Italian, you can express strong feelings with just a noun, adjective, or adverb — no verb needed. These short exclamations are complete, natural sentences on their own. Learning them lets you react and express emotion immediately, just like a native speaker.
en.explanation: ## The rule A proposizione esclamativa (exclamatory clause) expresses a strong feeling or reaction. In Italian, such clauses very often omit the verb entirely — the verb is sottinteso, meaning 'understood' or 'implied.' The remaining words — a noun, an adjective, an adverb, or a short phrase — carry the full meaning on their own, supported by tone of voice and context. This is not sloppy Italian. It is grammatically recognised and completely standard. The sentence is still considered dotata di senso compiuto — 'endowed with complete meaning' — even without a verb. ## How to form them The structure is simply: **[exclamatory word] + [noun / adjective / adverb / noun phrase] + !** Common exclamatory words used this way include: | Parola | Meaning | Notes | |---|---|---| | Che | What (a) / How | most common; used before nouns and adjectives | | Quanto / Quanta / Quanti / Quante | How much / How many | agrees in gender and number with the noun | | Come | How | often used with adjectives | | Quale / Quali | What (a) / Which | more formal or literary | ## Examples Che bella giornata! (What a beautiful day!) → The verb è ('is') is omitted. Full form would be: Che bella giornata è! — but that sounds unnatural and overly formal. Che fame! (I'm so hungry! / How hungry I am!) → Literally 'What hunger!' The noun alone, with no verb, perfectly expresses the feeling. Quanta gente! (So many people! / What a crowd!) → Quanta agrees with gente, which is feminine singular in Italian. Che buono! (How good this is! / This is so good!) → Said when tasting food. The adjective buono ('good/tasty') stands alone; no verb required. Quanti bambini! (So many children!) → Quanti is masculine plural to match bambini ('children', masculine plural). Che bello! vs. Che bella! → Both mean 'How lovely!' but the adjective changes to match what is being described. If you are reacting to a masculine noun (e.g. il vestito, 'the dress' — masculine in Italian), say Che bello! If reacting to a feminine noun (e.g. la casa, 'the house'), say Che bella! ## Agreement rules When the exclamation contains an adjective or quanto, it must agree in gender and number with the noun it describes — exactly as it would in a full sentence. | Noun | Gender / Number | Exclamation | |---|---|---| | il bambino (boy) | masc. sing. | Che bambino simpatico! | | la bambina (girl) | fem. sing. | Che bambina simpatica! | | i bambini (boys/children) | masc. pl. | Quanti bambini simpatici! | | le bambine (girls) | fem. pl. | Quante bambine simpatiche! | ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Forgetting agreement with quanto** *Quanto gente! ✗ — gente is feminine, so the correct form is Quanta gente! ✓ **Mistake 2: Adding a verb unnecessarily** Writing Che bella giornata è! instead of Che bella giornata! is not wrong, but it sounds stiff and unnatural. Native speakers almost always drop the verb in exclamations like these. **Mistake 3: Using come with a noun instead of an adjective** Say Che fame! (not *Come fame!). Come works best before adjectives (Come sei gentile!, 'How kind you are!'), while che works before both nouns and adjectives. **Mistake 4: Confusing che (exclamatory) with che (question word)** In a question, Che cos'è? means 'What is it?' In an exclamation, Che bello! means 'How lovely!' The exclamatory che always carries an emotional charge and ends with an exclamation mark, not a question mark.
en.why_this_matters: Exclamations are among the very first things you say in any language — surprise, joy, admiration, frustration. In Italian, many of the most common exclamations have no verb at all: the verb is simply left out because the emotion makes the meaning obvious. If you wait until you can build a full sentence, you will miss these moments entirely. Mastering verbless exclamations lets you sound natural from day one and helps you understand what native speakers say around you constantly.

unistr_label: Interrogative: totali (SÌ/NO) e parziali introdotte da: come, dove, quando, perché, quanto, chi, che, cosa, che cosa, quale?
label: Proposizioni interrogative totali e parziali

en.title: Asking questions: total and partial
en.tip: Italian has two kinds of questions: ones you answer with yes or no (total questions), and ones that ask for specific information using a question word like 'who' or 'where' (partial questions). Both are easy to form — word order often stays the same as in a statement, and your voice or a question mark does the rest.
en.explanation: ## The two types of question Italian grammar divides questions into two categories based on what kind of answer they expect. A **total question** (proposizione interrogativa totale, literally 'total interrogative clause') is a question that can be answered with a simple yes or no. The question is 'total' because the answer concerns the whole statement — either it is true or it is not. A **partial question** (proposizione interrogativa parziale, literally 'partial interrogative clause') is a question that asks about one specific part of a statement — a person, a place, a time, a thing. It requires a real piece of information as an answer, not just yes or no. These questions always begin with a **question word** (parola interrogativa). ## Forming total questions In English, yes/no questions require you to invert the subject and verb ('You are tired' → 'Are you tired?'). In Italian, **word order does not have to change**. You can form a total question simply by: 1. Raising your voice at the end when speaking, or 2. Adding a question mark at the end when writing. The statement and the question can be identical in written form except for the punctuation, and identical in spoken form except for intonation. You *may* also invert subject and verb (putting the verb before the subject), but this is optional and more common in formal or written Italian. At A1 level, the rising-intonation pattern is the most natural and widely used. ### Total question examples Statement: Tu parli italiano. (You speak Italian.) Question: Tu parli italiano? (Do you speak Italian?) Statement: Maria è a casa. (Maria is at home.) Question: Maria è a casa? (Is Maria at home?) With inversion (more formal): Parli tu italiano? (Do you speak Italian?) ## Forming partial questions Partial questions always begin with a question word. The question word comes at the **start of the sentence**, followed by the verb, then the subject (if stated). This is the standard word order for partial questions in Italian. Here are the most important question words at A1 level: | Parola interrogativa | English meaning | |---|---| | chi | who / whom | | che cosa / cosa / che | what | | dove | where | | quando | when | | come | how | | perché | why | | quanto / quanta / quanti / quante | how much / how many | | quale / quali | which / which ones | Note: che cosa, cosa, and che all mean 'what' and are used interchangeably in everyday speech. Che cosa is slightly more formal; cosa is the most common in informal conversation. Note: quanto agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to: quanto pane (how much bread), quanta acqua (how much water), quanti fratelli (how many brothers), quante sorelle (how many sisters). ### Partial question examples Chi è lei? (Who is she?) Cosa mangi a colazione? (What do you eat for breakfast?) Dove abita tua madre? (Where does your mother live?) Quando arrivi? (When are you arriving?) Come stai? (How are you?) Quanti anni hai? (How old are you? — literally 'How many years do you have?') ## A contrastive pair Notice how the same topic produces a very different sentence depending on which type of question you use: Total: Hai un fratello? (Do you have a brother?) — answer: Sì or No. Partial: Quanti fratelli hai? (How many brothers do you have?) — answer requires a number or name. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Translating English word order directly into Italian for total questions.** English requires 'do' or auxiliary inversion: 'Do you speak Italian?' Italian does not need this. Never add *fare as a dummy auxiliary. Incorrect: *Fai parli italiano? Correct: Parli italiano? **Mistake 2: Forgetting to put the question word first in a partial question.** The question word must open the sentence. Incorrect: *Tu abiti dove? (placing dove at the end) Correct: Dove abiti? (Note: placing the question word at the end does occur in very informal spoken Italian for emphasis, but it is not standard and should be avoided at A1 level.) **Mistake 3: Confusing come (how) with che / cosa (what).** Incorrect: *Come si chiama questo? — actually this is correct! But learners sometimes use cosa where come is needed: *Cosa ti chiami? instead of the standard Come ti chiami? (What is your name?) **Mistake 4: Using quale where che or cosa is needed, or vice versa.** Quale means 'which' and implies a choice among known options. Che cosa means 'what' in an open sense. Compare: Quale pizza preferisci? (Which pizza do you prefer? — from a menu) vs. Cosa mangi? (What are you eating? — open question). ## Summary | Type | Italian name | Starts with | Expected answer | |---|---|---|---| | Total question | interrogativa totale | No special word — intonation only | sì or no | | Partial question | interrogativa parziale | A question word (chi, cosa, dove…) | A specific piece of information |
en.why_this_matters: Questions are among the very first things you need in any language. From your first Italian conversation — ordering food, asking directions, meeting someone new — you will need to ask and understand questions constantly. Knowing the difference between the two types of question, and how to form each one correctly, removes one of the most common sources of confusion for beginners and immediately makes you sound more natural.

en.title: Joining sentences and words with 'e'
en.tip: The word 'e' (and) links two words or two sentences of equal importance. Before a word starting with 'e', use 'ed' instead to make pronunciation easier.
en.explanation: ## The rule Use e to link two elements that have the same grammatical role, or two complete sentences of equal importance. This type of linking conjunction is called congiunzione coordinativa copulativa (a joining coordinator). Both sides of e must carry the same weight — neither is more important than the other. **Linking two nouns (or names):** Marco e Sofia — Marco and Sofia (both are the subject, so they have the same role) **Linking two adjectives:** buono e fresco — good and fresh **Linking two verbs or two actions:** Mangio e bevo. — I eat and drink. **Linking two whole sentences:** Ho fame e voglio mangiare. — I am hungry and I want to eat. (Two complete sentences, equally important, joined into one.) ## The variant: 'ed' before a vowel When the word immediately after e begins with a vowel — especially the letter e — it is standard practice in written and careful spoken Italian to add a d and write ed. This is called a d eufonica (euphonic d), and its only purpose is to make pronunciation smoother. It is never required, but it is very common and always correct before a vowel. **Most common case — before a word starting with 'e':** pane ed acqua — bread and water Luigi ed Elena — Luigi and Elena **Also acceptable before other vowels:** bello ed intelligente — beautiful and intelligent **Plain 'e' before a consonant — never 'ed' here:** Marco e Luca — Marco and Luca ## Examples Ho una sorella e un fratello. (I have a sister and a brother.) — linking two noun phrases with the same grammatical role La minestra è calda e buona. (The soup is hot and good.) — linking two adjectives describing the same noun Mi alzo, faccio colazione e vado a scuola. (I get up, have breakfast, and go to school.) — linking three actions in a daily routine; 'e' appears only before the last item in a list, just as in English Parla italiano ed è di Roma. (She speaks Italian and is from Rome.) — 'ed' before 'è' (a vowel), linking two full sentences Mia madre lavora e mio padre cucina. (My mother works and my father cooks.) — two complete sentences of equal importance joined into one Il caffè è forte e amaro, ma mi piace. (The coffee is strong and bitter, but I like it.) — contrastive pair: 'e' links two adjectives of equal weight; 'ma' (but) then adds a contrast; notice only 'e' makes both adjectives equal, while 'ma' signals opposition) ## Lists: where does 'e' go? In a list of three or more items, Italian follows the same pattern as English: e appears only before the **last** item. A comma separates all earlier items. Ho comprato il pane, il latte e le mele. (I bought bread, milk, and apples.) Do **not** write il pane e il latte e le mele — that reads as clumsy repetition, though it is grammatically possible for emphasis in poetry or storytelling. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Using 'ed' before a consonant.** Incorrect: *Marco ed Luca* Correct: Marco e Luca The d eufonica is only for words starting with a vowel. Before a consonant, always use plain e. **Mistake 2: Placing 'e' between every item in a list.** Incorrect: *il pane e il latte e le mele* (as normal speech) Correct: il pane, il latte e le mele Only the last item in a list is introduced by e; the rest are separated by commas. **Mistake 3: Confusing 'e' (and) with 'è' (is).** These sound identical in speech but are written differently. è (with the grave accent) is the third-person singular of essere (to be). e (no accent) is the conjunction. Compare: Marco è a casa. — Marco is at home. (verb) Marco e Sofia sono a casa. — Marco and Sofia are at home. (conjunction) **Mistake 4: Assuming 'e' can express contrast.** Incorrect reasoning: thinking e can mean 'but'. It cannot. e always signals that the two elements are equal and compatible. For contrast, Italian uses ma (but) or però (however). Incorrect: *È gentile e non mi piace.* (intended as contrast) Correct: È gentile, ma non mi piace. — He is kind, but I do not like him. ## Quick-reference table | Form | When to use | Example | |---|---|---| | e | Before a consonant, or generally before any vowel | pane e burro | | ed | Preferred before a word starting with a vowel (especially 'e') | pane ed acqua |
en.why_this_matters: The conjunction e (and) is one of the most frequent words in Italian. Without it, you cannot list things, describe people, or connect two actions — all of which come up in the very first conversations you will have. Mastering this tiny word, including when to swap it for ed, removes a surprisingly common source of errors right at the start of your learning.

en.title: Joining alternatives with 'o'
en.tip: Use 'o' (or) between two words or sentences to show a choice between alternatives. It works exactly like English 'or' — place it between the two options you want to connect.
en.explanation: ## The rule The coordinating conjunction o (meaning 'or') joins two words, phrases, or whole sentences ('proposizioni coordinate disgiuntive' — disjunctive co-ordinate clauses) that are alternatives: choosing one logically excludes the other. Simply place o between the two items you want to contrast. **Basic pattern:** [option A] + o + [option B] There is no change for gender, number, or person — o is invariable. ## Variants and related words Italian offers several words that mean 'or'. They are interchangeable in most everyday situations, but each has a slightly different register or nuance: | Forma | English | Notes | |---|---|---| | o | or | the most common, neutral form | | oppure | or / or else | slightly more emphatic; very common in speech | | ovvero | or / that is to say | more formal; can also introduce a clarification | At A1 level, focus on o and oppure. You will hear and read both constantly. ### The doubled form: o...o When you want to stress that the choice is strictly between two options and no others, Italian repeats the conjunction: o... o... ('either... or...'). This is called a correlative use. O ora o mai più. (Either now or never.) You do not need to produce this form at A1, but you will encounter it, so it is worth recognising. ## Examples **Joining two nouns (a simple choice):** Vuoi tè o caffè? (Do you want tea or coffee?) **Joining two adjectives:** Il latte è caldo o freddo? (Is the milk hot or cold?) **Joining two verb phrases:** Mangi a casa o al ristorante? (Are you eating at home or at a restaurant?) **Joining two full sentences:** Non ho deciso se scrivere oppure telefonare. (I haven't decided whether to write or to call.) **Edge case — o versus e (and):** Prendo il pane e il latte. (I'm buying bread and milk.) — both items, no choice Prendo il pane o il latte. (I'm buying bread or milk.) — one item, a choice must be made This contrast is important: e adds things together, while o separates them into alternatives. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Confusing o with e.** Learners sometimes write e when they mean o because both connect two items. Ask yourself: are both things happening together? Use e. Is only one possible? Use o. ✗ Vieni martedì e mercoledì? (Are you coming Tuesday and Wednesday? — implies both days) ✓ Vieni martedì o mercoledì? (Are you coming Tuesday or Wednesday? — one day, a choice) **Mistake 2: Adding an accent — writing ò instead of o.** The conjunction o ('or') has no accent. The accented form ò does not exist as a standard word. Do not confuse this with è (accented form of e, meaning 'is'), which does carry an accent. Write simply o. **Mistake 3: Omitting o and listing options without a connector.** In English, informal speech sometimes drops 'or' ('Tea? Coffee?'). In Italian, it is normal and much clearer to include o between the final two options. ✗ Vuoi tè, caffè? ✓ Vuoi tè o caffè?
en.why_this_matters: Almost every conversation involves making choices or offering alternatives — 'tea or coffee?', 'today or tomorrow?', 'do you want to walk or take the bus?' Without o ('or'), you cannot express any of these ideas in Italian. This tiny word appears in questions, suggestions, and everyday decisions at every level of the language, so recognising and using it correctly from day one removes a constant gap in your speech.

en.title: Giving reasons with 'perché'
en.tip: Use 'perché' to explain why something happens. It connects two parts of a sentence, where the second part gives the reason for the first. This is one of the most common words in Italian — you will hear and use it every day.
en.explanation: ## The rule A causal clause, called a proposizione causale (reason clause), explains the cause or reason behind the action in the main clause, called the proposizione reggente (main/governing clause). At A1 level, you form it simply by placing perché between the main clause and the reason clause: **[main clause]** + perché + **[reason clause]** Both clauses use a normal, straightforward verb form — at A1, this is always the present tense (presente indicativo). No subjunctive, no special verb change is needed at this level. **Formation at a glance:** Mangio la pizza perché mi piace. (I eat pizza because I like it.) The sentence has two parts: - Mangio la pizza — main clause (what happens) - perché mi piace — reason clause (why it happens) ## Position: before or after? The reason clause with perché almost always comes **after** the main clause in everyday speech. This is the safest and most natural order at A1 level. In Italian it is also possible — though less common — to place another causal conjunction such as siccome (since/as) at the very start of the sentence, but perché does **not** normally open a sentence on its own in standard usage. ## Examples Studio l'italiano perché è bella lingua. (I study Italian because it is a beautiful language.) — giving a reason for a habit Non mangio la carne perché non mi piace. (I don't eat meat because I don't like it.) — giving a reason for a negative action Maria beve acqua perché ha sete. (Maria drinks water because she is thirsty.) — third-person subject in both clauses Siamo a casa perché fa freddo. (We are at home because it is cold.) — state of being, not an action Non dormo bene perché il bambino piange. (I don't sleep well because the baby cries.) — the subjects of the two clauses are different: 'I' and 'the baby' Vado al supermercato perché non c'è pane. (I'm going to the supermarket because there is no bread.) — everyday, A1-level scenario ## Important note: 'perché' has two meanings The word perché does **double duty** in Italian: it means both **'because'** (giving a reason) and **'why'** (asking a question). You tell them apart by context: | Use | Example | Meaning | |---|---|---| | Question | Perché studi? | 'Why do you study?' | | Answer/reason | Studio perché mi piace. | 'I study because I like it.' | When perché opens a question, it means 'why'. When it follows a main clause inside a sentence, it means 'because'. At A1, you will use both constantly — in question-and-answer pairs especially. ## Other causal conjunctions (for awareness) Italian has several other words that also introduce reason clauses. You do not need to use them at A1, but you may hear them: - siccome (since/as) — goes at the **start** of the sentence: Siccome ho fame, mangio. (Since I'm hungry, I eat.) - dato che (given that): Dato che è tardi, andiamo. (Given that it's late, let's go.) - visto che (seeing that): Visto che piove, resto a casa. (Seeing that it's raining, I'm staying home.) For now, focus on perché: it is by far the most frequent and the most useful. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Confusing 'because' and 'why':** Learners sometimes write *perché vuoi?* when they mean 'because I want to' (as an answer), or forget that the question form also uses perché. Remember: in an answer, perché always sits **after** the main clause, not at the start. **Mistake 2 — Using 'because' to start a standalone sentence:** In English, people sometimes write 'Because I like it.' as a full sentence (especially in informal writing). In Italian, perché must always be connected to a main clause. *Perché mi piace.* alone is not a complete sentence — it is a fragment. Always attach it: Lo faccio perché mi piace. (I do it because I like it.) **Mistake 3 — Using 'perché' with a noun instead of a verb:** Learners sometimes write *Sono stanco perché il lavoro.* This is wrong — perché must be followed by a full clause with a conjugated verb, not just a noun. Correct form: Sono stanco perché lavoro molto. (I am tired because I work a lot.) **Mistake 4 — Accent confusion:** Note that perché always carries an accent on the final é. Writing it without the accent (*perche*) is a spelling error in Italian.
en.why_this_matters: Every time you explain why you do something — why you are hungry, why you are tired, why you like something — you need a word to link the reason to the action. In Italian, that word is perché (because). Without it, you can state facts, but you cannot explain them. Mastering this one word immediately lets you answer questions like Perché studi l'italiano? (Why do you study Italian?) and unlocks a huge range of everyday conversation.

en.title: Expressing purpose with 'per' and the infinitive
en.tip: To say why you do something, use 'per' followed by the infinitive. This works whenever the subject of both verbs is the same person. It is the simplest and most natural way to express purpose in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The rule To express purpose — the reason or goal behind an action — Italian uses the preposition per ('in order to', 'to', 'for') followed by the **infinitive** of a verb. This construction is called an *implicit final clause* because the purpose is expressed without a full subordinate clause. **Formula:** Main clause + per + infinitive Example: Studio l'italiano per parlare con la mia famiglia. (I study Italian to speak with my family.) The infinitive is always in its base form — the form you find in the dictionary, ending in -are, -ere, or -ire. It does **not** change to agree with the subject. ## The key condition: same subject This structure is only used when **both verbs share the same subject** — that is, the person doing the main action and the person doing the purpose action are the same. ✔ Same subject (use per + infinitive): Vado al bar per prendere un caffè. (I go to the bar to get a coffee. — *I* go, *I* get.) ✘ Different subjects (do NOT use this structure — use affinché/perché + subjunctive instead): Ti scrivo perché tu sappia la verità. (I write to you so that *you* know the truth. — *I* write, *you* know.) At A1 level, you will almost always be dealing with the same-subject case, so per + infinitive is your go-to tool for expressing purpose. ## Forming the construction No changes are needed to the infinitive. Here is how the structure looks with verbs from all three conjugation classes: | Infinitive class | Example infinitive | With per | |---|---|---| | -are | mangiare (to eat) | per mangiare | | -ere | prendere (to take) | per prendere | | -ire | dormire (to sleep) | per dormire | Irregular verbs use their standard infinitive form too: | Infinitive | With per | |---|---| | essere (to be) | per essere | | avere (to have) | per avere | | fare (to do/make) | per fare | | andare (to go) | per andare | ## Position in the sentence The per + infinitive phrase most naturally comes **after** the main clause, but it can also appear at the **beginning** of the sentence for emphasis. Both positions are correct. After the main clause (most common): Apro la finestra per prendere aria. (I open the window to get some air.) At the start of the sentence (for emphasis): Per mangiare bene, andiamo al ristorante. (To eat well, we go to the restaurant.) ## Examples **1. Daily routine (basic use)** Mi alzo presto per fare colazione con la mia famiglia. (I get up early to have breakfast with my family.) **2. Movement with a goal (very common at A1)** Vado al supermercato per comprare il pane. (I go to the supermarket to buy bread.) **3. Learning a language** Studio l'italiano per capire i miei amici. (I study Italian to understand my friends.) **4.** Per at the start of the sentence Per dormire meglio, bevo una camomilla la sera. (To sleep better, I drink chamomile tea in the evening.) **5. Edge case — contrastive pair (same vs. different subject)** Chiamo la nonna per salutarla. (I call grandma to greet her. ← same subject: *I* call, *I* greet. ✔ Use per + infinitive.) Chiamo la nonna perché lei sappia che sto bene. (I call grandma so that *she* knows I am well. ← different subjects: *I* call, *she* knows. ✘ Cannot use per + infinitive here.) **6. Negative purpose (to avoid doing something)** Parlo piano per non svegliare il bambino. (I speak quietly so as not to wake the baby.) (Add non directly before the infinitive to make the purpose negative.) ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Conjugating the infinitive** ✘ Vado al bar per prendo un caffè. (Incorrect — prendo is a conjugated form, not an infinitive.) ✔ Vado al bar per prendere un caffè. **Mistake 2: Inserting a second subject pronoun** ✘ Studio per io parlare italiano. (Incorrect — no subject pronoun is used inside the per + infinitive phrase.) ✔ Studio per parlare italiano. **Mistake 3: Using** per **when the subjects are different** ✘ Le parlo per lei capisce. (Incorrect structure entirely.) ✔ Le parlo perché lei capisca. (Correct — use perché + subjunctive when subjects differ. This is a B1 structure; at A1 simply remember that per + infinitive requires the same subject.) **Mistake 4: Confusing purposive** per **with causal** perché These two words look similar but work differently. Resto a casa perché sono stanco. (I stay home *because* I am tired. ← perché gives a reason/cause with a full conjugated clause.) Resto a casa per riposare. (I stay home *in order to* rest. ← per + infinitive gives a purpose/goal.)
en.why_this_matters: Saying *why* you do something is one of the first things you need in any language. Without this structure, you cannot explain that you are studying Italian *to travel*, eating *to stay healthy*, or going to the shop *to buy bread*. The pattern per + infinitive appears in almost every real conversation, so mastering it early removes a major gap in your ability to communicate.

en.title: Basic word order in Italian sentences
en.tip: Italian sentences usually follow Subject–Verb–Object order, just like English. Getting this right from the start means you can build clear, correct sentences immediately, even with a very small vocabulary.
en.explanation: ## The basic rule: Subject – Verb – Object (SVO) In a simple Italian sentence (una frase semplice, a sentence with exactly one verb and one complete thought), the default, neutral word order is: **Subject → Verb → Object** This is called the ordine non marcato — the 'unmarked order', meaning the plain, neutral arrangement with no special emphasis. It is the order you should use unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise. - The **subject** (il soggetto) is who or what performs the action. - The **verb** (il verbo) expresses the action or state. - The **object** (l'oggetto) is who or what receives the action. ## Forming the sentence Simply place the three elements in order. There is no inversion or rearrangement needed for a basic statement: | Subject | Verb | Object | |---|---|---| | Marco | mangia | la pizza. | | La mamma | beve | il caffè. | | I bambini | guardano | la televisione. | ## Examples with translations Marco mangia la pizza. (Marco eats pizza.) — the classic S–V–O pattern. La mamma beve il caffè. (Mum drinks coffee.) — subject is a noun phrase with an article; order is unchanged. Il gatto dorme. (The cat sleeps.) — no object needed; a verb can stand alone after the subject when there is nothing to receive the action. Anna studia l'italiano. (Anna studies Italian.) — object includes its article; the article travels with the noun but does not change its position. I bambini mangiano il pane. (The children eat bread.) — plural subject and plural verb, same S–V–O order. Mio padre legge un libro. (My father reads a book.) — subject is a possessive noun phrase; order is still S–V–O. ## Important variants and notes **The subject pronoun is often dropped** Italian is a lingua pro-drop — a language that drops the subject pronoun when it is clear from the verb ending. This does not change the underlying S–V–O order; it simply removes the spoken subject: Mangio la pasta. (I eat pasta.) — io (I) is implied by the ending -o, so it is left out. The verb still comes before the object. **Sentences with no object** Many Italian verbs — especially verbs of motion or state — need no object at all. The sentence is simply Subject + Verb: Il bambino dorme. (The child is sleeping.) La nonna arriva. (Grandma is arriving.) **Adjectives after the noun (a side note)** Inside the noun phrases that make up your subject or object, adjectives most commonly follow the noun in Italian — una pizza buona (a good pizza) rather than before it as in English. This is a separate rule, but it is worth knowing it does not affect S–V–O order. **Marked order exists — but not at A1** Italian speakers sometimes move the object to the front of the sentence for emphasis or contrast: La pizza, Marco la mangia volentieri. (Pizza — Marco happily eats it.) This is called ordine marcato (marked order) and involves extra grammar (a repeated pronoun). You do not need to produce it at A1, but recognising that it exists explains why you will occasionally hear sentences that seem to start with the 'wrong' word. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Placing the verb at the end (influence from German or Japanese)** Some learners put the verb last: *Marco la pizza mangia. This is not standard Italian. Correction: Marco mangia la pizza. **Mistake 2 — Inverting subject and verb to form questions** In English, questions invert subject and verb: 'Does Marco eat pizza?' Learners sometimes copy this: *Mangia Marco la pizza? In everyday Italian, you can form a yes/no question simply by keeping S–V–O order and using a rising intonation, or by adding ? in writing: Marco mangia la pizza? (Is Marco eating pizza?) The inversion form does exist in formal or written Italian, but it is not the default at A1. **Mistake 3 — Omitting the article on the object** Learners sometimes drop the article thinking it affects the word order: *Marco mangia pizza. The article is a separate rule, but it belongs attached to its noun in the object slot: Marco mangia la pizza. Order and articles are independent — fix each separately. **Mistake 4 — Confusing subject and object because Italian nouns do not change form** Unlike Latin or German, Italian nouns do not have case endings to mark subject versus object. Word order does this job. So Il cane morde l'uomo (The dog bites the man) means something completely different from L'uomo morde il cane (The man bites the dog). Position in the sentence is the signal: first noun phrase = subject, noun phrase after the verb = object. Never swap them without meaning to change the meaning.
en.why_this_matters: Word order is the skeleton of every sentence you produce. Italian's default order — Subject, then Verb, then Object — matches English closely enough that you can transfer this instinct directly, making it one of the first things you get right without extra effort. Understanding it explicitly also prepares you to notice when Italian speakers deliberately change the order for emphasis, which you will encounter very soon after A1.

en.title: Dropping or keeping the subject pronoun
en.tip: In Italian, you usually leave out the subject pronoun — the verb ending already tells you who is acting. Keep the pronoun only when you need to avoid confusion, contrast two subjects, or add emphasis.
en.explanation: ## The basic rule: drop the pronoun by default Italian is a lingua pro-drop (a 'subject-dropping language'). Because each verb form has its own ending that identifies the person and number, the pronoun adds no new information and is normally left out. Compare English and Italian: | English (pronoun required) | Italiano (pronoun optional / usually dropped) | |---|---| | I speak | (Io) parlo | | You eat | (Tu) mangi | | He/She works | (Lui/Lei) lavora | | We are | (Noi) siamo | | You (pl.) have | (Voi) avete | | They go | (Loro) vanno | The forms in parentheses are grammatically correct but are usually omitted in normal speech and writing. ## When you MUST keep the pronoun There are three clear situations where the subject pronoun is required or strongly preferred. ### 1. Contrasting two different subjects When two clauses follow each other with different subjects, the pronoun makes it clear who does what: > Lui va in montagna, io vado al mare. > (He is going to the mountains; I am going to the sea.) Without lui and io, the sentence would be confusing because both verbs could belong to the same person. ### 2. Emphasis on who is acting When you want to stress that it is a particular person — and not someone else — who performs the action, you keep the pronoun. This is especially common after words like anche ('also'), neanche ('not even'), and pure ('too/also'): > Sei stato tu a dire questo. > (It was YOU who said this — not someone else.) > È venuta anche lei. > (She came too.) ### 3. Avoiding ambiguity Some verb forms are identical across different persons. In those cases, dropping the pronoun can make the sentence unclear: > È bene che vada. > (It is good that [someone] goes.) — Who? The pronoun is needed to clarify: È bene che tu vada / È bene che lui vada, etc. ## The subject pronouns: full list and notes on the third person The Italian subject pronouns are: | Person | Singular | Plural | |---|---|---| | 1st | io (I) | noi (we) | | 2nd | tu (you, informal) | voi (you all) | | 3rd masc. | lui / egli / esso (he / it) | loro / essi (they) | | 3rd fem. | lei / ella / essa (she / it) | loro / esse (they) | **Important note on the third person:** Historically, egli (he) and ella (she) were the 'correct' forms for referring to people, while esso / essa were reserved for animals and things. Today, egli and ella are very rare — even in writing — and have been largely replaced by lui and lei. At A1 level, use lui and lei without hesitation. **Rule for obligatory third-person pronouns:** Whenever the situation requires a subject pronoun in the third person (contrast, emphasis, clarity), the only acceptable forms are lui, lei, and loro: > Io sono italiana, lui è francese. > (I am Italian; he is French.) ## Reinforced pronouns Subject pronouns can be strengthened by adding stesso ('himself/herself/myself', etc.) after any pronoun: > io stesso, tu stesso, lui stesso, lei stessa, noi stessi, voi stessi, loro stessi There are also the combined forms noialtri and voialtri (written as one word), used regionally or for extra emphasis on 'we' and 'you all' as a group. These are less common and not essential at A1. ## Full examples covering main uses **Pronoun dropped (normal default):** > Mangio la pizza. > (I am eating pizza.) — Io is omitted; the ending -o already signals first person singular. > Parli italiano? > (Do you speak Italian?) — Tu is dropped in the question; the -i ending identifies second person singular. **Pronoun kept for contrast:** > Lei beve il caffè, io bevo il tè. > (She drinks coffee; I drink tea.) — Two different subjects require the pronouns to be explicit. **Pronoun kept for emphasis:** > L'ho fatto io! > (I did it! / It was ME who did it!) — Io placed after the verb for strong emphasis. **After anche:** > Viene anche lui alla festa? > (Is he coming to the party too?) — The pronoun is required after anche. **Avoiding ambiguity (contrastive pair):** > Spero che vada bene. > (I hope it goes well.) — Here no specific person is implied; the sentence is fine. > È importante che tu vada adesso. > (It is important that YOU go now.) — Without tu, it would be unclear who must go. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1 — Always copying English and using the pronoun:** Learners whose first language requires a subject (e.g. English, French) often write Io mangio, io bevo, io dormo in every sentence. This is not wrong, but it sounds unnatural and over-emphatic. Drop it unless one of the three conditions above applies. **Mistake 2 — Using egli or ella in speech:** Students who learn from older textbooks may use egli and ella in conversation. These forms sound archaic or overly literary today. Use lui and lei instead. **Mistake 3 — Confusing lei (she) with Lei (formal 'you'):** The pronoun Lei (with a capital L) is also used as the formal second-person singular ('you', polite). In writing, the capital letter marks the difference; in speech, context makes it clear. This is a separate topic, but be aware that lei and Lei are distinct uses of the same word. **Mistake 4 — Dropping the pronoun when it is needed for clarity:** In a sentence like Quando lavoro, non voglio essere disturbato, dropping both pronouns is fine — the context is clear. But in Lui va in montagna, vado al mare, omitting io from the second clause is confusing because the subject shifts. Keep io whenever the subject changes mid-sentence.
en.why_this_matters: Italian verb endings carry so much information that repeating the subject pronoun is usually unnecessary — and leaving it out is what sounds natural. From your very first lessons you will see sentences like Parlo italiano instead of Io parlo italiano, and you may wonder whether the pronoun has been forgotten. It has not: dropping it is the default. Understanding when to drop it — and when to keep it — removes one of the most persistent sources of unnatural-sounding Italian among beginners.

en.title: Word order in questions with question words
en.tip: When you ask a question using a question word like 'who', 'what', or 'where', put the question word first, then the verb, then the subject. This order is the most natural way to ask these questions in Italian.
en.explanation: ## The basic rule In Italian questions that begin with a question word (an interrogative pronoun or adverb), the standard word order is: **Question word → Verb → Subject (if stated)** Domanda word + Verbo + Soggetto — the subject, if you include it, comes *after* the verb. This is called Subject-Verb inversion, and it is the default in these questions. You do not add a separate word like English 'do' or 'does': the verb form alone carries the question. ## How to form it 1. Start with the interrogative word. 2. Follow immediately with the conjugated verb. 3. Place the subject noun or pronoun after the verb (or leave it out if it is obvious from context). Compare the statement and the question: | Statement | Question | |---|---| | Maria abita qui. | Dove abita Maria? | | (Maria lives here.) | (Where does Maria live?) | | Tuo fratello si chiama Luca. | Come si chiama tuo fratello? | | (Your brother is called Luca.) | (What is your brother called?) | ## The main interrogative words at A1 | Italian | Meaning | Notes | |---|---|---| | chi | who / whom | always singular, never changes | | cosa / che cosa / che | what | three equally correct forms | | dove | where | | | quando | when | | | come | how | | | perché | why | | | quanto / quanta / quanti / quante | how much / how many | agrees with noun in gender and number | ## Examples **1. Dove ('where') — verb immediately after:** Dove abita tuo padre? (Where does your father live?) **2. Chi ('who') — subject unknown, so chi itself acts as subject:** Chi parla italiano? (Who speaks Italian?) — here chi is the subject; no separate subject follows. **3. Cosa ('what') — verb then subject:** Cosa mangia Marco a colazione? (What does Marco eat for breakfast?) **4. Come ('how') — common greeting pattern:** Come stai? (How are you?) — subject tu is dropped because it is obvious from the verb ending. **5. Quanto ('how much') agreeing with the noun:** Quanti fratelli hai? (How many brothers do you have?) — quanti is masculine plural to match fratelli. **6. Contrastive pair — subject before vs. after verb:** ✓ Dove lavora tua madre? (Where does your mother work?) — correct inversion. ✗ Dove tua madre lavora? — this feels unnatural in standard Italian; avoid placing the subject between the question word and the verb. ## When the subject can come before the verb In informal spoken Italian, especially for emphasis or contrast, a noun subject sometimes appears before the verb: E Marco, dove abita? (And Marco, where does he live?) — the subject is fronted for emphasis, almost as a 'topic'. This is acceptable in conversation but is not the neutral default. At A1, practise the standard order first. ## Common learner mistakes **Mistake 1: Copying English 'do/does' word order without inversion.** ✗ Dove Maria abita? — subject between question word and verb, mirroring 'Where does Maria live?' literally. ✓ Dove abita Maria? — verb comes directly after the question word. **Mistake 2: Adding a redundant pronoun after the question word.** ✗ Dove lei abita? — the pronoun lei interrupts the pattern. ✓ Dove abita lei? — if you want to include the pronoun for clarity or emphasis, it goes after the verb. **Mistake 3: Using only che and forgetting cosa or che cosa.** All three forms — che, cosa, che cosa — mean 'what' when asking questions. Any one of them is correct: Che mangi? / Cosa mangi? / Che cosa mangi? are all fine. **Mistake 4: Forgetting gender/number agreement with quanto.** ✗ Quanto sorelle hai? ✓ Quante sorelle hai? — sorelle is feminine plural, so quanto becomes quante.
en.why_this_matters: Question words like chi ('who'), cosa ('what'), dove ('where'), and quando ('when') appear in almost every real conversation. Without knowing where to place them, you cannot ask basic questions about people, places, or things — and misplacing the verb or subject is one of the most noticeable errors beginners make. Getting this pattern right immediately makes your Italian sound natural.
